bill_title: DPA Modernization Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: The Defense Production Act is a 75-year-old bipartisan law that has helped our nation respond to war, natural disasters, and the COVID-19 pandemic. It was created to protect the American people in times of crisis, not to be misused for alternative political agendas or personal gain. Committee Democrats have worked across the aisle to put forward a stronger DPA that modernizes the law, reinforces clear guardrails, and ensures that it remains a tool for the public's good and not abused. This bill, which passed HFSC markup with a vote of 41-0, reauthorizes the Defense Production Act (DPA) of 1950 until 2031. The bill also modernizes and reorganizes DPA for structural clarity and improved oversight.
Background: Per the DPA's Declaration of Policy, ``the security of the United States is dependent on the ability of the domestic industrial base to supply materials and services for the national defense and to prepare for and respond to military conflicts, natural or man-caused disasters, or acts of terrorism within the United States.''\1\ Accordingly, the DPA ``provides the President with an array of authorities to shape national defense preparedness programs and to take appropriate steps to maintain and enhance the domestic industrial base.''\2\
\1\50 U.S.C. Sec. 4502(a)(1).
\2\50 U.S.C. Sec. 4502(a)(4).
Modeled after laws from World War II--particularly the War Powers Acts of 1941 (P.L. 77-354) and 1942 (P.L. 77-507), Congress enacted the DPA\3\ in September 1950 to enable President Harry S. Truman to respond to the industrial requirements of the Korean War. Due to the broad economic powers that the law conferred upon the President, this legislation fell under the sole jurisdiction of the House and Senate Committees on Banking and Currency (now the House Committee on Financial Services and the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs).\4\ As the Korean War ended in 1953, Congress allowed four DPA Titles to lapse, leaving only Title I (``Priorities and Allocations''), Title III (``Expansion of Productive Capacity and Supply''), and Title VII (``General Provisions'') in effect. Congress must periodically reauthorize most of the statute's provisions, although some parts, including a provision in Title VII that governs the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), are permanent. Congress has re-authorized and amended the DPA dozens of times, and the DPA's current authorization expires in September 2026.
\3\P.L. 81-774.
\4\CRS, The Defense Production Act of 1950: History, Authorities, and Considerations for Congress (Oct. 6, 2023).
Title I. ``Priorities and Allocations''--Title I authorizes the President to compel persons, including businesses, to perform and prioritize contracts or orders determined necessary for the national defense,\5\ helping to ensure the availability of scarce resources.\6\ The statute allows the U.S. government to place priority ratings and required delivery dates on individual contracts and purchase orders, including subcontracts and orders performed by entities down a contractor's supply chain.\7\
\5\Ibid, note 5.
\6\See, for example, Senate Committee on Banking and Currency, ``Hearings on the S. 3936,'' July 24-26, 1950 (Washington, D.C.: Government Printing Office, 1950), p. 91. Allocation actions are governed by 15 CFR Sec. 700.30-36.
\7\Commerce Department Bureau of Industry and Security, Defense Priorities and Allocations System Program (DPAS) (2020).
This authority, which allows a president to tell a private company that it must support U.S. national defense needs above all others, including existing contracts with other governments and private-sector firms, is significant and carries substantial impact. As seen in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, for example, the Department of Commerce extended its priority rating to critical infrastructure, allowing an owner/ operator to expedite the delivery of power generators and transfer switches needed to restore railroad operations around New Orleans.\8\ President Biden invoked Title I authorities to help Baxter International re-open its IV solutions and dialysis products manufacturing facility after Hurricane Helene caused damage that created a national shortage of those essential products.\9\ In some cases, however, the target of the priority rating pushes back. During the COVID-19 pandemic, 3M argued that President Trump's pandemic-era Title I classification towards its firm, forcing it to divert its global production of high-quality face masks to the U.S., would cause a decrease in the production of masks due to retaliatory trade measures by countries down its supply chain.\10\
\8\Virginia Department of Emergency Management, Overview And Application Of The Defense Production Act (Accessed Jun. 11, 2025).
\9\Scripps News, J. Boggs, Biden administration invokes Defense Production Act amid IV shortage caused by hurricane (Oct. 16, 2024).
\10\CNBC, K. Breuninger, 3M warns Trump: Halting exports under Defense Production Act would reduce number of masks available to US (Apr. 3, 2020).
Ultimately, the U.S. government and 3M settled their differences,\11\ but the dispute points to the unintended consequences of this extraordinary authority and the possible legal action that could occur if deployed in an irresponsible and illegal manner. There are examples, too, of the U.S. government exercising its Title I authority without deconflicting with another government, triggering diplomatic concern and, possibly, retaliatory action. Last month, the Trump Administration's standoff with the Trump Administration and Anthropic has caused concern regarding DPA.\12\ The Department of Defense attempted to require Anthropic to use its AI tools to conduct mass domestic surveillance and to create fully autonomous weapons.\13\ Having refused, President Trump threatened to both label Anthropic a ``supply chain risk'' (under Title 10) and label it ``critical'' to the national defense, under DPA, allowing the government to force the company to act at the government's direction. Ultimately, the Trump Administration chose the first option, directing all federal agencies to immediately stop using Anthropic's AI tools.\14\ Whether the DPA threat re-appears against Anthropic or another firm is unknown, but it's clear that the President sees the law as a cudgel with which he can bend companies to his will.
\11\CNN, S. Westwood, J. Diamond, Trump announces face mask manufacturing deal with 3M after contentious negotiations (Apr. 7, 2020).
\12\Brendan Bordelon, `Attempted corporate murder': Trump's threats against Anthropic chill AI industry, Politico (Feb. 27, 2026).
\13\Anthropic, Statement from Dario Amodei on our discussions with the Department of War (Feb 26, 2026).
\14\Brendan Bordelon, `Attempted corporate murder': Trump's threats against Anthropic chill AI industry, Politico (Feb. 27, 2026).
To advise the President on the effective use of DPA authorities, the statute established the Defense Production Act Committee (DPAC), comprised of agency heads and other senior government leaders.\15\ Led by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA),\16\ the DPAC chair's current role is not to direct the actions of the individual member agencies, but to coordinate among the agencies to expedite the supply of and expand the productive capacity for materials and services essential to the national defense.\17\
\15\E-mail correspondence from CRS to House Financial Services Committee minority staff (Feb. 29, 2024).
\16\See 50 U.S.C. 4567, The Chairperson of the DPAC, ``shall be the head of the agency to which the President has delegated primary responsibility for government-wide coordination of the authorities in this chapter.''
\17\FEMA, The Defense Production Act Committee Report to Congress: Calendar Year 2020 (Sep. 20, 2021).
Title III. ``Expansion of Productive Capacity and Supply''--Title III allows the President to expand the production and supply of critical materials and goods\18\ via loans, loan guarantees, direct purchases, and purchase commitments to eligible businesses (i.e., those that meet the definition of domestic sources). That can include the creation or improvements to facilities and initiatives to address skilled workforce shortages in critical industries. Notably, the U.K. and Australia were added to the definition of domestic sources in the FY24 NDAA but while even though these countries are considered domestic sources, the President must first look to the U.S. and Canada as a primary source of production, and only if such a source is not possible, are they able to look to these allies.\19\ Title III activities are paid for by DPA Fund appropriations almost exclusively via grants. Appropriations generally remain available to the executive until expended, but per the current statute, the fund's unobligated balance at the end of each fiscal year may not exceed $750 million.\20\
\18\Projects under Title III include investments in ``select kinetic capabilities, microelectronics, castings and forgings, critical materials, and batteries and energy storage,'' per Assistant Secretary of Defense, Defense Production Act Title III (2024).
\19\50 U.S.C. Sec. 4552.
\20\Ibid. Supra, page 1, note 5.
Title VII. ``General Provisions''--Title VII contains provisions pertaining to the DPA as a whole, including key definitions. It also authorizes the National Defense Executive Reserves (NDER), which establishes of a pool of volunteer executives who could be called to public service in the name of national defense, and DPA voluntary agreements, which bring together business and government to collaborate on solving vexing problems that impact the national defense.\21\ Examples include a recently expired pandemic-era voluntary agreement to enhance coordination and cooperation related to critical healthcare resources\22\ and a series of newer ones focused on nuclear energy technologies.\23\
\21\DefenseOne, J. McGinn, D. Kaniewski, Where Does the Defense Production Act Go from Here? (Nov. 24, 2020).
\22\FEMA, Voluntary Agreement With Private Industry To Respond To Pandemics (Jan. 15, 2021).
\23\The White House, Reinvigorating The Nuclear Industrial Base (May 23, 2025).
``National Defense'' and the Scope of DPA--DPA activities are shaped by the definition of the term national defense, a term that has changed significantly since the law's enactment. In 1992, the term was defined as, ``programs for military and energy production or construction, military assistance to any foreign nation, stockpiling, space, and any directly related activity.''\24\ In 1994, however, emergency preparedness was added to this definition, and in 2003, ``critical infrastructure protection and restoration'' was included. In 2009, P.L. 11-67 added ``critical infrastructure assistance to any foreign nation'' and ``homeland security'' to the definition.\25\
\24\GovInfo, Code of Federal Regulations Title 10--Energy (Jan. 1, 2023).
\25\See ``Amendments'' section of 50 U.S.C. Sec. 4552.
This definition is critical to how the law can be applied. For example, in light of growing competition with China, Title III has been a significant tool to address aggressive and often illegal Chinese economic practices\26\ and has received strong bipartisan support for investments in areas such as critical minerals, rare-earth processing, batteries, magnets, and microelectronics.\27\ It has been used to refill stocks of supplies after the U.S. has distributed weapons to allies like Ukraine.\28\ In June 2022, the Biden Administration issued multiple Presidential Determinations (PDs) allowing the Department of Energy to execute Title III projects relating to renewable energy, ``to lower energy costs for families, reduce risks to our power grid, and tackle the urgent crisis of a changing climate.''\29\ While the Trump Administration has reversed these PDs,\30\ a future president could choose to refocus the application of the law on such technologies.

bill_title: DPA Modernization Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: \26\George Mason University, J. McGinn, No. 6 Building Resilience: Mobilizing the Defense Industrial Base in an Era of Great-Power Competition (Sep. 28, 2020).
\27\E.O. 13806, Assessing and Strengthening the Manufacturing and Defense Industrial Base and Supply Chain Resiliency of the United States (Jul. 26, 2017); E.O. 14017, America's Supply Chains (Feb. 24, 2021).
\28\White House, Memorandum on the Presidential Waiver of Statutory Requirements Pursuant to Section 303 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended (Oct. 3, 2022).
\29\White House, FACT SHEET: President Biden Takes Bold Executive Action to Spur Domestic Clean Energy Manufacturing (Jun. 6, 2022).
\30\White House, Additional Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions (Mar. 14, 2025).
Analysis: H.R. 7688 is a strongly bipartisan bill that expands oversight, improves function, limits the president's power where it matters, and strengthens the law. Generally, the bill would narrow the use of Title I authorities to a declared national emergency, a Stafford Act natural disaster, or a public health emergency. It would allow the President to delegate certain responsibilities to designated agencies, and it would affirmatively anchor the DPA Fund in the Department of the Treasury. Further, civil penalties would rise from $10,000 to $100,000, while potential criminal penalties would be removed.
The bill would increase the DPA Fund cap from $750 million to $2 billion, expanding potential application of the law's authorities. It would also raise the threshold at which Congressional notice is required from $50 million to $100 million. At the same time, however, the bill would require significantly more detailed planning for the use of those funds: After restructuring the DPAC, the bill would mandate a DPA Strategy to identify potential threats, live ``table-top'' exercises to devise mobilization plans to address those threats (reflecting a bill from Rep. Green, H.R. 8071, the ``Strengthening and Improving Mobilization Act of 2026''), and a supply-chain strategy covering medical materials, critical minerals, and naval shipbuilding capacity. The bill would also require an analysis of foreign adversary control risks and another, from Rep. Fields' H.R. 8136, the ``DPA Advanced Procurement Act of 2026,'' on long-lead items and stockpiling. Reporting to Congress (in a far more extensive manner than is currently required) would be required for all activities.
H.R. 7688 addresses several industrial areas critical to the national defense. For critical minerals, there would be a targeted initiative to speed planning, procurement, and infrastructure permitting. For emerging technologies, reflecting a bill from Rep. Lynch, H.R. 8053, the ``DPA Emerging Technologies Act,'' there would be established a subcommittee of the DPAC that would examine how artificial intelligence and robotics, biotechnology, cryptography and quantum computing, materials science, semiconductors, space might be leveraged for the national defense within and across agencies and sectors. This subcommittee would study the potential for a strategic biomaterials reserve, as recommended by members of the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology. The DPAC would be permitted to establish additional subcommittees. It would also require outreach and support to firms that offer goods and services necessary to the national defense, consistent with a bill from Rep. Beatty, H.R. 8038, the ``DPA Private-Sector Outreach Act of 2026.''
To address critical skills gaps, the bill reflects legislation from Rep. Casten, H.R. 8133, the ``DPA Workforce and Skilled Labor Needs Act of 2026,'' affirming that DPA funds could be used to support recruitment, training, placement, or retention of defense-critical workers and apprenticeships. Agencies would be required to report to Congress on steps needed to bolster the workforce to support the national defense. The bill would also adopt language from Rep. Gottheimer's H.R. 8138, the ``DPA Specialized Staffing Act,'' that would grant special hiring authority for subject matter experts to assist agencies with specialized financing focus and decisions.
Reflecting concern about trends of the last 13 months, the bill would cap future DPA-funded equity investments to 15% and would require a determination that private capital is unavailable. The bill would also require timely liquidation of such equity, when commercially feasible. Further, the bill would require the agencies using DPA authorities to take equity shares to provide Congress with the terms of the agreements-- information that has not been shared for most of the transactions where President Trump has used taxpayer dollars for private-sector equity ownership.
Addressing ethics issues, the bill includes Ranking Member Waters' H.R. 8030, the ``DPA Transparency Act of 2026,'' that would enact conflicts-of-interest language that would cover the President, Vice President, certain cabinet officials, or their immediate family members, including sons- and daughters-in-law. If those individuals hold 20% or more ownership in an entity, DPA assistance would be barred to those entities. In cases where there are two or more covered individuals that have an interest in an entity, those interests are aggregated to determine if they meet the cap. The bill would also require DPA agencies to institute fraud risk management standards.
The bill also incorporates components of Rep. Himes' H.R. 3542, the ``CLEAR (Committee Leadership and Enhanced Accountability for Resilience) Defense Production Act of 2025,'' which would make improvements to DPAC management and function, are also included, as are elements to support future health emergencies, drawn from a bill from Rep. Vargas.
While the bill is a product of collaboration between Chairman Hill and Ranking Member Waters, two amendments that would have improved the bill were offered by the Democratic caucus and denied by the majority. Both represent critical, timely issues raised in the headlines during the week prior the markup.
The first amendment, offered by Ranking Member Waters, would have established a rule of construction to prevent DPA authorities from being used in presidentially declared emergencies related to domestic federal elections. The Washington Post\31\ and other media\32\ reported that the Trump Administration has been circulating a 17-page draft executive order that claims that China interfered in the 2020 election. In that draft order, Trump refers to the Defense Production Act authorities three times, attempting to build the case for being able to suggest voting machines are invalid and must be replaced by his own approved methods of vote casting and counting. The amendment was rejected on party lines.
\31\Washington Post, A. Arnsdorf, Trump, seeking executive power over elections, is urged to declare emergency (Feb. 26, 2026).
\32\Democracy Docket, M. Cohen, J. Saksa, Read a draft of the emergency executive order for Trump to take control of elections (Feb. 27, 2026).
The second amendment was offered by Rep. Liccardo, reflecting the Trump Administration's highly unusual actions towards Anthropic. His amendment aimed to stop the Department of Defense from using DPA to retaliate against developers for instituting safeguards on high-risk technologies. Noting the Trump Administration's ire at Anthropic for the AI company's effort to set guardrails that would prevent its products and services from being used for mass surveillance of U.S. citizens or autonomous weapons, the amendment proposed to prevent such abuses. It was rejected on party lines.
We support the underlying bill will continue to work on these amendments and to improve the bill as it moves to the floor.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Al Green,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,
Juan Vargas,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Members of Congress.

bill_title: HEATS Act
content:
<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 5587 would exempt certain geothermal exploration and production activities from longstanding federal oversight and permitting requirements. Specifically, the bill allows projects occurring on non-federal surface estate and involving less than 50 percent federal subsurface estate to proceed without a federal drilling permit and without review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Endangered Species Act (ESA), and National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). This is an extreme waiver of the federal government's responsibilities to steward public resources.
Under current law, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) must conduct environmental review under NEPA before approving any project involving federal subsurface resources. Even where projects occur on non-federal surface estate, operators are still required to obtain a geothermal drilling permit when federal subsurface resources are involved. Subsurface activities can have significant surface impacts, including induced seismicity, land subsidence, the creation of sinkholes, and impacts on groundwater used for drinking and irrigation.
H.R. 5587 would eliminate essential safeguards, including environmental review, consultation under the ESA, engagement with Tribal governments, and opportunities for public input. In previous Congresses, BLM testified in opposition to the legislation, noting that it would strip the Secretary of the Interior's authority necessary to ensure geothermal development is conducted safely, in compliance with applicable laws, and consistent with the agency's multiple-use and sustained-yield mandate. The bill would undermine the BLM's core responsibility to ensure that activities affecting federal resources protect the environment, nearby communities, Tribal interests, other landowners, and the taxpayers.
Split-estate landowners rely on the federal government to protect their land. The mineral estate is the dominant estate, giving those with mineral rights priority over surface rights. The federal drilling permit process is often the only mechanism for considering how a proposed plan of operations would affect many resources on private land, including water impacts, ranching, and wildlife impacts. Any shortcomings in a state's permitting process would inappropriately leave federal taxpayers responsible for obligations created by the state.
Finally, H.R. 5587 continues an alarming pattern of proposals to waive federal environmental review for energy development--Republicans have attempted similar waivers for oil and gas development for years, which Democrats have strongly opposed. Regardless of the energy source involved, surface landowners deserve a say in the development of federal minerals beneath their land. This bill would set a dangerous precedent by eroding bedrock environmental laws and weakening accountability.
For these reasons, I oppose H.R. 5587.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
bill_title: American Broadband Deployment Act of 2025
content:
<Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.>: In November 2021, President Biden signed into law the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, or the ``Bipartisan Infrastructure Law,'' which made historic and long overdue investments in surface transportation, energy, healthcare, and communications infrastructure. These investments included $42.45 billion for the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment Program to deploy broadband infrastructure to Americans who lack reliable access to high-speed internet service.
Committee Democrats do not dispute that there are barriers in the way of deploying broadband infrastructure. H.R. 2289 addresses none of them, unfortunately. The Republican Majority could have worked with Democrats on comprehensive legislation that addresses the concerns that all witnesses raised at legislative hearings--most notably, the lack of adequate resources and qualified personnel to review permit applications at Federal agencies. Instead, the Republican Majority ignored the fact that President Trump ordered the firings of thousands of federal workers, many of whom were hired under the prior administration specifically to cut down on permit review times. The result is this package, which is composed of dozens of partisan bills masquerading as legislative ``solutions'' in search of problems, rather than addressing the very real problem of the lack of resources that agencies need to conduct the permitting review process.
H.R. 2289 regrettably proposes to eliminate standard environmental and historic preservation protections that simply do not affect the overwhelming majority of communications infrastructure projects as suggested by Republicans. For example, H.R. 2289 proposes blanket exemptions to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). However, many projects to deploy communications infrastructure already qualify for expedited review and approval under existing categorical exclusions, which Federal agencies apply to predetermined activities that do not have a significant environmental impact. If a project does not qualify for an existing categorical exclusion, the project can still be approved under an Environmental Assessment and a Finding of No Significant Impact. There is little evidence to suggest that communications infrastructure projects regularly trigger the highest level of scrutiny under NEPA, which require applicants to develop and submit an Environmental Impact Statement, let alone warrant the proposed blanket NEPA exemptions.
Perhaps most troubling are H.R. 2289's provisions to eliminate local communities' roles in decision-making over the placement and construction of utility infrastructure. The bill imposes heavy-handed ``deemed granted'' provisions on local governments by setting narrow and arbitrary deadlines to approve requests to install communications infrastructure in areas managed by county or municipal governments. The 60-day ``shot clock'' to approve or deny an application implies an unfamiliarity with the realities of local government calendars. At the local level, construction application and review processes are often designed to comply with ``sunshine'' laws to ensure transparency and provide residents with sufficient opportunity to be heard on important community matters. While the Republican Majority seems intent on helping big corporations evade scrutiny in communities they wish to serve, Democrats understand that our friends and neighbors who serve our communities as mayors, council members, and local zoning board members represent the best interests of their constituents, and they disagree with attempts by Republicans to constrain their ability to do so.
Local officials are responsible for ensuring the safety and welfare of residents. Efforts like this bill by House Republicans to automatically approve certain construction projects will put people in harm's way. Communications providers that proceed with construction without the proper approvals from state, county, or municipal governments should recognize the liability to which they are exposing themselves. These are just some of the reasons why H.R. 2289 is opposed by the National League of Cities, United States Conference of Mayors, the National Association of Counties, and the National Association of Telecommunications Officers and Advisors.
If Committee Republicans were truly committed to expediting the deployment of high-speed internet to rural communities, they should have advocated that the Trump Administration carry out the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law as intended. Instead, the Trump Administration, with the support of Congressional Republicans, has delayed progress by at least a year just to change program rules that force inferior broadband technologies onto unserved and underserved communities across the country.
Frank Pallone, Jr.,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Main Street Capital Access Act
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Cleo Fields>: We strongly support community banks and credit unions and stand ready to work with Republicans to advance sensible reforms to do just that. However, this package of overwhelmingly Republican and partisan bills represents the greatest amount of bank deregulation since before the 2008 global financial crisis. Instead of focusing on sensible improvements to support community banks and credit unions on Main Street, this bill will help megabanks on Wall Street and harm consumers. It undermines consumer protection, community reinvestment, and anti-discrimination safeguards, as well as impairs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) ability to issue any new rules. It also includes reforms that will chill international regulatory cooperation, as well as fuel faster industry consolidation by effectively exempting most bank mergers from review. In other words, this legislation does not provide access to capital for Main Street.
This bill's partisan approach is a departure from recent action the House took to support community financial institutions. Specifically, Ranking Member Maxine Waters and Committee Democrats recently worked with Chairman French Hill and Committee Republicans to include 12 provisions to help community financial institution in H.R. 6644, the ``Housing for the 21st Century Act.'' Five of those provisions were led by Committee Democrats, with four others co-led by Committee Democrats. In February 2026, the House passed that package overwhelmingly by a vote of 390 to 9.
POISON PILLS UNDERMINING SENSIBLE RELIEF FOR COMMUNITY FINANCIAL
INSTITUTIONS
This bill falls well short of what we know can be done on a bipartisan basis to promote, preserve, and enhance access to banking services for Main Street communities. H.R. 6955 consists of 30 Republican bills and only a few Democratic bills. Unlike our package of community bank reforms included in the housing bill, fully nine of the provisions in this package are poison pills and opposed by all Democratic members of this committee, and another seven provisions were opposed by most. Below are the nine provisions opposed by all Committee Democratic Members that were included in the package:
• Sec. 201: H.R. 3380--the ``Taking Account of
Institutions with Low Operation Risk (TAILOR) Act''
(Loudermilk), (5/21/25 markup, 29-23). This section
contains sweeping and harmful partisan reforms that
would require banking regulators and the CFPB to tailor
all regulations for all their regulated entities, not
just community banks, to account for a wide variety of
risk profiles and industry costs (but not benefits).
Given this bill requires any new rule to be tailored
not just to types of institutions but individual
institutions, any one of thousands of banks, credit
unions, or nonbank financial companies would have a
basis to sue and block any new rule from being
implemented. The ANS eliminated a lookback provision
but would still require any new rule to follow this new
procedure. This section would significantly impair the
CFPB and the banking regulators' ability to issue or
update any rules, including those that apply to the
largest financial companies that community banks and
credit unions compete with.
• Sec. 202: H.R. 2835--the ``Small Bank
Holding Company Relief Act'' (Donalds), (6/10/25
markup, 30 20). This section would double the
consolidated asset threshold from $3 billion to $6
billion for bank holding companies (BHCs) and savings
and loan holding companies (SLHCs) to be eligible for
the Federal Reserve's Small Bank Holding Company and
Savings and Loan Holding Company Policy Statement. This
statement exempts small BHCs and SLHCs from
consolidated risk-based capital and leverage
requirements, reduces reporting requirements, expedites
bank mergers, and allows them to have higher debt
flexibility to finance bank acquisitions. This policy
was first implemented by the Fed in 1980 to help the
smallest banks with less than $150 million in assets,
and Congress has subsequently increased this threshold
three times, last in 2018, to $3 billion today. While
the ANS reduces the proposed threshold from $25 billion
to $6 billion, this is still a sizable increase and
much higher than an inflation-based increase to $4
billion. This also ignores other sweeping rollbacks for
capital requirements for these same banks provided in
other sections of the bill, like the next one.
• Sec. 301: H.R. 3379--the ``Halting Uncertain
Methods and Practices in Supervision (HUMPS) Act''
(Fitzgerald), (5/21/25 markup, 29-23). This section
would significantly rollback oversight of bank
management by requiring the banking regulators, through
the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council
(FFIEC), to develop recommendations and modify their
implementation of the CAMELS ratings framework, where
depository institutions are given composite and
component exam ratings for Capital adequacy, Asset
quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, and
Sensitivity to market risk (CAMELS). In doing so,
regulators would be required to either eliminate the
management component or significantly limit its use.
The bill also eliminates the consideration of
management with respect to certain provisions of the
Bank Holding Company Act, including with respect to
acquiring other banks and expanding the bank's
financial activities. This will significantly diminish
the ability to hold bank management, like Silicon
Valley Bank (SVB) following their failure or Wells
Fargo after their repeated violations resulting in
consumer harm, accountable for their actions.
• Sec. 401: H.R. 3446--the ``FDIC Board
Accountability Act'' (Huizenga), (7/23/25 markup, 26-
23). This section represents an attack on Biden's
appointed regulators and mandates the appointment of a
member with experience in small depository
institutions, and limits board members' terms to twelve
years. Originally, this section would also remove the
CFPB Director as a voting member of the FDIC board,
though that was removed in the ANS. Nonetheless, this
section does nothing to prevent Trump's attacks on the
independence of the FDIC or require the President to
fill the vacant FDIC Board member positions with
Democratic nominees.
• Sec. 402: H.R. 4460--the ``Stop Agency Fiat
Enforcement of Guidance (SAFE Guidance) Act'' (Meuser),
(7/23/25 markup, 26-23). The bill requires the head of
Federal financial departments and agencies--
specifically Treasury, HUD, Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC,
NCUA, SEC, CFPB, and FHFA--to provide a so-called
``guidance clarity statement'' on a wide variety of
agency statements stipulating that they don't have a
binding effect. This would require endless numbers of
disclaimers that could chill agency communications and
hinder guidance that could be helpful for industry
participants to understand their legal obligations.
Moreover, this bill would not apply to President Trump,
who issues chaotic and contradictory policy statements
on social media, who has seized control over the
rulemaking process for these agencies. The bill also
does not overturn the action of Trump's CFPB to rescind
nearly 70 guidance documents that could help regulated
entities understand their legal obligations.
• Sec. 403: H.R. 6544--the ``Regulatory
Efficiency, Verification, Itemization, and Enhanced
Workflow (REVIEW) Act'' (Timmons), (12/17/25 markup,
30-23). This section would amend the Economic Growth
and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act of 1996 (EGRPRA)
to increase the frequency of a comprehensive regulatory
review conducted every 10 years by Federal banking
regulators to every 8 years (previously 7 years before
it was changed in the ANS) and require them to conduct
a further review of the cumulative impact of their
regulations with additional cost-benefit analysis that
ignores certain benefits, like consumer protection. The
EGRPRA process is already an elaborate one, with
extensive stakeholder engagement that typically last
three years. Moreover, with the combination of Section
302, this section arguably includes the CFPB to do this
comprehensive lookback too, despite the fact they
already do a 5-year lookback review on its regulations,
among other requirements that banking regulators are
not subject to. Furthermore, regulators already have
authority to update rules whenever it may be
appropriate, and doing an exhaustive regulatory review
every 8 years would distract regulators, including the
CFPB, from their day-to-day duties to oversee the
banking system and protect consumers.
• Sec. 404: H.R. 6550--the ``American
Financial Institution Regulatory Sovereignty and
Transparency (American FIRST) Act'' (Loudermilk), (12/
17/25 markup, 29-23). This section requires the Fed,
OCC, FDIC, and NCUA to include unusually extensive
information about their interactions with global
financial regulatory or supervisory forums, like the
Basel Committee or the Network for Greening the
Financial System, undermining and chilling such
engagement by U.S. regulators and addressing risks,
like climate-related financial risk. While certain
reporting requirements were simplified through the ANS,
the requirements are still robust and would likely
chill efforts for U.S. regulators to coordinate with
foreign regulators through these forums. This section
also ignores the many ways U.S. regulators already keep
Congress informed of such engagements and advance our
national interests with their foreign counterparts to
shape global financial regulatory policy. Committee
Republicans passed a similar bill last Congress (H.R.
4823, 118th) on a party-line vote.
• Sec. 601: H.R. 5262--the ``Bank Competition
Modernization Act'' (Fitzgerald), (9/16/25 markup, 28-
24). The section amends several banking laws to
completely waive a review for mergers that would result
in a bank under $10 billion in assets related to
competition, regardless of whether the bank would
become the only lender in a community. The section also
includes an annual adjustment calculation based on
nominal GDP, which would quickly increase the threshold
as opposed to a more typical inflation-based
adjustment. These sweeping reforms will accelerate
consolidation and lead to fewer community banks.
• Sec. 604: H.R. 1900--the ``Bank Failure
Prevention Act'' (Barr), (5/21/25 markup, 29-21). This
section would modify the bank merger review process by
limiting the Fed's ability to consider feedback from
affected stakeholders on proposed mergers. It would
also force the Fed, FDIC, and OCC to either approve or
deny a merger application within 120 days (previously
90 days before it was changed in the ANS) of receiving
an initial application, even if the application is not
complete and the merging parties have not provided all
the information regulators request to adequately assess
the merger application. These reforms will bring less
scrutiny to a rubber-stamping process that has wiped
out community banks and significantly increased the
market share of the largest banks. Previously, this
section was section 103 in the introduced version of
the bill before it was moved here.
FORGOTTEN LESSONS FROM PAST FINANCIAL CRISES
In the nearly two decades since the 2008 global crisis, we've learned a great deal about how to maintain a resilient financial system in the face of many obstacles, including through the pandemic. But this partisan package ignores those lessons and will plant the seeds for the next crisis. Moreover, while the nation grapples with an affordability crisis and surge in financial scams and fraud, costing consumers tens of billions of dollars, this package would hamper the CFPB's ability to issue any new rules, undercutting the very agency Congress established to combat financial abuses and empower consumers to protect their finances. At a time when the Trump Administration has largely shut down the CFPB and this Committee has failed to fulfill our statutory duty to have Acting Director Russell Vought testify, the last thing Congress should be doing is undermining the CFPB any further.

bill_title: Main Street Capital Access Act
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Cleo Fields>: Furthermore, this bill ignores the lessons from the failure of Silicon Valley Bank and other regional banks which failed a few short years after Congress and President Trump's regulators rolled back enhanced prudential standards on these banks. Instead, this bill lets even more of these regional banks escape critical safeguards that promote safety and soundness. Instead of rolling back progress to pursue deregulation that enables unnecessary risk-taking, speculation, and weakens our financial system, we should work together to strengthen community banks, credit unions, and consumer protections, as well as promote access to affordable financial products and services.
Committee Democrats offered several amendments to improve the bill that were rejected. This included an amendment from Ranking Member Waters that would provide funding and reforms to support community development financial institutions (CDFIs) and minority depository institutions (MDIs). This was based on her bill, H.R. 9767 (118th Cong.), the ``Promoting and Advancing Communities of Color Through Inclusive Lending Act.'' The Majority rejected another amendment by Ranking Member Waters to strip the bill of harmful provisions that would roll back various consumer protections. It would have also restored the CFPB of its original funding levels from the Federal Reserve, and required the CFPB to resume supervision of the largest banks that compete with community banks at the same frequency and with the same number of staff as in 2024.
The Majority rejected another amendment by Ranking Member Waters to modernize the deposit insurance framework and enhance tools to hold culpable executives of a failing bank accountable. The latter amendment was based on her legislation, H.R. 4551, the ``Employee Paycheck and Small Business Protection Act,'' and H.R. 7886, the ``Failed Bank Executives Accountability and Consequences Act.'' Finally, the majority rejected an amendment from Rep. Sean Casten to require the Federal Reserve to report on any activities they have carried out as Treasury's fiscal agent relating to Venezuela's oil proceeds.
There were a number of organizations that either opposed H.R. 6955 or bills included in the package, including: Americans for Financial Reform (AFR), Center for Responsible Lending (CRL), Consumer Action, Consumer Federation of America, Consumer Reports, Institute for Agriculture and Trade Policy, Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility, National Association of Consumer Advocates, National Community Reinvestment Coalition (NCRC), National Consumer Law Center, on behalf of its low-income clients (NCLC), National Consumers League, New Economy Project, Private Equity Stakeholder Project, Public Citizen, Public Justice Center, Rise Economy, The People's Justice Council, Transparency Task Force, and 20/ 20 Vision.
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 6955.
APPENDIX--ADDITIONAL DETAILS AND ANALYSIS OF OTHER SECTIONS OF THE BILL
Below is a section-by-section description and analysis of the other sections in H.R. 6955. Title I--New Bank Formation and Local Community Access
• Sec. 101: H.R. 478--the ``Promoting New Bank
Formation Act'' (Barr), (4/2/25 markup, 28-21). This
section, which Republicans passed through Committee
last Congress by a party-line vote, requires new banks
and their holding companies to have lower capital
requirements than they otherwise should have for their
first three years, with additional capital reductions
for rural de novo community banks by allowing them to
be subject to below 8% Community Bank Leverage Ratio
(CBLR) in their first two years before reaching 8% in
their third year. New banks are much more vulnerable to
failure than other banks, which is why appropriate
capital is key to ensure they can stay in business and
grow. There were technical changes in the amendment in
the nature of a substitute (ANS), for example, adding a
U.S. Code citation, but substantively this is the same
as the standalone version of H.R. 478 instead of the
more targeted, pilot program version that Democrats
agreed to include in the Housing for the 21st Century
package.
• Sec. 102: H.R. 6551--the ``New Bank
Application Numbers Knowledge (New Bank) Act''
(Loudermilk), (12/17/25 markup, 53-0). The section
would require annual reports relating to applications
for new Federal depository institution charters, bank
holding companies, credit unions, Federal deposit
insurance, and State depository institution charters.
It would require the reporting of timelines and common
reasons for denial of such applications.
• Sec. 103: H.R. 6536--the ``Rural
Depositories Revitalization Study Act'' (Norman), (12/
17/25 markup, 50-0). The section would require the Fed,
FDIC, OCC, and NCUA to study ways to improve the
growth, capital adequacy, and profitability of rural
depository institutions, as well as the creation of de
novo depository institutions in rural areas. The ANS
modifies this section to provide for two separate
studies--one by the 3 banking regulators, and a
separate one by NCUA. This previously was section 104
in the introduced version; the old section 103 was
moved down in the bill to become section 604.
• Sec. 104: H.R. 5913, the ``Community
Investment and Prosperity Act'' (Lawler)--increase
public welfare investment (PWI) cap for banks, included
in Housing for 21st Century. This section was added by
the ANS and would increase the public welfare
investment cap for the OCC and the Federal Reserve from
15% to 20% to enhance the capacity of banks to make
investments in affordable housing and would require the
OCC and Federal Reserve to study and publish routine
reports on how these investments are made and used to
support communities.
• Sec. 105: H.R. 3161 (118th), the ``CDFI Fund
Transparency Act'' (Rose), (5/16/24 markup, voice
vote). This section was added by the ANS and requires
the Treasury Secretary (or their designee) to testify
annually on the CDFI Fund. This section does not
include reporting requirements that were added by
Ranking Member Waters, Rep. Velazquez, and Rep. Beatty
when the bill was passed by voice vote through the
Committee in 2024. Those omitted Democratic provisions
were designed to gain more granular data and better
learn how Treasury and the CDFI Fund were taking steps
to support community financial institutions.
• Sec. 106: H.R. 7733 (117th), the ``CDFI Bond
Guarantee Program Improvement Act'' (Cleaver) (5/17/22
markup, voice vote), previously passed in 2022 by FSC
and House by voice vote. This section was added by the
ANS bill and would reauthorize and improves the CDFI
Bond Guarantee Program. Specifically, the section
lowers the CDFI Bond Guarantee Program minimum issuance
threshold from $100 million to $25 million to expand
access, and revises the amount to be held in a CDFI's
relending account. Instead of extending this program by
4 years as the Committee and the House previously
approved in the 117th Congress to provide certainty to
market participants, this section would only extend the
program until 2028. Title II--Tailoring Bank Regulation
• See description of Section 201 (H.R. 3380,
the ``Taking Account of Institutions with Low Operation
Risk (TAILOR) Act,'' Loudermilk) and Section 202 (H.R.
2835, the ``Small Bank Holding Company Relief Act,''
Donalds) above in the section on poison pills.
• Sec. 203: H.R. 5276--the ``Community Bank
Leverage Improvement and Flexibility for Transparency
(Community Bank LIFT) Act'' (Kim), (9/16/25 markup, 33-
19). This section would permit community banks to have
significantly less capital by lowering the statutory
range for the community bank leverage ratio (CBLR) from
8-10% to 6-9% (the standalone bill provided a range of
6-8%, the ANS modified this to 6-9%). Trump's
regulators in his first term previously set the CBLR at
9%, though more recently have proposed lowering this to
8%. However, most community banks (83%) have over 9%
CBLR, but are not utilizing the CBLR framework for
other reasons, raising serious questions that reducing
the CBLR ratio is necessary for more banks to utilize
the framework. The section also increases the threshold
from $10 billion to $15 billion.
• Sec. 204: H.R. 6553--the ``Tailoring and
Indexing Enhanced Regulations (TIER) Act'' (Barr), (12/
17/25 markup, 33-19). This section would significantly
increase the thresholds for enhanced prudential
standards (i.e. capital, liquidity, stress testing,
risk management, etc.) that apply to the largest banks.
Specifically, the bill increases the threshold when
mandatory enhanced standards apply from $250 billion to
$370 billion in assets, and the minimum threshold for
when regulators have the discretion to apply such
standards from $100 billion to $150 billion. As we
approach the three year anniversary when we had 3 of
the 4 largest bank failures in U.S. history and
regulators were forced to use systemic risk tools to
resolve Silicon Valley Bank ($212 billion) and
Signature Bank ($110 billion), this approach ignores
lessons from that crisis and will reduce safeguards
relating to these large institutions. Furthermore, the
section indexes these thresholds to rapidly grow based
on nominal GDP (e.g. between 2015 and 2025, nominal GDP
grew by 67%, compared to 25% growth based on real GDP),
an approach Trump's FDIC recently rejected when
adjusting much smaller regulatory thresholds when they
adopted an inflation-based approach to index such
thresholds.
• Sec. 205: H.R. 7056, the ``Community Bank
Regulatory Tailoring Act'' (Barr), (1/22/26 markup, 33-
21). This section was added by the ANS. The section,
which the Committee did not hold a hearing on,
increases 37 regulatory thresholds for financial
institutions regarding a wide range of topics,
including capital, consumer protections, fair lending,
anti-discrimination, community reinvestment, Volcker
Rule's prohibition on proprietary trading, executive
compensation, GAAP accounting, independent audits, and
more without any study or analysis to justify these
changes. These thresholds are in a number of Federal
banking and consumer protection laws, specifically, the
Bank Holding Company Act of 1956 (``BHCA''), Community
Reinvestment Act of 1977 (``CRA''), Depository
Institution Management Interlocks Act (``DIMIA''),
Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection
Act (``Dodd-Frank''), Federal Credit Union Act, Federal
Deposit Insurance Act (``FDI Act''), Federal Home Loan
Bank Act of 1932 (``FHLB Act''), Federal Reserve Act,
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act of 1975 (``HMDA''), Home
Owners' Loan Act (``HOLA''), International Lending
Supervision Act of 1983, Real Estate Settlement
Procedures Act of 1974 (``RESPA''), Revised Statutes of
the United States (which includes the National Bank
Act), and Truth in Lending Act (``TILA''). Some of
these thresholds have not been adjusted in decades and
would include sizable increases with little
justification. Instead of focusing on small
institutions, several of the threshold increases would
benefit large banks with up to $175 billion in assets,
and all of the changes reduce safeguards with no
threshold changes that would benefit consumers.
Furthermore, these revised thresholds would all
continue to rapidly grow based on nominal GDP, an
approach that Trump's FDIC recently found to be
inappropriate and too aggressive when they updated some
similar thresholds using a more modest and typical
inflation-based indexing approach.
• Sec. 206: H.R. 975, the ``Credit Union Board
Modernization Act'' (Vargas). This section was added by
the ANS, and previously passed House several times with
broad bipartisan support, including in the Housing for
21st Century Act. This section would reduce board
meeting requirements for well-managed credit unions,
aligning Federal standards with similar credit union
board requirements for many states. Title III--Fair and Transparent Bank Supervision

the ``Halting Uncertain Methods and Practices in

content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Cleo Fields>: Supervision (HUMPS) Act,'' Fitzgerald) above in the
section on poison pills.
• Sec. 302: H.R. 940--the ``Fair Audits and
Inspection for Regulators'' Exams (FAIR Exams) Act''
(Hill), (5/21/25 markup, 35-17). This section would
impose certain timelines for examiners from the Federal
Reserve, FDIC, OCC, NCUA, and CFPB to share exam
reports, as well as all supporting documentation, with
a financial institution they supervise following an
exam. This bill would also establish an Office of
Independent Examination Review (OIER) within the FFIER
to review appeals of material supervisory
determinations (MSD) issued by these Federal agencies
for financial institutions they supervise, including
the largest banks, which would further be subject to
judicial review. GAO and other experts said the problem
with Silicon Valley Bank was not due process, but
rather, that supervisory concerns were not elevated
quickly enough to ensure they were addressed. The
Committee found similar dynamics at Wells Fargo, as the
bank received various citations that snowballed into
significant and repeated consumer harm. Accordingly,
this bill would significantly weaken the supervisory
framework and undermine consumer protection as well as
the safety and soundness of depository institutions.
While the ANS makes some changes to this section, Fed staff have indicated that this section would make it more difficult to bring routine supervisory actions and could result in significant delays before the Fed could require an institution to address a serious safety and soundness concern, which would adversely impact the effectiveness of their enforcement program. This approach is the exact opposite of what is needed following the SVB failure, where the Fed's slow supervisory and enforcement approach was heavily criticized for contributing to SVB's failure.
• Sec. 303: H.R. 4437--the ``Supervisory
Modification for Appropriate Risk-Based Testing (SMART)
Act'' (Timmons), (7/22/25 markup, 53-1). This section
provides exam relief for well-managed and well-
capitalized banks and credit unions with under $6
billion in total assets, provided they are not subject
to an enforcement action or recently went through a
merger. Specifically, the bill provides these
institutions with alternating full-scope and limited-
scope exam as well as a combined exam (safety and
soundness; consumer compliance; and/or cybersecurity
and information technology), however regulators retain
discretion to do additional targeted or full-scope
exams to ensure safety and soundness and compliance
with applicable laws.
• Sec. 304: H.R. 4478--the ``Tailored
Regulatory Updates for Supervisory Testing (TRUST)
Act'' (Moore-NC), (7/23/25 markup, 48-0). This section
raises the consolidated asset threshold from $3 billion
to $6 billion for well-capitalized and well-managed
banks (including not being subject to an enforcement
action) to qualify for an 18-month full-scope
examination cycle instead of a 12-month exam. Congress
last raised this threshold in 2018, when this threshold
covered 94.2% of banks. After first proposing to raise
this threshold to $10 billion, Republicans agreed to
lower this to a $6 billion threshold, which would cover
94.6% of banks today.
• Sec. 305: H.R. 2702--the ``Financial
Integrity and Regulation Management (FIRM) Act''
(Barr), (5/21/25 markup, 33-19). Instead of focusing on
debanking resulting in closed or frozen accounts, this
section would completely eliminate reputational risk as
a component of the supervision of depository
institutions. For the first time, regulators would be
prevented from considering certain types of risk, in
this case reputational risk, when promoting safety and
soundness. Republicans adopted an amendment offered by
Rep. Sherman to exempt reputational risk concerns
related to terrorist financing, however there remain
many other types of issues, including repeat offenders
and other instances of money laundering, that could be
tougher to curb based on this section. Title IV--Regulatory Accountability and Transparency
• See description of Section 401 (H.R. 3446,
the ``FDIC Board Accountability Act,'' Huizenga),
Section 402 (H.R. 4460, the ``Stop Agency Fiat
Enforcement of Guidance (SAFE Guidance) Act,'' Meuser),
Section 403 (H.R. 6544, the ``Regulatory Efficiency,
Verification, Itemization, and Enhanced Workflow
(REVIEW) Act,'' Timmons), and Section 404 (H.R. 6550,
the ``American Financial Institution Regulatory
Sovereignty and Transparency (American FIRST) Act,''
Loudermilk) above in the section on poison pills. Title V--Strengthening Local Bank Funding
• Sec. 501: H.R. 3390--the ``Bringing the
Discount Window into the 21st Century Act'' (De La
Cruz), (7/23/25 markup, 48-1). This section would
require the Federal Reserve to conduct a review,
develop a plan, and issue reports on steps they are
taking to enhance and modernize the functioning of the
Fed's discount window where banks obtain emergency
liquidity. This is in response to concerns raised by
banks that had problems accessing the Fed's discount
window during the 2023 regional bank failures.
• Sec. 502: H.R. 3234--the ``Keeping Deposits
Local Act'' (Emmer), (9/16/25 markup, 51-0). This
section would modify limits first set by Congress in
2018 to increase the amount of reciprocal deposits
exempted from brokered deposit restrictions, utilizing
a tiered approach based on a bank's total assets and
total liabilities. Reciprocal deposits are part of a
network operated by a third-party where a bank, for a
fee, may provide insurance for a customer on funds
greater than $250,000. Funds over the cap are
distributed to other banks in the network, and those
banks reciprocate and provide the originating bank
matching funds so it may use the full amount of the
deposit for lending or other purposes. A bipartisan
amendment was adopted to narrow the scope to ensure
community and mid-size banks benefit the most.
• Sec. 503: H.R. 5317--the ``Community Bank
Deposit Access Act'' (Hill), (9/16/25 markup, 48-2).
This provision would allow banks to maintain custodial
deposits and have them exempted from brokered deposit
restrictions. Custodial deposits allow smaller banks to
ensure a customer with more than $250,000 in deposits
can obtain FDIC insurance for the full amount of their
deposit, spreading the funds across other banks in a
custodial deposit network. A bipartisan amendment was
agreed to that narrowed the bill to ensure it focuses
on community banks with less than $10 billion. Title VI--Promoting Bank Competition and Merger Clarity
• See description of Section 601 (H.R. 5262,
the ``Bank Competition Modernization Act,'' Fitzgerald)
above in the section on poison pills.
• Sec. 602: H.R. 6570--the ``Merger Agreement
Approvals Clarity and Predictability Act''
(Fitzgerald), (12/17/25 markup, 52-0). This section
requires GAO to study the use of commitments and
conditions by Federal prudential regulators in
connection with bank merger applications, as well as
other aspects of bank merger reviews and the impact
mergers have had on affected communities, competition,
and financial stability.
• Sec. 603: H.R. 6546--the ``Merger Process
Review Act'' (Williams), (12/17/25 markup, 52-0). This
section requires the Inspectors General of Federal
banking regulators to every three years review the
regulator's handling of bank merger applications,
including the impact bank mergers have had on affected
communities, competition, and financial stability. It
also requires the regulators to respond to the IG
reports with a written plan on how they will improve
the bank merger review process.
• See description of Section 604 (H.R. 1900,
the ``Bank Failure Prevention Act,'' Barr) above in the
section on poison pills.
Title VII--Strengthening Transparency and Involvement in Bank
Resolutions
• Sec. 701: H.R. 6547--the ``Least Cost
Exception Act'' (Flood), (12/17/25 markup, 50-0). This
section would allow the FDIC to waive the least cost
resolution test when selecting a bid for a failed bank
if the FDIC and Federal Reserve make a determination
that any risks to the FDIC's Deposit Insurance Fund are
outweighed by limiting the concentration in Global
Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs) if the FDIC
chooses a bid from a bank other than a G-SIB. The
alternative bid will need to meet certain criteria,
including agreeing to pay the difference of their bid
and that of a G-SIB, subject to case-by-case discounts
and other criteria established by the FDIC.
• Sec. 702: H.R. 6555--the ``Enhancing Bank
Resolution Participation Act'' (Huizenga), (12/17/25
markup, 51-0). This section requires a study by Federal
banking regulators on the use of so-called ``shelf
charters'' and modified bidder qualifications since
2008 to allow nonbank companies to buy a failing bank.
Republicans agreed to expand the study to also consider
safety and soundness, the availability of financial
products and services provided to consumers, and the
risks and benefits of private equity's involvement in
such acquisitions.
• Sec. 703: H.R. 6556, the ``Failing Bank
Acquisition Fairness Act'' (Lynch), (12/17/25 markup,
51-0). This section was added by the ANS and previously
passed the House with broad support when it was
included in Housing for 21st Century. This section
would promote competition in banking by narrowing the
exception that allows a megabank with more than 10% of
U.S. total deposits or liabilities to bid to acquire a
failing bank. Specifically, this bill would prevent
such megabanks from bidding for a failed bank if there
are other eligible bids from other well-capitalized and
well-managed banks that meet FDIC's typical
requirements. Only when there are no such bids would
these megabanks be permitted to acquire a failing bank.
• Sec. 704: H.R. 3716, the ``Systemic Risk
Authority Transparency Act'' (Green), (6/10/26 markup,
51-0). This section was added by the ANS and previously
passed the House with broad support when it was
included in Housing for 21st Century. This section
would require GAO and bank regulators to issue reports
if regulators invoke the systemic risk exception, as
they did to manage the failures of Silicon Valley Bank
and Signature Bank in 2023. These reports would provide
Congress and the public an analysis to identify the
causes of the bank failures, including any management,
supervisory, or regulatory shortcomings.
Title VIII--Facilitating Innovation and Bank Partnerships
• Sec. 801: H.R. 5291--the ``Merchant Banking
Modernization Act'' (Williams), (9/16/25 markup, 35-
17). This section would permit financial holding
companies (FHCs), a type of bank holding company, to
hold merchant banking investments for up to 15 years.
The Fed's regulations currently set a limit of 10 years
on these investments, though they may grant individual
extensions based on the circumstance and could modify
the regulation. Most of these investments are done by
the largest banks, and allow the bank to make engage in
non-financial business activities that may pose unusual
risks. Without more data about these kind of unique
investments, such a reform could undermine the safety
and soundness of large banks operating in this space.
• Sec. 802: H.R. 6552--the ``Bank FinTech
Partnership Enhancement Act'' (Barr), (12/17/25 markup,
53-0). This section requires the Federal banking and
credit union regulators to conduct a study of how
fintech partnerships could help banks and credit unions
better compete and serve their communities. Republicans
added considerations for consumer protection as well as
availability of financial products and services for
consumers.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Stephen F. Lynch,
Al Green,
Emanuel Cleaver, II,
Joyce Beatty,
Juan Vargas,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Nikema Williams,
Cleo Fields,
Members of Congress.
