committee_name: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
bill_title: To prohibit the District of Columbia from requiring tribunals in court or administrative proceedings in the District of Columbia to defer to the Mayor of the District of Columbia's interpretation of statutes and regulations, and for other purposes.
content:
<Rep. Robert Garcia>: Committee Democrats strongly oppose H.R. 3766. The bill would prohibit the District of Columbia (D.C.) from requiring a reviewing tribunal to defer to the D.C. executive branch's interpretation of a statute or regulation. The bill would also repeal a D.C. law that codified the longstanding deference the local D.C. courts had given to the D.C. executive branch's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute or regulation.\1\ The bill is opposed by D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser, D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson, and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb.\2\
\1\Review of Agency Action Clarification Amendment Act of 2025, D.C. Law 26-37.
\2\Letter from District of Columbia Mayor Muriel Bowser, District of Columbia Council Chairman Phil Mendelson, and District of Columbia Attorney General Brian Schwalb to Chairman James Comer and Ranking Member Robert Garcia, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (Dec. 1, 2025) (online at https://www.congress.gov/119/meeting/ house/118712/ documents/HMKP-119-GO00-20251202-SD017.pdf).
In 2024, in Loper Bright, the right-wing United States Supreme Court held that federal courts may not defer to a federal agency's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute and instead must exercise their independent judgment.\3\ While Loper Bright is not binding on the local D.C. courts, after Loper Bright, D.C. codified the longstanding deference the local D.C. courts had given to the D.C. executive branch's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute or regulation.
\3\Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024).
The bill would violate D.C.'s right to self-government. Moreover, the bill would give the local D.C. courts authority to overrule the longstanding deference they had given to the D.C. executive branch's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute or regulation. Such a ruling would disrupt D.C.'s legal system, substitute the judgment of the local D.C. courts for that of expert D.C. agencies, and transfer interpretative responsibility from D.C.'s political branches, which are accountable to D.C. residents, to local D.C. judges, who are appointed by the President, subject to Senate confirmation.
Robert Garcia,
Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: FLEX Act
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
The Charter School Program (CSP) is authorized by the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965 (ESEA)\1\ for the purpose of ``supporting innovation; providing financial assistance for the planning, design, and initial implementation of charter schools; increasing the number of high-quality charter schools; encouraging states to provide charter schools facilities financing; and strengthening the charter school authorizing process.''\2\ H.R. 7082, the Fostering Learning and Excellence in Charter Schools (FLEX) Act, introduced by Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-PA),\3\ would alter CSP by shifting reserved funds for different sections of the program, expanding the allowable uses of funds under the supporting high-quality charter schools section of the program, and eliminating oversight provisions, among other things.\4\ By doing so, the bill would significantly reduce funding for high-quality charter schools, reduce guardrails and transparency, and open the door for potentially greater waste, fraud, and abuse in the program.\5\
\1\20 U.S.C. Sec. Sec. 7221-7221j.
\2\Rebecca R. Skinner & Isobel Sorenson, Cong. Rsch. Serv., IF12601, ESEA: Charter Schools Program, (2024), https://www.crs.gov/ Reports/IF12601; see 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221(1)-(8).
\3\Fostering Learning and Excellence in Charter Schools (FLEX) Act, H.R. 7082, 119th Cong. (2026).
\4\Id.
\5\Id.
SUMMARY OF CONCERNS
H.R. 7082 Would Slash Funding and Erode Safeguards for the High-Quality
Charter Schools Section of CSP
H.R. 7082 Would Slash Funding for High-Quality Charter
Schools
Pursuant to current law, CSP authorizes funds to support charter schools in three ways, and each of these ways has its own specific funding set-aside/reservation:\6\ supporting high-quality charter schools (65% of CSP funds);\7\ facilities financing assistance (12.5% of CSP funds);\8\ and national activities (22.5% of CSP funds).\9\ H.R. 7082 would change the amounts reserved for each of the three sections.\10\ Specifically, the bill would: (1) increase the reservation of funds for facilities financing assistance from 12.5 to 15 percent;\11\ (2) increase the amount reserved for national activities from 22.5 to 25 percent;\12\ and (3) reduce the amount of funds reserved for supporting high-quality charter schools from 65 to ``at least 30 percent'' and allow the remaining 35 percent to be distributed among all three sections as determined by the Secretary.\13\ The latter change is the most significant. Republicans assert that H.R. 7082 would ``reduce red tape and provide greater flexibility [in CSP] . . . ensuring resources reach classrooms more efficiently and respond to the needs of students and families.''\14\ In fact, H.R. 7082 would do the opposite. Rather than continue to emphasize supporting high-quality charter schools as CSP currently does, the bill would allow funding for high-quality charter schools to be reduced by more than half. It would permit the Secretary to more than triple the amount of funds used for facilities financing assistance and more than double the amount used for national activities. As a result, significantly less funding would go directly to students, families, and classrooms.
\6\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221a(a)-(b); Skinner, supra note 2.
\7\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221a(b)(3). This funding provides grants to State Entities (defined as state educational agencies (SEAs), state governors, state charter school authorizing boards, or charter school support organizations), which in turn provide subgrants to eligible applicants (defined as charter school developers that have applied to a charter authorizer to open a charter school) to open a new charter school or replicate or expand a high-quality charter school. 20 U.S.C.
Sec. 7221b.
\8\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7721a(b)(1). This reservation funds two types of programs: (1) Credit Enhancement Grants, which ``are made to public or private entities (or a combination of the two) for the development of credit enhancement initiatives to assist charter schools in acquiring, constructing, or renovating facilities''; and (2) Facilities Incentive Grants (also called Per-Pupil Facilities Grants or the Per-Pupil Facilities Aid Program), which ``provide[] funds to states to establish or enhance and administer per-pupil facilities allowances to help charter schools obtain facilities'' in states that permit such per-pupil facilities aid. Skinner, supra note 2; 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221c.
\9\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7721a(b)(2). This reservation funds: (1) Replication and Expansion of High-Quality Charter Schools Grants, which provide funding to non-profit Charter Management Organizations ``to replicate or expand one or more high-quality charter schools''; (2) Developer Grants, which are provided to ``charter school developers in states that do not have a current CSP grant to a state entity [and] may apply directly to the Secretary of Education (the Secretary) for a competitive grant to open a new charter school or replicate or expand a high-quality charter school; and (3) Dissemination and Evaluation Grants to provide technical assistance, disseminate best practices, and evaluate the impact of CSP, including its impact on student achievement. Skinner, supra note 2; 20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d.
\10\H.R. 7082 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
\11\Id.
\12\Id.
\13\Id.
\14\Press Release, Congressman Mackenzie's FLEX Act Advances Through Committee (Jan. 21, 2026), https://mackenzie.house.gov/media/ press-releases/congressman-mackenzies-flex-act-advances-through-committee.
H.R. 7082 would also expand the allowable uses of funds authorized to support high-quality charter schools in the CSP. The bill would permit funding under that section to be used for ``curricular or other offerings,'' ``new academic programs or delivery models,'' ``personalized learning,'' or ``a new curricular approach.''\15\ However, the bill does not define these terms, and it is unclear what they mean or how they could be interpreted by the Department of Education (Department). Thus, the bill would significantly reduce the funds that may be available for high-quality charter schools while at the same time dilute what the remaining funds may be used for by inserting these new and amorphous terms. The bill states that this change must done in a way that would ``enable additional students to enroll in and benefit from the school,'' but as written, the language would be satisfied with the enrollment of only two additional students, and how the term ``benefit'' would be assessed is unclear.
\15\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate Oversight by the Secretary
Current law requires that the Secretary conduct interim reviews of grants to state entities to ensure a grant is being used appropriately and determine whether the full grant amount will be needed; based on that review, the Secretary may reduce or terminate the grant.\16\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate this oversight review.\17\
\16\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(d)(3).
\17\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
Research has shown that some CSP funds awarded to plan and open charter schools are used by entities that either never ultimately open a charter school or open a school and close it shortly thereafter.\18\ In fact, data has shown that charter schools close at a much higher rate than traditional public schools. More than 25 percent of charter schools close within five years of opening, and this increases to 49 percent within fifteen years of opening.\19\ According to then-Secretary of Education Betsy DeVos, from school year 2006-2007 to school year 2013-2014, $70,000,000 in CSP funding was provided to 634 charter schools that did not open or were not likely to open.\20\ More recently, from school year 2022-23 to school year 2023-24, there were 218 ``charter schools that closed or never opened.''\21\
\18\Peter Greene, Report: The Department Of Education Has Spent $1 Billion On Charter School Waste And Fraud, Forbes (Mar. 29, 2019), https://www.forbes.com/sites/petergreene/2019/03/29/report-the-department-of-education-has-spent-1-billion-on-charter-school-waste-and-fraud/; Network for Pub. Educ., Still Asleep at the Wheel: How the Federal Charter Schools Program Results in a Pileup of Fraud and Waste (rev. Jan. 2020), https://networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/ uploads/2025/06/Still-Asleep-at-the-Wheel.pdf; Nat'l Ctr. for Charter Sch. Accountability & Network for Pub. Educ., Doomed to Fail: An Analysis of Charter School Closures from 1998 to 2022 (Nov. 2024), https://networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/DTM- Final.pdf; Nat'l Ctr. for Charter Sch. Accountability & Network for Pub. Educ., Charter School Reckoning: Decline, Disillusionment and Cost, Part I: Decline (July 2025), https:// networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/Charter- School-Reckoning-FINAL-1.pdf.
\19\Doomed to Fail, supra note 18, at 2.
\20\Letter from the Honorable Betsy DeVos, Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Educ., responding to oversight request regarding the Charter Schools Program, to the Honorable Ral M. Grijalva, Member of Congress (June 28, 2019) (on file with the Comm. on Educ. and Workforce Min. Staff); see also Still Asleep at the Wheel, supra note 18, at 2 (stating that the numbers for that same time period are much higher--$502,468,123 was awarded to schools that never opened or opened and closed).
\21\Charter School Reckoning, supra note 18, at 6.
Charter schools generally close due to low enrollment (which impacts their funding directly) or fraud and mismanagement.\22\ Some charter supporters believe that ``school closures are considered a natural consequence of the marketplace model.''\23\ But failure at this alarmingly high rate has a substantial impact on students and their families. Unfortunately, this occurs even with the oversight included in current law. By removing this oversight provision, H.R. 7082 would open the door to further misuse of funds and harm to students and families.
\22\Still Asleep at the Wheel, supra note 18, at 26-27.
\23\Doomed to Fail, supra note 18, at 5.
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate State Entity Reporting and
Oversight
Current law requires that each state entity that receives a grant submit an interim and a final report to the Secretary.\24\ The law further delineates what must be included in the report, including: the number and amount of subgrants awarded; the number of students served by each subgrant as well as the number of new students served each year of the subgrant; and how the state entity met the objectives in its grant application.\25\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate the interim report.\26\ In so doing, it would eliminate the need for the state entity to conduct oversight of its subgrantees and report back to the Secretary as well as eliminate a tool the Secretary may use in its own evaluation of the state entity and determination of whether to reduce or terminate the state entity's grant. This provision of the bill would eradicate an entire chain of oversight and transparency.
\24\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(i).
\25\Id.
\26\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Emphasize Obligating Funds Quickly Over
Quality and Oversight of the Program
Current law permits the Secretary to award one grant at a time to any state entity.\27\ In contrast, H.R. 7082 would permit the Secretary to award additional grants as long as the funding for an existing grant has been obligated.\28\ This change would encourage state entities to obligate funding as quickly as possible in order to remove any barrier to receiving a new grant award. Combined with the elimination of the Secretary's oversight review of such grants, there is no mechanism to ensure responsible allocation and spending of a grant award.
\27\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(e)(1).
\28\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate Peer Review Quality Assurance

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: FLEX Act
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: Pursuant to current law, both applications for grants from the Secretary to a state applicant and applications for subgrants from states to eligible applicants must utilize a peer review process.\29\ H.R. 7082 would still require the Secretary to use the peer review process in evaluating grant applications by states, but states would no longer be required to utilize the peer review process in evaluating subgrant applications by eligible applicants.\30\ This would provide tremendous leeway to states when choosing subgrant recipients without the benefit of the critical, impartial, and knowledgeable quality control and standards of peer review.
\29\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(d)(2).
\30\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Weaken Requirements of Subgrant
Applications to State Entities
Current law requires state entities, in their application for a grant, to describe how the state entity will determine and award competitive subgrants, including how it will evaluate applications for subgrants and certain requirements that subgrant applications must include.\31\ H.R. 7082 would depart from this by permitting state entities to accept an application for becoming a charter school within the state ``in lieu of'' an application for a subgrant, as long as state laws for becoming a charter school are met.\32\ In other words, if state law requirements for becoming a charter are more lenient than the federal law requirements for a subgrant, then the federal requirements may be ignored. For example, federal law currently requires that applicants for subgrants describe how they will include parent and community input about the charter school; however, if a state does not require this, and it chooses to use an eligible applicant's application to be a charter school, then that requirement would no longer be necessary. This change would eliminate important aspects of subgrant applications, allow state laws to trump federal requirements that Congress deemed necessary to receive a subgrant, and create inconsistency in the application process across states.
\31\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(f)(1).
\32\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate Consistency in Planning
Current law permits subgrantees to use up to 18 months for planning purposes.\33\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate this and leave the amount of planning time up to each state, though it may not exceed two years.\34\ This would eliminate consistency in the program across states lines. Moreover, some management organizations operate in more than one state; therefore, it's possible that this change could potentially lead to inconsistency in their ability to plan accordingly.
\33\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(d)(1)(B).
\34\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Open the Door for Significant Additional
and Extended Expenditures
Current CSP law contains numerous provisions to help plan for, open a new, or replicate or expand a high-quality charter school, but federal funding for these supports is short term. This requires charter schools and management organizations to plan for alternative financial support in the long-term. H.R. 7082 would flip this model on its head. Current law permits subgrant funding to be used for hiring and compensation for teachers, school leaders, and specialized instructional support personnel during the planning period of the grant.\35\ H.R. 7082 would eradicate the limited time period and instead permits funding to be used for compensation throughout the grant period.\36\ Similarly, current law permits funding to be used for ``one-time, startup costs associated with providing transportation to students to and from the charter school.''\37\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate the restriction for ``one-time, startup,'' enabling funding to be used for transportation throughout the grant period.\38\ Current law also permits the use of funding for certain ``appropriate, non-sustained costs'' when funding is not otherwise available.\39\ H.R. 7082 would similarly jettison the limitation on the use of funds for those other costs.\40\
\35\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221b(h)(1)(B).
\36\H.R. 7082 Sec. 3, 119th Cong. (2026).

H.R. 7082 would also add a provision to allow subgrant funding to be used for ``necessary renovations, upgrades, or facilities repairs, or acquiring portable classrooms.''\41\ This would constitute an expansion of facilities language into the high-quality charter schools section of the program rather than the section devoted to facilities financing assistance. Facilities related spending can be costly, and there is no limit included in the new provision, so the funding could eat up the entire allocation for the high-quality charter schools section of the program. Furthermore, the use of portable classrooms raises questions about health and safety for students and teachers.\42\ H.R. 7082 would also add a provision that would permit funding for ``costs associated with operations and management of the charter school facility.''\43\ As written, it is unclear if this means the physical facility itself, or the entire existence of the charter school. Overall, these changes would establish a reliance on subgrant funding for the duration of the subgrant and would not require or even encourage charter schools or management organizations to plan for continuity and self-sustainment once the subgrant period ends, potentially exacerbating the existing problem of charter schools that either never open or open only to close shortly thereafter.
Changes to the National Activities Section of CSP May Lead to Greater
Waste, Fraud, and Abuse
H.R. 7082 Would Allow for Significantly Increased Funding for Charter
Management Organizations and the Potential for Waste, Fraud,
and Abuse
Currently, the bulk of funding under the national activities section of CSP flows to eligible entities, which are defined as charter management organizations--organizations that manage charter schools. H.R. 7082 would permit the Secretary to more than double the amount of funding that may be used for national activities, significantly increasing the amount of money these organizations may receive. This increase in funding to charter management organizations is problematic because of allegations and reports of waste, fraud, and abuse in CSP.
A2016 audit by the Department's Office of Inspector General (OIG) concluded that charter school relationships with charter management organizations lacked strong internal controls and oversight related to conflicts of interest, insufficient segregation of duties, and related-party transactions. This increased the risks of: lack of accountability of federal funds; waste, fraud, and abuse; and schools not providing students the services required by federal programs.\44\ Additionally, a 2022 OIG audit found that for CSP funds distributed between 2013 and 2016, grantees (including management organizations) opened or expanded only 51 percent of the schools promised and for which they received funding.\45\ Most recently, a 2023 OIG audit found that charter management organizations did not always address compliance issues relating ``to their uses of Replication and Expansion grant funds, fiscal control, and fund accounting'' and that charter schools ``with highly problematic applications'' still received millions of federal dollars from CSP.\46\ It is also worth noting that the National Center for Charter School Accountability recently reported identifying ``$858 million wasted due to fraud, theft, profiteering, or incompetence.\47\
\44\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Inspector Gen., Nationwide Assessment of Charter and Education Management Organizations--Final Audit Report at 2 (Sept. 2016), https://www.oversight.gov/sites/ default/files/oig-reports/a02m0012.pdf.
\45\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Inspector Gen., Effectiveness of Charter School Programs in Increasing the Number of Charter Schools at 3 (Sept. 21, 2022), https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/oig-reports/ED/FY22A21IL0034020724v100SECURED.pdf.

\47\Nat'l Ctr. for Charter Sch. Accountability and Network for Pub. Educ., Charter School Reckoning: Decline, Disillusionment and Cost, Part II: Disillusionment at 7 (Dec. 2025), https://networkforpubliceducation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/ Charter-School-Reckoning- Disillusionment.pdf.
H.R. 7082 would do nothing to address these problems, yet it would more than double the amount of funding that could go to charter management organizations, thereby increasing the potential scale of any waste, fraud, and abuse.
H.R. 7082 Would Reduce Understanding of the Overall Impact
of Charter Schools
Under current law, at least 11 percent of funding under national activities must be used for technical assistance, disseminating best practices, and evaluating the impact of CSP, including on student achievement.\48\ H.R. 7082 would reduce this amount to not more than ten percent.\49\ At the same time, the legislation would expand the allowable uses of those limited funds to include funding and financing for charter school facilities, early-stage charter school planning, and grants made by the Secretary to state entities.\50\ In so doing, the legislation would effectively eliminate any requirement that the funding be used to disseminate best practices or evaluate the impact of CSP, thus eliminating transparency about the health and effectiveness of the overall program.

H.R. 7082 Would Eliminate the Requirement to Plan for
Financial Sustainability
Under current law, an eligible entity applying for a grant under national activities must include in its application a description of how it will continue to sustain itself after the grant period is over, including a ``multi-year financial and operating model.''\51\ H.R. 7082 would eliminate the requirement for a multi-year model.\52\ This is yet another example of how the bill would provide charter school funding without incentivizing or even encouraging long term success and would further widen the door for school finance challenges and school closures.

<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: In determining grants under national activities, current law permits the Secretary to give priority to charter management organizations that: will serve racially and socioeconomically diverse student populations; have demonstrated success with schools needing comprehensive support and improvement; will use funds to expand or replicate high-quality charter high schools; or plan to focus on dropout recovery.\53\ All four of these priorities focus on students. In contrast, H.R. 7082 would add a priority for applications by charter management organizations that plan to enter a state in which they do not currently operate a charter school or a state ``with limited charter school options.''\54\ This priority demonstrates greater interest in expanding the management organization rather than in serving the students who need it most. Moreover, it is unclear what constitutes a state ``with limited charter school options''' or how that would be determined. Considering that charter school laws are determined by each state, this seems an odd interference by the federal government.
\53\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d(b)(5).
\54\H.R. 7082 Sec. 4, 119th Cong. (2026).
In addition, the fact that the bill slashes funding for high-quality charter schools in order to increase funding for charter management organizations does not consider that demand for CSP funding has declined in recent years. In 2024, the Biden Administration indicated that the demand for CSP funding to open and expand charter schools declined from 2019 to 2023, and that awards were reduced due to the inability to meet grantees' original targets.\55\ In 2023 2024, there were 8,010 charter schools.\56\ In 2024 2025, there were only 38 more (8,048).\57\ Still, President Trump's Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 budget proposal included a $60 million (14%) increase to CSP for a total of $500 million,\58\ and on May 16, 2025, Education Secretary McMahon announced that the Department would give CSP an additional $60 million in funding for FY 2025, unilaterally effectuating the President's request for that fiscal year.\59\ President Trump's FY 2027 budget again requests Congress to increase CSP funding to $500 million.\60\ Despite the dwindling demand for new charter schools, the need for funding across so many areas of education, and inflation that continues to outpace appropriations, this bill would take funding away from students and classrooms and instead give it to charter management organizations.

H.R. 7082 Would Negatively Alter Definitions and Applicability
H.R. 7082 Would Sow Confusion Regarding the Definition of
Charter School
Current law defines a charter school as ``a public school that provides a program of elementary or secondary education, or both.''\61\ H.R. 7082 would change the definition of a charter school to ``a public school that provides a program of elementary or secondary education (which may include other educational programs, pursuant to State law), or both.''\62\ The bill's language is confusing and its intent is unclear. Further, the new language could create inconsistency across states. For example, it is unclear if the new language is age related, so intended to permit, for example, early childhood education as part of a charter school (which is already permitted) or adult education or something else. Alternatively, it is unclear if the language is intended to be program specific, so intended to permit, for example, a school focused solely on a specific disability. This lack of a clear definition of what constitutes a charter school--the most fundamental definition necessary for this entire program-- exemplifies the lack of clarity and transparency found throughout the bill.
\61\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221i(2)(D).
\62\H.R. 7082 Sec. 7, 119th Cong. (2026) (emphasis added).
H.R. 7082 Would Allow Grantees to Decide When to Apply to
the Law
Rather than applying the changes to the law on or after the date of enactment should the legislation become law, H.R. 7082 would permit current grantees and subgrantees to decide whether they want the changes to apply to them.\63\ This would make applicability inconsistent and enable grantees and subgrantees to unilaterally self-elect to change the terms of their grant or subgrant contracts. In other words, this provision would leave it up to the states to decide whether to enact or enforce federal law and would make it impossible for the federal government to conduct its own responsibilities to implement the law and conduct oversight over a federal program and how federal taxpayer dollars are spent.
\63\H.R. 7082 Sec. 8, 119th Cong. (2026).
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING THE MARKUP OF H.R. 7082
Committee Democrats proffered three amendments to improve the bill. These amendments would have prohibited funding from being used for virtual charters schools, required charter funding applicants to assess segregation in the community and propose how to address it, and required a study to identify disparities and address discrimination of historically underrepresented students in and by charter schools. bill_title: Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027
content:
<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Grace Meng>: Pursuant to the provisions of clause 3(a)(1) of House rule XIII and sec. 6(i) of the Committee Rules, the dissenting views of the minority party of the House of Representatives, are printed below:
We appreciate Chairman Rogers's efforts this year as chair of the Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS) Subcommittee, including the hard work that has gone into the crafting of this appropriations bill. However, the harsh reality is that this bill does not fulfill the very real needs of the American people across a wide range of critical areas, including crime prevention; job creation; efforts to ensure fair trade; the advancement of American innovation and climate science research; and much more. Therefore, we must strongly oppose this bill in its current form.
This bill defunds law enforcement by gutting the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) by more than 25 percent, forcing the agency to lose more than 1,000 law enforcement personnel nationwide. The bill also includes numerous harmful policy riders designed to further impede the efforts of law enforcement officers to fight gun violence, including a rider that completely shuts down the enforcement of all ATF measures, regulations, or guidance issued or finalized between January 2021 and January 2025. This will inevitably result in more illegal firearms trafficking, more guns falling into the hands of dangerous criminals, and more victims of gun violence in both large and small communities across our country.
Handicapping the ATF will also further burden our State and local law enforcement officers, who rely on their ATF counterparts to help them keep communities safe from gun violence.
In this bill, grants for local communities to prevent and respond to juvenile delinquency are also cut by $50 million below the current level. The bill further eliminates funding for Community Violence Intervention and Prevention grants and several other grants aimed at keeping communities safe.
Working Americans are facing a cost-of-living crisis that is only worsening. Yet the Majority's bill slashes funding for Economic Development Administration grants by 36 percent below the current level. These grants help create jobs and economic opportunity, improve public infrastructure, and ultimately help revitalize communities facing decline and disinvestment throughout our nation, particularly in rural areas. The bill also guts funding for the International Trade Administration. This will negatively impact the American economy in two ways:
(1) by reducing the agency's capacity to promote the expansion of U.S. exports, and (2) by degrading the agency's efforts to fight the unfair trade practices of other countries.
Perhaps most shortsighted of all, this bill makes deep cuts to the scientific research that drives American innovation, technological leadership, and economic competitiveness. At a time when other countries are increasing scientific investment to compete in the global economy, this bill cuts the National Science Foundation by more than $1.7 billion, sharply reducing cutting-edge American research and abandoning the next generation of scientists and engineers. NASA's Science account is cut by more than $1.3 billion, including a massive cut of $828 million (38 percent) to Earth Science, and NASA's Aeronautics research account is cut by $85 million, or 9 percent. The bill also makes massive cuts to the programs of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, which has helped American industry overcome technical challenges, innovate manufacturing, and work on the cutting edge of emerging technologies.
This bill also irresponsibly ignores the reality of global warming and the need for the United States to lead efforts to advance humanity's scientific understanding of climate change and our ability to prepare for, respond to, and mitigate its impacts. Such research also helps improve future weather forecasting, as carefully studying and tracking changes in the climate helps scientists better understand and predict the range of possible weather extremes, including the influence of the changing climate on extreme weather events such as hurricanes, wildfires, and flooding. In addition to the bill's huge cut to NASA Earth Science, the bill cuts funding for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)'s Climate Laboratories and Cooperative Institutes by 11 percent and cuts NOAA's Competitive Climate Research program by 23 percent.
As noted in a September 2023 report by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, ``climate change already imposes substantial financial costs on communities across the United States.'' According to NOAA, in 2024, the United States experienced 27 weather and climate disasters costing at least $1 billion each, totaling $182.7 billion. (The current Administration has unacceptably directed NOAA to discontinue compiling this statistic). In every decade since the 1980s, the average annual cost of these disasters has increased. Increasingly frequent extreme weather events disrupt crop yields, displace people from their homes, burden emergency service systems, and destroy critical infrastructure. However, the funding cuts in this bill turn a blind eye to this reality and will damage our capacity to improve the scientific understanding of our planet and its changes. This, in turn, will weaken our ability to protect the health and safety of Americans from climate change.
Within the NOAA program table, we also note with disappointment that the Majority is once again proposing to remove the name of former Representative Jose Serrano from NOAA's Educational Partnership Program with Minority Serving Institutions--in addition to sharply cutting this program's funding. Representative Serrano served for more than 30 years in Congress and was a distinguished former chair of the CJS Subcommittee.
The bill undermines efforts to promote justice and opportunity for all Americans. Besides gutting the Legal Services Corporation, which provides basic civil legal aid to the poorest American families, seniors, and veterans, the bill also drastically cuts funding for the Minority Business Development Agency and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The Community Relations Service, which for more than 60 years has worked honorably to help mediate and end community conflicts across our country, is eliminated in this bill. Despite historically high levels of hate crimes recorded by the FBI, this bill eliminates DOJ programs aimed at preventing and prosecuting hate crimes. Furthermore, the bill prohibits funding for agency programs focused on diversity, equity, and inclusion.
The bill's funding level for the Census Bureau is very inadequate, especially as the Bureau must ramp up efforts in fiscal year 2027 to prepare for the 2027 Economic Census, the 2030 Decennial Census, and other census surveys. The bill also includes policy riders that would lower the quality of census surveys and implement an unconstitutional change to Census Bureau apportionment count procedures.
Furthermore, the bill continues the Majority's attacks on women's health and safety by barring funding for: (1) DOJ's Reproductive Rights Task Force, (2) enforcement of certain protections for women in the workplace, and (3) litigation against States or local governments over laws that limit access to abortion.
There are many additional harmful and irresponsible policy riders contained in this bill that must be removed, including riders impacting fisheries restoration, federal employee unions, and much more.
Last, but not least, we note that the lawless behavior of the current Administration requires that efforts be undertaken to ensure transparency and accountability. With that in mind, we are deeply distressed that this bill discontinues the requirement enacted in the Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2025 and 2026 that agency spend plans must contain the same level of detail as provided in the spend plans for fiscal year 2024. We believe that the Appropriations Committee has a serious and vital duty to ensure transparency in the spending of taxpayer dollars, and removal of this provision is a dereliction of duty.
These and other issues must be addressed before this bill is enacted into law, and we stand ready to help improve the CJS appropriations bill for fiscal year 2027 in conference.
Rosa DeLauro.
Grace Meng.

bill_title: Making appropriations for the Legislative Branch for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
content:
<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Adriano Espaillat>: We appreciate the efforts of Chairman Valadao and his staff in producing the Fiscal Year 2027 Legislative Branch bill. While the bill incorporates several Democratic priorities, it ultimately fails to adequately fund the needs of the Legislative Branch and includes a partisan policy rider that undermines Congress's constitutional responsibilities and institutional independence.
The interim allocation for the Legislative Branch totals $7.3 billion, slightly more than one-half of one percent above the Fiscal Year 2026 enacted level. Consistent with longstanding practice, under which each chamber determines its own housekeeping requirements and the other concurs without intervention, the House bill does not include funding for the Senate or Senate office buildings. Excluding Senate items, the bill provides $5.4 billion, which is $125 million, or 2.2 percent, below the Fiscal Year 2026 enacted level and $1.2 billion below the budget request.
These funding levels are insufficient to meet the operational and infrastructure needs of the Legislative Branch. With such a constrained allocation, the bill fails to adequately fund critical projects managed by the Architect of the Capitol that are necessary to address the deterioration of House office buildings and broader campus infrastructure. Delaying these investments will only increase long-term costs and further jeopardize the safety, functionality, and preservation of the Capitol complex.
The funding levels, combined with the inclusion of the partisan policy rider in section 116, are unworkable, and Democrats cannot support the legislation as drafted. Most notably, the bill proposes nearly a 25 percent cut to the Government Accountability Office (GAO).
Weakening GAO weakens Congress's ability to hold the Executive Branch accountable and ensure taxpayer dollars are spent as intended. The proposed reduction would force GAO to eliminate more than 1,000 positions, severely undermining the workforce responsible for audits, investigations, and oversight conducted on behalf of Congress.
The Committee considered an amendment that would have struck section 116, a provision restricting GAO's ability to bring independent civil actions under the Impoundment Control Act of 1974 unless Congress first adopts a concurrent resolution authorizing such action. The amendment failed.
The inclusion of this provision undermines Congress's constitutional oversight authority by limiting GAO's longstanding independent enforcement role under the Impoundment Control Act, authority that has existed for more than fifty years and was reaffirmed by Congress following the Supreme Court's decision in Bowsher v. Synar. These concerns are particularly significant given GAO's ongoing investigations into whether the Administration unlawfully withheld fiscal year 2025 appropriated funds. At a time when strong oversight is essential, the bill both weakens GAO's enforcement authority and proposes nearly a 25 percent cut to the agency responsible for identifying waste, fraud, abuse, and unlawful executive actions across the federal government.
The bill also reflects the Majority's refusal to adopt amendments to prohibit certain judgment fund payments to elected officials and to permit Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients to receive compensation as employees of the Legislative Branch.
The Legislative Branch bill should not be used to weaken Congress's oversight capacity or undermine the independence of the institutions that support its constitutional responsibilities. Instead, this legislation should provide the resources necessary for Congress to function effectively as a coequal branch of government, conduct meaningful oversight, safeguard the Capitol complex, and serve the American people. Because this bill fails to meet those standards, Democrats cannot support the legislation as drafted.
Rosa DeLauro.
Adriano Espaillat.

bill_title: Energy and Water Development and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027
content:
<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Marcy Kaptur>: Due to concerns about spending levels, harmful cuts to the clean energy economy and programs meant to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, and partisan policy riders, we are unable to support the bill as written. The bill will make energy more expensive, from gasoline to electricity for homes and businesses, while families struggle to keep up with the rising cost of living. It will set us back, decreasing our investments in energy technologies of the future, while our adversaries race ahead. It will jeopardize national security by weakening our efforts to stop the spread of nuclear weapons. And it will leave our communities vulnerable to radioactive waste leftover from our nation's atomic weapons program.
U.S. energy independence in perpetuity is an imperative. Respect for Mother Earth must be our North Star. Our citizenry suffers from rising costs for transportation, fuel, heating, electricity, and so much more. Energy is woven deeply into all of these. The bill does not address these problems. In fact, it will make many of them worse.
America cannot remain energy vulnerable. We need broad innovation, and we need competition and investment across the broad range of the energy sector. Yet this bill cuts investments that support the production of new energy.
To reach bipartisan agreement, funding levels and provisions require adjustments. First, we must revise balances of top line funding for defense and non-defense spending. The bill increases defense programs by $774 million, or 2 percent, while non-defense programs are cut by $1.8 billion, or 6 percent. We cannot cede our future to the past. This imbalance needs correction so that domestic energy and water programs are enhanced. Our citizenry wants a secure energy future, not captivity.
We must address the most harmful cuts in the bill. The bill guts funding for the Department of Energy's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation program by $1.3 billion, or 40 percent. This slows us down while our adversaries race ahead in the contest for energy independence by investing in clean energy and efficiency. It looks backwards as our competitors are pressing forwards. And by limiting the amount of new energy we can produce, it ensures costs will not come down anytime soon.
To meet the challenges of the future, we need to be creative. We need to innovate, conduct research, and find solutions to problems before they erupt into crises. Yet this bill proposes cutting funding for the Advanced Research Projects Agency--Energy by $50 million, or 14 percent.
With energy prices rising, a $25 million cut for the Department of Energy's electricity and grid deployment programs harms our ability to modernize our aging grid and to drive down electricity prices.
This bill threatens our national security by cutting funding for the Nuclear National Security Administration's Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation account by $282 million, or 12 percent. This hampers our efforts to track down, secure, and dispose of material that can be used to develop a nuclear weapon. We cannot retreat as nuclear threats increase globally.
Additionally, this bill would put our communities at risk by impeding the cleanup of radioactive waste left over from America's atomic weapons development. This bill includes total elimination of funding for the Army Corps' Formerly Utilized Sites Remedial Action Program and cuts the Department of Energy's Office of Environmental Management by $863 million, or 10 percent. This slows down cleaning up nuclear contamination across this country.
Critically, this bill should only repurpose Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act funds through bipartisan agreement embracing an all-of-the-above energy strategy. That means supporting a diverse portfolio of daunting technologies like geothermal, electric grid upgrades, fusion, and advanced nuclear.
The bill must be free of controversial policy riders. Glaringly, the bill is missing key provisions necessary to protect Congress' power of the purse. Any bipartisan bill must prevent and reverse the Department of Energy's project terminations, and the bill should require transparency and accountability for federal spending.
At a time when Americans are struggling to navigate rapidly rising costs; when our adversaries are increasing their investments in the future; and when our communities remain burdened by the hazardous remnants of atomic weapons; this bill fails to meet the moment. We must work on a bipartisan basis to craft an agreement that supports our communities, protects national security, and invests in the future. We know we must work together to meet the new frontiers of energy and water.
Rosa L. DeLauro.
Marcy Kaptur.

bill_title: Student Aid Fraud Oversight and Accountability Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 7891, the Student Aid Fraud Oversight and Accountability Act of 2026, amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA) to codify an expedited program review and investigation process for institutions of higher education that disburse federal student aid. The bill would give the Department of Education (Department) the power to initiate this process if a school disbursed federal aid to a student whose application for aid presented ``a reasonable suspicion of identity fraud.''\1\ The bill would work in conjunction with H.R. 7892, the No Aid for Ghost Students Act of 2026, which requires the Department to establish an identity fraud detection system within the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) process.\2\ While, in theory, the framework proposed under these bills may help mitigate identity fraud in student aid, Committee Democrats have concerns around the necessity of the legislation and potential weaponization new oversight mechanisms to target specific institutions. At the time this bill was marked up, Ranking Member Bobby Scott (D-VA) was committed to work with the Majority to perfect the language of H.R. 7891 before it was brought to the floor and voted to report it out of Committee. Subsequently, that negotiation process stalled, and these views outline the problems with the bill as drafted.
\1\Student Aid Fraud Oversight and Accountability Act of 2026, H.R. 7981, 119th Cong. (2026).
\2\No Aid for Ghost Students Act of 2026, H.R. 7982, 119th Cong.
(2026).
IDENTITY FRAUD IN FEDERAL STUDENT AID
It is critical for Office of Federal Student Aid (FSA) to prevent any waste, fraud, and abuse of the federal student aid system. One rising challenge within the student aid system is the increase number of individuals enrolling specifically to commit fraud. In most cases, these individuals, often referred to as ``ghost students'',\3\ are fraudulent applicants that enroll using fake or stolen identities and obtain federal student aid, including Pell Grants, with no intention of attending classes or earning a degree. These students ``use their access to register for low-cost classes and apply for grants only to withdraw upon receipt of tuition reimbursement.''\4\
\3\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of the Inspector Gen., Glossary--Ghost Students-Higher Education, https://oig.ed.gov/taxonomy/term/146.
\4\Jeremy Green & James Densley, Pell Grant Fraud Awareness: White- Collar Crime Challenges, FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin, Fed. Bur. of Investigation (Feb. 4, 2014), https://leb.fbi.gov/articles/featured-articles/pell-grant-fraud-awareness-white-collar-crime-challenges.
Over the past several years, these fraudulent activities have been traced to fraud rings targeting institutions, primarily targeting low-cost community colleges and distance education programs due to their lower barriers of access.\5\ Institutions have reported that some of these fraudulent individuals are using artificial intelligence and bots to pose as real students.\6\ For example, the California Community College system has reported several instances where individuals used AI and bots to submit FAFSAs for nonexistent students. The individuals were disbursed student aid under these fake identities, and then disappeared with the funds, leaving no ties to their actual identities. These schemes divert federal student aid from legitimate students and have forced institutions to use additional resources to identify and prevent fraudulent enrollment and improve their identity verification processes.\7\
\5\Sara Weissman, California Community Colleges Battle Against the Bots, Inside Higher Ed (May 23, 2025), https://www.insidehighered.com/ news/institutions/community-colleges/2025/05/23/calif-community-colleges-ramp-battle-against-bots; Sharon Lurye, How scammers are using AI to steal college financial aid, Associated Press (Jun. 10, 2025), https://apnews.com/article/ai-scam-college-financial-aid-identity-theft-aa1bc8bcb4c368ee6bafcf6a523c5fb2.
\6\How scammers are using AI to steal college financial aid, Identity Theft Resource Center (Jan. 5, 2026), https:// www.idtheftcenter.org/post/ai-steal-college-financial-aid/.
\7\Weissman, supra note 5.
ONGOING FRAUD DETECTION AND PREVENTION EFFORTS
Federal law enforcement, including the Department's Office of Inspector General (OIG), have been aware of these matters for many years and have taken a variety of actions to address the issue.\8\ For example, the OIG noted in its most recent Semiannual Report to Congress,
\8\See e.g., U.S. Dep't of Educ. Off. of Inspector Gen., Title IV of the Higher Education Act Programs: Additional Safeguards Are Needed to Help Mitigate the Risks That Are Unique to the Distance Education Environment (Feb. 2014), https://oig.ed.gov/sites/default/files/ reports/2024-05/a07l0001.pdf; U.S. Dep't of Educ. Off. of Inspector Gen., Final Management Information Report: Student Aid Fraud Ring Assessment (Jan. 17, 2013), https://oig.ed.gov/sites/default/files/ reports/2024-04/x18m0001.pdf; U.S. Dep't of Educ. Off. of Inspector Gen., Investigative Program Advisory Report: Distance Education Fraud Rings (Sep. 26, 2011), https://oig.ed.gov/sites/default/files/reports/ 2023-06/l42l0001.pdf.
Prosecutive actions were taken against the leaders
and participants in student aid fraud rings that
targeted millions in Federal student aid, including the
arrest of 2 people for allegedly running separate 10-
year schemes in Michigan involving more than 1,200
people, 100 schools in 24 States, and more than $12
million in Federal student aid. Additionally, a 5-year
prison sentence was handed down for the leader of a
North Carolina-based ring who recruited approximately
80 people to participate in the scam that targeted more
than $5 million in Federal student aid.\9\
\9\U.S. Dep't of Educ. Off. of Inspector Gen., Semiannual Report to Congress, No. 91, ii (Feb. 17, 2026), https://oig.ed.gov/sites/default/ files/reports/2026-02/FY25%20SAR%2091%20%282.17. 26%29v101_508_SECURED.pdf.
The OIG has also produced materials aimed at informing the public on this issue\10\ and has provided resources to help financial aid administrators identify and stop fraud rings.\11\
\10\See e.g. U.S. Dep't of Educ. Off. of Inspector Gen., Eye on ED Podcast--Episode 12 Student Aid Fraud Rings (Sep. 30, 2024), https:// oig.ed.gov/sites/default/files/document/2024-09/ fy24_student_aid_fraud_podcast_transcript_9.30.24v100_508.pdf.
\11\U.S. Dep't of Educ. Off. of Inspector Gen., Student Aid Administrators: Help Spot and Stop Student Aid Fraud Rings, (updated Sep. 2024), https://oig.ed.gov/sites/default/files/document/2024-09/ fy24_identify_and_stop_student_aid_fraud_ring_info_sheet_8.27.24v100_508 _ secured.pdf.
Efforts Under the Biden Administration
Despite the Trump Administration claiming the Biden Administration ``created a prime opportunity for fraudsters to exploit the [FAFSA] process,'' the Department has consistently worked to mitigate fraud while trying to decrease verification burdens for institutions. On December 27, 2020, Congress passed the FAFSA Simplification Act,\12\ which streamlined the federal student aid application process. One key provision of the Act required the Department ``to the maximum extent practicable, streamline and simplify the process of verification for applicants.''\13\ In July of 2021, recognizing the need to address fraud prevention while responding to the unique challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic, ``the Department issued a waiver of certain verification requirements in order to provide relief to students and colleges facing challenges resulting from the COVID-19 emergency while retaining a strict focus on identity and fraud. In accordance with that policy, requirements remain for institutions to verify identity.''\14\ Financial aid officers and student aid stakeholders supported this decision because ``too many vulnerable students were flagged for verification in the standard process, which yielded little evidence of fraud. They argued that focusing on identity theft, which requires a different form of verification, made more sense.''\15\ In July 2024, the Department announced further verification rate reductions, in an effort to continue reducing institutional burdens by leveraging partnerships with the IRS for income verification processes.\16\ The Department emphasized this was done to ``more effectively target verification efforts'' to identity verification.\17\
\12\Pub. L. No. 116 260, Title VII, Div. FF (2020).
\13\20 U.S.C. Sec. 1090(b)(6).
\14\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Fed. Stud. Aid, Electronic Announcement, Reminder--Identity Verfiication (Sep. 2, 2021), https:// fsapartners.ed.gov/knowledge-center/library/electronic-announcements/2021-09-02/reminder-identity-verification-ea-id-general- 21-54.
\15\Danielle Douglas-Gabriel, Students applying for financial aid will face stricter ID verification, The Wash. Post (Jun. 6, 2025), https://www.washingtonpost.com/education/2025/06/06/student-aid-identification-verification-requirements-change/; see Press Release, Nat'l Assn of Stud. Fin. Aid Admins., NASFAA Statement on 2021-22 Verification Changes (July 13, 2021), https://www.nasfaa.org/ nasfaa_statement_on_2021-22_verification_changes.

\17\Id.
Efforts Under the Trump Administration
Admittedly, the Trump Administration has taken several steps to build on the ongoing fraud prevention efforts. In June 2025, the Department announced that it would ``require institutions of higher education to validate the identity of certain first-time applicants . . .'' and required an applicant to ``present, either in person or on a live video conference, an unexpired, valid, government-issued photo identification to an institutionally authorized individual and the institution must preserve a copy of this documentation.''\18\ In response, advocates highlighted the importance of fighting against fraud and abuse, but emphasized that there must be a stronger balance between that and student access and burden on under-resourced schools.\19\ In December 2025, the Department claimed that their recent efforts ``halted more than $1 billion in attempted financial aid theft by fraudsters, including coordinated international fraud rings and AI bots pretending to be students.''\20\
\18\Press Release, U.S. Dep't of Educ., U.S. Department of Education to Implement New Identity Validation Processes to Combat Student Aid Fraud (Jun. 6, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-implement-new-identity-validation-processes-combat-student-aid-fraud.
\19\Douglas-Gabriel, supra note 15 (``Protecting against fraud and abuse is important, but must be balanced against access,' said Elizabeth Morgan, chief external relations officer for the nonprofit National College Attainment Network. `Barriers that delay students' ability to receive aid could harm their ability to attain a postsecondary degree.'').
\20\Press Release, U.S. Dep't of Educ., U.S. Department of Education Prevents More Than $1 Billion in Federal Student Aid Fraud This Year, Additional Crackdowns Expected in 2026, (Dec. 11, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-prevents-more-1-billion-federal-student-aid-fraud-year-additional-crackdowns-expected-2026.

content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott>: Last month, the Trump Administration launched a new fraud prevention framework built into the FAFSA process.\21\ Starting with the 2026 2027 FAFSA cycle, FSA will implement a new screening technology embedded into the FAFSA that places applicants into various risk categories, to help target verification efforts.\22\ This framework will be launched ``in coordination'' with the newly launched White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.\23\ Again, the Department estimates these upcoming efforts will prevent over $1 billion in federal student aid fraud.\24\
\21\Press Release, U.S. Dep't of Educ., U.S. Department of Education Launches Comprehensive, Nationwide Federal Student Aid Fraud Prevention Effort (Apr. 27, 2026), https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-launches-comprehensive-nationwide-federal-student-aid-fraud-prevention-effort.
\22\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Fed. Stud. Aid, Electronic Announcement, FAFSA Real-Time Fraud Detection (Apr. 15, 2026), https:// fsapartners.ed.gov/knowledge-center/library/electronic-announcements/ 2026-04-15/fafsa-real-time-fraud-detection.
\23\Id; Exec. Order No. 14395, 91 Fed. Reg. 13485 (2026).
\24\Press Release, U.S. Dep't of Educ., U.S. Department of Education Launches Comprehensive, Nationwide Federal Student Aid Fraud Prevention Effort (Apr. 27, 2026), https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-launches-comprehensive-nationwide-federal-student-aid-fraud-prevention-effort.
H.R. 7891 ESTABLISHES BROAD ENFORCEMENT MECHANISM WITH LOW TRIGGER
H.R. 7891 establishes an oversight and enforcement mechanism to hold institutions accountable for disbursing aid to fraudulent applicants. Specifically, it would give the Secretary broad authority to prioritize for a program review\25\ any institution that makes a single disbursement of federal student aid funds to any one student whose application the Department flags as having a ``reasonable suspicion of identity fraud'' that cannot be verified as a real student via the mechanisms proposed in H.R. 7892.\26\ In addition to triggering a program review, the bill alarmingly authorizes the Secretary to use any finding of improper disbursement to also inform ``audits, investigations, and other oversight activities'' authorized under title IV of the Higher Education Act. Since the focus of discussion on this legislation during the markup was around the prioritization of program reviews, it is unclear why such broad discretion for investigations and oversight activities is also necessary. Without more clarity, Democrats cannot support the proposed codification of an expanded review process that would vest the power to open widespread federal investigations, which would include subpoena power,\27\ and broad, unspecified oversight activities to the Secretary's discretion with little underlying evidence.
\25\For details on program review process, see U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Fed. Stud. Aid, 2025 2026 Federal Student Aid Handbook, Ch. 8-- Program Reviews, Sanctions, & Closeout, https://fsapartners.ed.gov/ knowledge-center/fsa-handbook/2025-2026/vol2/ch8-program-reviews-sanctions-closeout.
\26\No Aid for Ghost Students Act of 2026, H.R. 7982, 119th Cong.
(2026).
\27\20 U.S.C. Sec. 1097a.
Institutions undergoing scheduled program reviews typically have ample opportunity to review and respond to any claims or allegations of wrongdoing, and the penalties are typically expressly indicated for each violation.\28\ However, H.R. 7891 remains silent as to whether these same protocols will be applied if institutions are subjected to snap investigations based on as little as a single improper aid disbursement. This is especially troubling considering the inherent suggestion these powers are being granted to help the Department expose suspected fraud and wrongdoing. Some stakeholders even argue that ``the Committee's drafting of [this] language deliberately bypassed the typical safeguards afforded to colleges, because it was inserted to avoid the protections contained in existing law (Section 498A(b) [of the HEA])''\29\ and the new authorities ``go far, far beyond any power granted to a previous Secretary of Education to withhold financial aid to specific institutions.''\30\
\28\See 34 C.F.R Part 668 Subpart H (updated May 14, 2026); See U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of Fed. Stud. Aid, 2025-2026 Federal Student Aid Handbook, Ch. 8--Program Reviews, Sanctions, & Closeout, https:// fsapartners.ed.gov/knowledge-center/fsa-handbook/2025-2026/vol2/ch8-program-reviews-sanctions-closeout.
\29\Bryce McKibben & Michael H. Gavin, The Hidden Power Grab in ``Fraud Prevention''--and the Students Who Will Pay, Hope Ctr. For Stud. Basic Needs (Apr. 29, 2026), https://hope.temple.edu/newsroom/ hope-blog/hidden-power-grab-fraud-prevention-students-who-will-pay.
\30\Id.
Further, this process envisioned in H.R. 7891 threatens to directly conflict with the directives of the FAFSA Simplification Act to reduce the verification burdens and hurdles for institutions. Since any of the enforcement mechanisms in H.R. 7891 could be triggered after just one improper disbursement; something as innocuous as a clerical error could trigger a hasty compliance review that could risk a school's Title IV eligibility. Stakeholders have urged Congress to instead calibrate the review triggers to ``actual patterns of institutional noncompliance'',\31\ reasoning that ``[a]n isolated disbursement error shouldn't land an institution on a prioritized program review list--and certainly not subject them to a limitless audit or investigation.''\32\ Other higher education stakeholders also argue that ``this bill is likely to have a disproportional impact on community colleges and other open access [colleges] since they have been a key target for fraud''\33\ and also typically have to navigate smaller operating budgets.\34\
\31\Id.
\32\Id.
\33\Nat'l Coll. Attainment Network, Three Federal Student Aid Bills Slated for Markup (Mar. 16, 2026), https://www.ncan.org/Web/News/ 722348.aspx.
\34\Victoria Yuen, The $78 Billion Community College Funding Shortfall, Ctr. for Amer. Prog. (Oct. 7, 2020), https:// www.americanprogress.org/article/78-billion-community-college-funding-shortfall/.
During the markup, Ranking Member Scott offered an amendment to narrow the review trigger to institutions that display a pattern of disbursing student aid to fraudulent applicants and to allow institutions an opportunity to correct any mistakes. This amendment was withdrawn after the Majority and Minority publicly discussed working together to properly tailor the enforcement mechanisms before the bill reached the House Floor. Unfortunately, discussions to create enforcement mechanisms agreeable to both sides were not productive. Without narrowing the scope of enforcement strictly to existing program reviews or giving institutions a chance to provide additional information prior to triggering noncompliance status, H.R. 7891 creates unnecessary risks to upsetting the administration of federal student aid for too many students.
H.R. 7891 IS TOO BROAD TO NARROWLY DETECT IDENTITY FRAUD
H.R. 7891 establishes a new term, ``reasonable suspicion of identity fraud,'' that is not currently utilized in higher education statutes or regulations. Reasonable suspicion is a legal evidentiary standard stronger than simple speculation but lower than probable cause necessary to support a search warrant.\35\ Generally reasonable suspicion requires law enforcement to present specific and articulable facts beyond a ``hunch'' to justify a search.\36\ H.R. 7981 does not include any definition of ``reasonable suspicion of identity fraud'' to clarify how this standard will operate in the identity fraud verification setting. Following from the common law concept of reasonable suspicion, it is foreseeable that H.R. 7891 could be interpreted as giving the Secretary fairly broad power to identify institutions for potential investigations and program reviews since the standard for determining if an application presents a reasonable suspicion of identity fraud would be relatively low.
\35\Cassandra J. Barnum & Peter G. Berris, Cong. Rsch. Serv., IF13169, Fourth Amendment Search Warrant Requirements (2026).
\36\E.g. Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1, 27 (1968) (``And in determining whether the officer acted reasonably in such circumstances, due weight must be given not to his inchoate and unparticularized suspicion or ``hunch,'' but to the specific reasonable inferences which he is entitled to draw from the facts in light of his experience.).
However, other language of the bill suggests that the Department will interpret ``reasonable suspicion'' well past the bounds of common law. The bill text suggests the Department may identify for further investigation any institution that does not require live or video identity verification for students the Department considers to under reasonable suspicion of identity fraud. This is because the bill allows an institution to avoid this reasonable suspicion framework entirely if it
``demonstrates to the Secretary that, with respect to
each such student, before the disbursement of Federal
financial aid to the student, the institution, in
accordance with procedures established by the
Secretary, determined that a reasonable suspicion of
identity fraud was not present by confirming the
identity of such student using in-person verification
or live, synchronous audiovisual verification and
notified the Secretary that the identity of the student
has been verified, and maintains a record of such
identity verification.''\37\
\37\Student Aid Fraud Oversight and Accountability Act of 2026, H.R. 7981, 119th Cong. (2026) (emphasis added).
While the identity fraud detection system that will determine how the Department establishes reasonable suspicion is not the subject of this bill, that is moot from the perspective of an institution. H.R. 7891 will greatly incentivize institutions to implement in-person or audiovisual verification for all students at some point prior to disbursement of funds.
During the markup, Democrats expressed that, consistent with established law, ``reasonable suspicion'' should be a standard based on specific, articulable facts to prevent any administration from being able to target specific institutions or student populations due to concerns unrelated to identity fraud. Some stakeholders urged Congress to ensure ``such powers cannot be weaponized against perceived political enemies-- perhaps a state or college that isn't politically aligned with the Administration.''\38\
\38\McKibben & Gavin, supra note 29.
To successfully implement the proposed verification framework, we believe the definition of reasonable suspicion must be narrowed to protect institutions and student populations from being politically targeted due to founded or unfounded concerns unrelated to identity fraud and to mitigate longstanding concerns about the impact of verification on real students flagged for additional reviews. Ranking Member Scott also offered an amendment to narrow the definition of ``reasonable suspicion of identity fraud.'' This amendment was withdrawn after Members of the Majority and Minority publicly discussed working together to establish a narrow and articulable standard of reasonable suspicion before the bill reaches the House Floor.
H.R. 7891 COULD BE WEAPONIZED TO ADVANCE THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S
ATTACKS ON POLITICAL ENEMIES

CONCLUSION
It is critical to protect federal student aid from waste, fraud, and abuse, including identity fraud by ghost students and fraud rings. Due to the severity of this issue, Congress must work closely and thoughtfully with a wide range of stakeholders to ensure narrow fraud enforcement, decrease institutional verification burdens, and support students flagged for verification.
The majority of Committee Democrats supported H.R. 7891 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on March 17, 2026, under the condition of addressing the concerns discussed in these views. As those negotiations produced no meaningful changes to the bill text, we cannot support this bill on the floor in its current form. Given the ongoing politicization of federal fraud prevention efforts and broad enforcement authority, we have concerns with how the Trump Administration may further weaponize federal student aid laws to unfairly target students or institutions. We urge the House of Representatives to oppose H.R. 7891 unless there is a significant narrowing of enforcement authority, adjustments to the program review trigger, and wider consultation of higher education stakeholders.
