committee_name: House Committee on Ways and Means
bill_title: Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act
content:
<Rep. Richard E. Neal>: Ways and Means Democrats have long supported improving opportunities for Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) beneficiaries who wish to explore a return to work. To advance this goal, Congress has previously granted the Social Security Administration (SSA) with time-limited demonstration authority to test improvements to its return-to-work policies and services. Prior demonstration projects have explored many options including enhanced education and work supports, increased access to health care, and earnings limits that were more favorable than under current law. In some projects, this led to improved health outcomes and mental health status, greater rates of employment, and higher earnings; however, none of the findings showed that the demonstrations tested would likely lead to a substantial reduction in SSDI participation or savings to the Social Security trust funds.
Yet during his first Administration, President Trump repeatedly proposed using SSA's demonstration authorities to slash disability benefits by approximately $50 billion over 10 years. President Trump's attempts to impose devastating cuts on SSDI beneficiaries did not stop there. During his first term, his budgets included long lists of hoped-for SSDI benefit cuts, and his Administration proposed a rule that would have thrown people of Social Security disability benefits by subjecting them to more frequent continuing disability reviews. As recently as 2025, the Trump Administration was considering a rule to strip away Social Security disability benefits from older, severely disabled workers by making it harder to qualify for benefits. The Administration only pulled back from these and other planned benefit cuts after massive public outcry and strong opposition by Ways and Means Democrats.
It is with this lens that we are forced to consider H.R. 8884, the Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act, which proposes to reauthorize the SSDI demonstration authority through 2030.
In the past, prior to any reauthorization of the SSDI demonstration authority SSA typically worked with Congress to closely review its intended projects; this ensured that the planned use of the authority was well-understood before enactment. In contrast, at this time SSA has not disclosed any information on how it would use the SSDI demonstration authority, if reauthorized under H.R. 8884. While Ways and Means Republicans have cited the Purple Heart Freedom to Work Act (H.R. 1841) as an example of a potentially beneficial use of the authority, H.R. 8884 does not commit SSA to testing this or any other specific plan. Instead, the bill leaves the SSDI demonstration project(s) open-ended, for the Trump Administration to determine.
At the same time, H.R. 8884 fails to add sufficient guardrails that could address concerns about what the Trump Administration might do with such broad authority, given its track record of repeated attempts at sweeping benefit cuts. For example, while participation in demonstrations would remain voluntary (as under current law), the bill does not protect participants against demonstrations that could result in their benefits being reduced compared to current law. Instead, the amendment in the nature of a substitute prevents an individual's total income from being reduced due to participation. Under this provision, beneficiaries could have lower benefits than under current law, and applicants who would be found eligible under current law could have even fewer protections against claim delays or denials of their benefit claims. In addition, while H.R. 8884 extends the window for Congressional notification from 90 days to 120 days prior to implementation of a demonstration, it fails to require public notice and comment or allow for Congressional disapproval.
H.R. 8884 also adds a new requirement that SSA must use its operating budget to fund the administrative costs of any SSDI demonstration projects; the operating budget funds the agency's customer service and is subject to annual appropriations limits. In contrast, current law authorizes SSA to use mandatory disability trust fund dollars for all SSDI demonstration costs, including administrative costs. This can help to prevent demonstration project costs from reducing scarce resources for front-line customer service. The Trump Administration has already thrown SSA into a customer service crisis. Forcing the agency to take away from its customer service budget in order to pursue ideologically-driven demonstrations may only worsen SSA's service to the public.
Social Security Subcommittee Ranking Member John B. Larson ordered an amendment to H.R. 8884 to address these concerns. Unfortunately, the Majority failed to support the amendment's commonsense protections.
Sincerely,
Richard E. Neal,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2027
content:
<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Betty McCollum>: Pursuant to the provisions of clause 3(a)(1) of rule XIII of the Rules of the House of Representatives and section 6(i) of the Committee Rules, the views of the minority party of the House of Representatives, are printed below:
The Fiscal Year 2027 Defense Appropriations Bill totals $1.072 trillion. The Administration's total request for both mandatory and discretionary levels $1.5 trillion for the coming fiscal year for defense. This sum is an unprecedented topline request.
Broken out, this is a base budget increase of over $200 billion above last year's enacted level; mandatory funding is requested at $350 billion. The request is nearly a 44% increase in defense spending over last year.
This massive increase for defense comes as the President also proposes to cut domestic investments in the non-defense budget by $73 billion, or 10%. We know that cuts to other appropriations bills will deeply impact our national security-- particularly cuts to education and diplomacy.
In addition to the immense cuts to non-defense programs, we continue to have concerns about the Administration's split between discretionary funding that we control, and mandatory funding that we do not.
The Administration's reconciliation request includes many of their priorities such as Golden Dome, Drone Dominance, munitions and defense industrial base support. As of today, there is no guarantee it will pass. And if it does not, it will be nearly impossible to fix all the ``broken glass'' in a conferenced bill. The Administration must forego this approach in the fiscal year 2028 process.
In addition to the $1 trillion provided in fiscal year 2026 and the $1.5 trillion requested in Fiscal year 2027, the Administration is now requesting an additional $67 billion for the President's war with Iran. As of the writing of this document, the Committee is still waiting for the details of what this request encompasses. What the President said would be a six week conflict has evolved into a four month mess.
Our brave men and women in the military have won this war tactically, however, the strategic costs to our nation have been immense. The question must be answered at the end of this crisis--what will we have accomplished and at what cost?
Unfortunately, yet again, the bill did not include additional military support funding for Ukraine. The hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have now lasted longer than World War I--more than 1500 days. Every enacted Defense bill for the past eleven years has included funding for Ukraine and there remains broad Congressional support for the funding these programs. Therefore, we believe funding should be included. We look forward to working through the process to ensure funding continues.
It was disappointing that an amendment to follow the language in Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (P.L. 119-60) for troop levels in European Command (EUCOM) failed in committee. The Administration's recent announcement of a six-month review of our personnel in NATO countries causes concern for many members, especially given the Administration's rash decisions over the past six months on troop levels and exercises in the EUCOM area of operations. Any additional removal of personnel and assets from EUCOM is exactly what Putin is hoping that the United States will do.
The bill now will include support for changing the name of the Department of Defense to the Department of War. This cosmetic alteration could cost up to $125 million to cover the costs of the necessary changes. When Congress and the Truman Administration reorganized our national security agencies in 1947, they made the decision to create the Department of Defense--and bring all the military services underneath it. The reason they chose ``defense'' instead of ``war'' was because they did not want to be overtly aggressive towards the Soviet Union. We should heed their wise decision. War is something we should want to avoid.
Finally, we were optimistic that going into the full committee markup the bill included only one poison pill provision. Unfortunately, an amendment to restore anti-LGBTQ, anti-DEI, anti-CRT and restrictions on reproductive health provisions were added to the bill in a party-line vote. Partisan riders bog down the appropriations process. They only extend deliberations until they are finally removed.
It should also be noted that none of these provisions are necessary under the current Administration. The Department of Defense does not conduct research on fetal tissue from abortions; does not have DEI programs; does not teach critical race and does not provide for the reproductive health needs of service members to the fullest extent necessary. Yet the attacks against equality for women, the LGBTQI community and diversity continue.
We are consistently concerned about what effect these provisions could have on recruitment and retention of military personnel. Any person, if they have the desire to serve, should have the opportunity to enlist in the U.S. Armed Forces. This bill should be laser focused on serving our warfighters and their families; that they have the equipment, training and support they need to execute their missions. It should not be focused on issues that divide us.
We have the most powerful military in the history of humankind. We are extraordinarily grateful to the men and women of our armed services who sacrifice everything to keep us safe. Their devotion to duty is exemplary, and it must be matched by the seriousness and sobriety of those at the very top of the chain of command.
For all of these reasons, we cannot yet support the bill as it is currently drafted. We look forward to working with the majority through the process of crafting a law that we all can support.
Rosa DeLauro.
Betty McCollum.

bill_title: Small Business Health Options Awareness Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: H.R. 5498 would require the Small Business Administration (SBA) to distribute materials on Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Accounts (ICHRAs).
It is important to provide information to small businesses so they can better meet the health care needs of their workers. However, small businesses should have a complete view of all options available to them, not just ICHRAs. Over half of all the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace enrollees are small businesses owners, employees, or self-employed. By directing SBA to provide information only on ICHRAs, without requiring information on the ACA Marketplace, creates a significant gap in the guidance available to small businesses.
With that said, ICHRAs are problematic in that they lead to health care discrimination against certain classes of workers. While nondiscrimination provisions were included in the original rule to protect employees from being targeted based on age, health status, or other features, ICHRAs could be offered to specific classes of workers to reduce group health plan costs, and better coverage could be offered to top executives.
ICHRAs will also make the marketplace risk pool sicker and increase premiums. A Brookings Institution analysis found that allowing employers to offer ICHRAs alongside a traditional group health insurance plan could increase marketplace premiums by 16% to 93%. If employers shift high-cost or high-risk workers onto the individual market, the adverse selection will drive up premiums in the individual market.
ICHRAs leave small business employees worse off for healthcare coverage. If an employee is offered an ICHRA, the employee is not eligible for subsidized marketplace coverage, unless their share of the premium is more than 9.96 percent of household income. For many low-wage workers, they may be better off without an ICHRA and use the marketplace premium tax credits for more generous and affordable coverage.
Aside from the underlying policy concerns, it makes little sense at this time to require the Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) to disseminate information about them while President Trump's budget eliminates their funding, and the SBA is withholding funds. Expanding responsibilities while reducing resources is not only unsustainable, but it is the textbook definition of an unfunded mandate. Moreover, several agencies are already required to educate individuals and employers about ICHRAs, making additional SBDC dissemination on ICHRAs duplicative.
Small businesses--already squeezed by Trump's tariffs--are getting squeezed by Republicans' health plan. Get less, pay more. And it means higher costs and worse health for working Americans. To help with the affordability crisis, we should ensure small businesses and their employees have a comprehensive slate of health care information to make informed decisions. Doing so would mean the very survival of the operation. That is why Democrats supported an amendment offered by Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-MI), which would require the SBA to publicly post information about all health care plans, and supported an amendment offered by Rep. Kelly Morrison (D-MN) requiring a notice that ICHRAs could limit an individual's eligibility for the ACA premium tax credits. The amendments were defeated by Republicans.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Protecting Small Business Competitions Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Section 15(a)(1)(C) of the Small Business Act states that the Small Business Administration (SBA) shall ``assur[e] that a fair proportion of the total purchases and contracts for goods and services of the Government . . . are awarded to small business concerns.''\1\ The main authority federal agencies use to create a level playing field for small businesses is to set aside contracts for small business-only competitions. Contracting officers can, and in some cases must, exclude other-than-small firms from participation, therefore allowing small businesses to compete with firms of similar size and scale while maintaining the competitive requirements in the Competition in Contracting Act.
\1\15 U.S.C. 644(a)(1)(C).
Currently, the Small Business Act requires that federal agencies default to small business set asides for contracts with values under the Simplified Acquisition Threshold (SAT/ $350,000), unless there is not a reasonable expectation that two small businesses can and will make competitive offers. For contracts above the SAT, contracting officers must conduct market research and determine if there are two or more responsible small businesses that will make offers and can perform the work at fair market prices.\2\ If contracting officers have a reasonable expectation that offers will be received from two or more small businesses, they must set the contracts aside and allow only small businesses to compete. This analysis is known as the ``Rule of Two'' and is the process that triggers small business competition.
\2\13 CFR 125.2(f); 48 CFR 19.502-2.
The Rule of Two has been a regulatory requirement for forty years and is the foundation of the Federal Government's support for small business prime contracting. The requirement for a Rule of Two analysis was put in place in recognition of the fact that if small businesses were required to compete with large corporations, it would be nearly impossible for any small business to win a contract, let alone be awarded a ``fair proportion.'' This is especially true for small businesses seeking federal contracts for the first time.
The data bears this out: with the Rule of Two in place, over $100 billion dollars is now awarded annually to small business government contractors through small business-only competitions. In fiscal year 2024 alone, $72 billion was awarded through general small business set-asides.\3\ That does not include contracts awarded through one of SBA's procurement programs--which this legislation protects and enables.
\3\U.S. Small Bus. Admin., Final FY23 Corrective Action Report with Agency Reports and Addenda, (Sep. 9, 2024) and Small Business Data HUB. https://datahub.certify.sba.gov/ (last accessed Apr. 24, 2026).
The Rule of Two has been retained during changes to federal procurement regulations since its initial inclusion in the Federal Acquisition Regulations (FAR) 40 years ago. On April 15, 2025, the President issued Executive Order (EO) 14275 requiring the government to review and rewrite the FAR, initiating the most recent round of reviews.\4\ The newest version of the FAR retained the Rule of Two. However, both EO 14275 and the revised FAR (which has not yet moved through the formal rulemaking process) include a section that stated any provision retained in the revision, but not based on statute, would expire in four years unless extended by the FAR Council.\5\ As a result, the Rule of Two's future as a regulatory requirement is less secure.
\4\Exec. Order No. 14275, 90 Fed. Reg. 16447 (Apr. 15, 2025).
\5\FAR Part 1.109: ``All FAR sections that are not required by statute must expire 4 years after the effective date of the sections, unless renewed by the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council.''
The Committee believes that retaining and codifying the Rule of Two must be a top priority and has consistently and publicly highlighted the need to do so since the signing of EO 14275--including through hearing records, press releases, op-eds, and outreach to the community. This effort has demonstrated the overwhelming support among the small business community for retaining the Rule of Two and enacting H.R. 2804. The Protecting Small Business Competitions Act is formally endorsed by more than 35 organizations and hundreds of small businesses.
For example, the Committee record includes testimony from a September 10, 2025, Small Business Subcommittee on Contracting and Infrastructure hearing entitled: ``Leveling the Playing Field: Fostering Opportunities for Small Business Contractors,'' which discussed the FAR rewrite and the necessity of retaining the Rule of Two. The witnesses invited by both sides of the aisle highlighted the need to codify the Rule of Two and the strong, bipartisan support for doing so. Ms. Sue Tellier stated: ``The Rule of Two has historically been a bedrock protection for us. Its erosion results in a less welcoming environment--reducing opportunities for small innovative firms and instead accelerating consolidation.'' Mr. Michael Ramos stated: ``If we remove the Rule of Two, that will be damaging to the defense industrial base. I think that's pretty critical to understand. If you remove that rule and you do not codify it, you have this scenario where not only will [small businesses] leave, but you will just create massive entrenchment of the existing larger small businesses.''\6\
\6\Leveling the Playing Field: Fostering Opportunities for Small Business Contractors. Hearing before the H. COMM. ON SMALL BUS., 119th Cong. (2025).
The purpose of H.R. 2804 is to codify the current requirement and application of the Rule of Two as included in the Federal Acquisition Regulation, while retaining and preserving the existing exemptions, including those found in the Revolutionary FAR Overhaul's 19.104-1. H.R. 2804 does not expand the Rule of Two to procurements outside of its current application. In particular, procurements governed by different laws and processes, such as procurements made pursuant to the Javits-Wagner-O'Day Act (41 U.S.C. 8501, et seq.), or current, specific requirements at federal agencies, are not covered by H.R. 2804.
Preserving and codifying the Rule of Two as applied today will ensure that both small business competitions and other important procurement programs and structures remain consistent with the purpose of their enactment. For example, non-competitive procurements--including acquisitions with a statutorily mandated source such as Federal Prison Industries or AbilityOne--or procurement processes with alternative structures--such as procurement conducted for Architect and Engineering services via the Brooks Act, and small business direct award authorities--have been deliberately and specifically crafted to ensure the industrial base can efficiently support agency missions while realistically supporting Congressionally directed policy objectives. Among other objectives, Congress has directed federal agencies to use specific authorities--through mandatory and competitive procurements--to promote American's small business (contracts set-aside for small business competitions), American products and services (ie: Buy America Act) and American jobs (AbilityOne and competitions restricted to small firms in HUBZones). This bill does not repeal any existing laws and retains, codifies and protects that structure in statute for the future.
Similarly, the Committee adopted an Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute to remove the underlying bill's expansion of the Rule or Two's applicability to task and delivery orders. On January 15, 2025, the FAR Council issued a proposed rule to increase small business participation on certain multiple-award contracts by among other provisions, expanding the Rule of Two to placement of task and delivery orders.\7\ At the time of introduction of H.R. 2804, this rule remained in the proposed rule stage, and therefore, the bill's text included ``contracts, task order and delivery orders.'' The proposed rule was withdrawn on June 12, 2025\8\ and no expansion of the Rule of Two was included in changes made by the FAR Council.
\7\90 Fed. Reg. 3753 (Jan. 15, 2025).
\8\90 Fed. Reg. 24773 (Jun. 12, 2025).
The bill, as amended and passed, aligns with the current acquisition regulations regarding the applicability of the Rule of Two to task and delivery orders.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: Stop the Sexualization of Children Act
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Frederica S. Wilson, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark Takano, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Summer L. Lee, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 7661, the Stop the Sexualization of Children Act, would prohibit public schools, from using funds authorized under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965\1\ (ESEA) to ``develop, implement, facilitate, host, or promote'' programs, activities, literature, or materials for minors that include ``sexually oriented material.''\2\ This bill defines ``sexually oriented material'' as content depicting, describing, or simulating sexually explicit conduct,\3\ including material that exposes ``children to nude adults, individuals who are stripping, or lewd or lascivious dancing,'' and any material involving gender dysphoria or transgenderism.\4\ This bill is yet another attempt to promote culture wars by forcing public schools to follow partisan ideology in order to receive federal education funds. The bill negatively targets transgender people under the guise of stopping students from seeing sexually explicit material. In actuality, this bill does nothing to protect students in the classroom. However, it does have the potential to cause further marginalization and harm to trans students and potentially limit access to books, historical artifacts, and even state flags. Ultimately, this bill does nothing to address the actual challenges public K-12 schools are currently facing.
\1\20 U.S.C. Sec. 6301 et seq.
\2\Stop the Sexualization of Children Act, H.R. 7661 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
\3\The bill incorporates by reference parts of the definition of ``sexually explicit conduct'' from 18 U.S.C. Sec. 2256(2)(A)-(B). Id.
\4\H.R. 7661 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
SUMMARY OF CONCERNS
This Bill Aims To Infuse Curriculum and All Other Aspects of Public
Schools With Divisive Ideology
ESEA already prohibits schools from using federal dollars provided by programs authorized under ESEA to promote sexual activity generally. Current law also prohibits ESEA funds from being used to distribute or aid in the distribution of legally obscene materials to minors on school grounds, teach sex education/ HIV prevention, or distribute contraception in schools.\5\ These prohibitions do not tell school districts how or what they can teach but merely set guardrails on how federal funds can be spent. As such, they do not infringe on the longstanding prohibition that prevents the federal government from exercising ``any direction, supervision, or control over the curriculum, program of instruction, administration, or personnel of any educational institution, school, or school system . . .''.\6\ Schools are free to use state and local funds to provide sex education and HIV prevention classes, and often do, tailoring their curricula and programs to the prevailing opinions of the locality and not the federal government.
\5\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7906. Even current law prohibitions on sex education allow for federal funds to be used if, ``that instruction is age appropriate and includes the health benefits of abstinence;''. Id.
\6\20 U.S.C. Sec. 1232a.
On its face, it would appear that the prohibition in H.R. 7661 operates in the same manner. However, the broad definitions tied to its funding restrictions could significantly affect school-based health education, library collections, curriculum, field trips, enrichment activities, and federally supported student services. The bill will likely influence local decisions about instructional materials and student support.
School districts already face pressure campaigns over books they buy for their libraries and curriculum they use in their classrooms. These campaigns often have nothing to do with the educational value or generally understood age-appropriateness of some material.\7\ For example, in Tennessee, a school board voted to remove Maus, a Pulitzer Prize-winning graphic novel, in part because of images of nudity despite its clear educational purpose as Holocaust literature.\8\ Similarly, Holocaust education materials often include documentary photographs of nude survivors or victims, not because the material is sexually provocative but because it is historical evidence of the gross inhumanity of the Holocaust.\9\ But, since H.R. 7661 deems any material that ``exposes children to nude adults''' as ``sexually explicit'' without exception, schools would have no leeway to argue that such materials, however educational or age-appropriate, were not in fact prohibited. The same issue arises with respect to materials that fulfill state curricular requirements for LGBTQ-inclusive instruction.\10\ By defining any material that ``involves gender dysphoria or transgenderism''\11\ as ``sexually oriented'', H.R. 7661 will prevent ESEA funds from being used to purchase such materials, even if they only contain age-appropriate, non-sexually explicit material.
\7\Tovia Smith, School Book Bans Show no Signs of Slowing, New PEN America Report Finds, NPR, Sep. 21, 2023, https://www.npr.org/2023/09/ 21/1200725104/book-bans-school-pen-america.
\8\Tim Stelloh, `Maus,' Pulitzer Prize-winning Book about Holocaust, is Pulled from Tennessee School District, NBC News, Jan. 27, 2022, https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/maus-pulitzer-prize-winning-book-holocaust-pulled-tennessee-school-dis-rcna13730.
\9\Group Portrait of Naked Survivors in Mauthausen Concentration Camp, U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, May 05, 1945, https:// collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/pa1032317.
\10\Equality Maps: LGBTQ Curricular Laws, Movement Advancement Project, Apr. 20, 2026, https://www.lgbtmap.org/equality-maps/ curricular_laws.
\11\It is worth noting ``trangenderism'' is recognized as hate speech by Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation (GLAAD). Online Anti-LGBTQ Hate Terms Defined: `Transgenderism', GLAAD, https:// glaad.org/transgenderism-definition-meaning-anti-lgbt-online-hate/.
Supporters of H.R. 7661 would say that the bill is not prohibiting schools from teaching or purchasing anything--it is simply prohibiting what can be done with federal money. In this case this is a distinction without a difference. It has been established that certain curricula material like textbooks vary depending on the state they are used in.\12\ Commonly Texas and California are cited as the two large markets that drive left v. right editorial differences in textbooks.\13\ But, H.R. 7661 inserts a third player in these markets, the federal government. The bill's prohibitions would supersede state preferences since schools in any state might use funds to purchase textbooks or other curricular materials. As such, publishers that do not adhere to H.R. 7661's prohibitions could find their materials remaining unsold on the shelf. While it is not direct, H.R. 7661 would unleash an indirect censorship power over any school that receives ESEA funds. ESEA funds can support a wide array of activities including teacher salaries, programs to help students meet challenging state academic standards, well-rounded education services, and school-based mental health programs. Any service or program where a transgender student or teacher could be involved would force a school to confront whether ESEA funds could be used, or if doing so would involve ``transgenderism'' or ``gender dysphoria''. In practice this would be an unworkable standard for schools. Schools should be able to use federal dollars without the threat of micromanagement of every decision to determine if it adheres to the Majority's ideology.
\12\E.g., Dana Goldstein, Two States. Eight Textbooks. Two American Stories, N.Y. Times, Jan. 12, 2020, https://www.nytimes.com/ interactive/2020/01/12/us/texas-vs-california-history-textbooks.html.
\13\Id.
Finally, it must be noted that H.R. 7661 does include a rule of construction that prevents the bill from interfering with the teaching of ``standard science coursework'', ``the texts of major world religions'', ``classic works of literature'' or ``classic works of art.''\14\ This again puts the federal government at the center of determining what will be taught in schools since H.R. 7661 includes definitions of both classic works of literature and art. Those definitions come in part from materials published by Compass Classroom, a provider of homeschool curricula whose website prominently promotes its ``Christian worldview'' and ability to ``[t]each your kids to think Biblically about the world.''\15\ In its letter of opposition, the publisher Penguin Random House expressed the problems inherent in H.R. 7661's approach:
\14\H.R. 7661 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2026).
\15\Compass Classroom, Christian Homeschool Video Curriculum, https://compassclassroom.com/ (last visited June 17, 2026).
Rather than allowing educators and librarians to
select appropriate titles that reflect the maturity,
reading ability, and interests of their students, H.R.
7661 offers subjective and often biased lists of
``classics''' assembled by Encyclopedia Britannica, and
two reading lists published by a single curriculum
provider, Compass Classroom, written by Thomas Purifoy,
Jr. and Mary Pierson Purifoy. If a book is not a
classic in the eyes of those three sources, it is
deemed unworthy of consideration. Not only does this
rule out classic titles such as The Great Gatsby (F.
Scott Fitzgerald), Of Mice and Men (John Steinbeck),
and The Crucible (Arthur Miller) it also forbids
consideration of any new works.
While framed as addressing explicit content, the
bill's ambiguous language and definitions extend beyond
explicit material to include content related to
identity and ideology, narrowing the range of stories
and perspectives available to students of all
identities and backgrounds. Reading fosters empathy,
critical thinking, and civic understanding, and when
access to books is limited, these benefits are
diminished. Furthermore, being able to read,
comprehend, and interpret philosophically complex and
ambiguous writing such as Fitzgerald, Steinbeck and
Miller mentioned above is crucial to honing independent
thinking skills that are routinely called for on
standard college admission exams.\16\
\16\Letter from Skip Dye, Sr. Vice-Pres. & Dir. Sales Operations & Library Sales, Penguin Random House, to H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce (Apr. 13, 2026), https://global. penguinrandomhouse.com/announcements/penguin-random-house-sends-letter-to-congress-urging -opposition-to-h-r-7661/.
The Bill Does Nothing To Address Genuine Issues for Schools and
Students and Intentionally Causes Harm for a Vulnerable
Population of Young People
While the Majority continues to center culture war issues as Committee business, K-12 schools continue to face pressing issues. H.R. 7661 does nothing to address the slew of concerns public schools have faced since this Administration began. Last year, the Department of Education (ED) failed to disburse over $6 billion of federally mandated funds to schools and organizations on time creating chaos and forcing schools and districts to scramble to ensure services continued for students.\17\ Additionally, a court ruled the Administration could move forward with canceling all Teacher Quality Partnership (TQP) and Supporting Effective Educator Development (SEED) grants\18\ at a time when educator preparedness is at a crisis level in many states.\19\ Finally, the Administration is attempting to illegally dismantle ED through executive order,\20\ interagency agreements (IAAs),\21\ and a Reduction in Force (RIF) which cut ED staff in half,\22\ and most recently, plans to shutter the doors of ED's headquarters.\23\ Now is simply not the time to consider H.R. 7661.
\17\Lexi Cochran, Trump Administration Withholding $6B for After- School, Summer Programs, The Hill, Jul. 02, 2025, https://thehill.com/ homenews/education/5381348-trump-administration-after-school-funding-summer-programs/.

<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Frederica S. Wilson, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark Takano, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Summer L. Lee, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 7894, the Truman Scholarship Clean House Act, sponsored by Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-NY), amends the Harry S Truman Memorial Scholarship Act to make significant changes to the operation of the Harry S. Truman Scholarship Foundation (``Truman Foundation'') and the processes by which recipients of the Harry S. Truman Memorial Scholarship (``Truman Scholars'') are selected. 19 million students enrolled in American higher education are facing a system that is becoming increasingly harder to access and afford. This is due in part to actions recently taken by this Committee.\1\ Given that context, the Majority has decided to focus the Committee's time and attention on a small program that provides graduate school scholarships to approximately 60 students yearly, to pursue careers in public service. The Majority does this under the rationale that the Truman Scholarship is riddled with political bias disfavoring conservative students and academic subjects of study.\2\
\1\Pub. Law. No. 119-21 Sec. Sec.  81001, 82001 (2025).
\2\Infra notes 3-32 and accompanying text.
H.R. 7894 is a bundle of policy ``solutions'' looking for a problem. The Committee has no credible evidence of wrongdoing or bias on behalf of the Foundation, relying instead on flimsy non-academic papers and ``exposes'' by entities with established conservative ties. It is not clear if the bill's policies would even bring about the Majority's desired solutions if passed into law. What is clear is that the bill would give President Trump power to remake the Scholarship as he saw fit. Based on the President's established track record of remaking political institutions with little regard to his authority or the law, this Committee should not empower him further.
BACKGROUND INTO TRUMAN SCHOLARSHIP ``OVERSIGHT''
Starting in the 118th Congress, the Majority has conducted oversight of the Truman Foundation based on allegations of left-wing bias. Because these allegations are the driving force behind all Committee action in regard to the Truman Foundation, it is important to analyze and dismiss them before addressing the substance of H.R. 7894.
On May 20th, 2024 then Committee Chair Virginia Foxx (R- NC), Higher Education and Workforce Development (HEWD) Subcommittee Chair Burgess Owens (R-UT), and Rep. Robert Aderholt (R-AL), Chair of the Subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies of the Committee on Appropriations, sent a letter to Dr. Terry Babcock-Lumish, Executive Secretary of the Truman Foundation.\3\ The letter leveled accusations of bias at the Foundation, alleging it displayed a ``stark partisan tilt''.\4\ These accusations were based wholly on analysis conducted by scholars at the American Enterprise Institute, a right-wing think tank.\5\
\3\Letter from Rep. Virginia Foxx, H. Comm. on Educ. & the Workforce Chair., et al., to Dr. Terry Babcock-Lumish, Exec. Sec'y, The Harry S. Truman Scholarship Foundation (May 20, 2024), https:// edworkforce.house.gov/uploadedfiles/5.20.24_truman_letter.pdf.
\4\Id.
\5\Over the last two Congresses, Committee Republicans have called AEI scholars and fellows as witnesses at least eight different full Committee or subcommittee hearings.
In that AEI report, Frederick Hess and Joe Pitts alleged that the Rhodes Scholarship Program (privately funded) and Truman Scholarship Program (in part publicly funded) evinced left-wing bias in their recipient selection processes.\6\ In their report, Hess & Pitts conducted analysis of 182 Truman Scholar biographies from 2021-2023 and the Scholars' policy issue interests. The biographical analysis proved nothing; the majority of Truman Scholars could not be classified under AEI's standards as either progressive or conservative from a reading of their biographies.\7\ Further, their analysis found that 90 percent of Scholars reported no affiliation with partisan officials, candidates, or organizations in their biographies.\8\
\6\Letter from Rep. Virginia Foxx, supra note 3; Frederick M. Hess & Joe Pitts, Do the Rhodes and Truman Scholarships Have Any Room for the Right? Am. Enterprise Inst., May 2024, https://www.aei.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Do-the-Rhodes-and-Truman-Scholarships-Have-Any- Room-for-the-Right.pdf?x85095.
\7\Hess & Pitts, supra note 6, at 3 (``After examining the biographies, we concluded that there weren't enough data on affiliation with partisan officials, candidates, or organizations to support credible analysis. While scholars were vastly more likely to report left-leaning associations than right-leaning ones, more than 90 percent didn't report any such affiliation.'').
\8\Id.
Researchers with no pre-conceived notions regarding the Truman Foundation might have stopped there. However, Hess & Pitts continued to a strained policy issue analysis classifying policy issues that Truman Scholars expressed interest in as ``progressive,'' ``centrist,'' or ``conservative.''\9\ Progressive issues included: LGBT+ advocacy; racial justice and diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI); climate and the environment; and immigration rights. Centrist issues included mental health, cybersecurity and technology, national and international security and sexual violence prevention. Conservative issues included free markets, religious freedom, pro-life advocacy, and gun rights.
\9\Id. at 3-5. Hess & Pitts coded the scholars' policy issue interests by 12 categories, four belonging to each ideological framework. They emphasized that each policy issue category was ``uncontested'' and therefore is unarguably belonging to its respective ideological framework.
Hess & Pitts found ``[O]f the 182 Truman scholars, 74 cite interest in at least one progressive issue, while just six note interest in a conservative issue.''\10\ This was seen by them as a damning indictment of the Truman Scholarship as being overrun with progressive scholars. That analysis fails to mention by their own standards, if a survey of 182 scholars showed that 80 scholars expressed interest in partisan policy issues, that leaves 102 of scholars who expressed interest in policy issues that could not be classified as either progressive or conservative. To put this in terms our Majority colleagues might better understand, the percentage of scholars who expressed either centrist or non-partisan policy issue interests (56%) is greater than the current percentage of House Republicans' majority in Congress (50.58%).\11\
\10\Id.at 4.
\11\Based on the Clerk of the House's tally of 218 Republicans, 212 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 4 vacancies. If the Independent who caucuses with the Republicans is included, their majority is 50.81%.
A sober conclusion could be drawn that Truman Scholars on the whole were mostly interested in centrist or non-partisan policy issues. Hess & Pitts instead called on the Truman Foundation to recruit a more diverse scholar pool that ``true to the nation's breadth of perspectives, views, and values'' and on institutions to reevaluate their engagement with the Foundation if matters do not improve.\12\ This request was then parroted in the May 20th letter from Reps. Foxx, Owens and Aderholt.\13\
\12\Hess & Pitts, supra note 6, at 5.
\13\Letter from Rep. Virginia Foxx, supra note 3, at 1-2 (``. . . the Truman Scholarship should, at a bare minimum, be reflective of the country's breadth of values, viewpoints, and interests.'') (no internal citations omitted).
In response to the May 20th letter highlighting the AEI study,\14\ Executive Secretary of the Foundation, Dr. Terry Babcock-Lumish responded with a comprehensive critique of the AEI analysis for its broad characterization of issues as conservative or progressive.\15\ She also called the findings misleading because the researchers did not acknowledge all applicants, only those students who were selected.\16\ Dr. Babcock-Lumish claimed that the Foundation has no knowledge of applicants' ideological orientations unless they explicitly share them.\17\ She criticized the researcher's methods flagging that categorizing an issue as conservative, progressive, or neutral is subjective.\18\ She added that in the report ``[e]ven within issues, there is no allowance made for students who wish to take a conservative approach to a topic already deemed `progressive.'''\19\ Dr. Babcock-Lumish also noted that AEI ignored the fact that applicants work in apolitical settings where they are required to avoid partisan politics. Therefore, most applicants are neither obviously progressive nor obviously conservative. For example, she noted that ``a Naval Academy midshipman interested in studying the environmental impacts of the nuclear fleet would be characterized as progressive for the purposes of AEI's report.''\20\ Similarly, at a December 3, 2025 HEWD Subcommittee Hearing on the Truman Foundation, Ranking Member Bobby Scott (D-VA) challenged the report's classification of certain policy issues as inherently progressive:

Committee Oversight of the Truman Foundation was also driven by ``reporting'' from The College Fix, a conservative leaning news website. In June 2024, The College Fix published an ``expose'' on the Truman Scholarship and political ideology.\22\ Using a combination of winners' official biographies, self-reported work histories on LinkedIn, and social media profiles and posts, the author's found that of the 599 recipients since 2015, only 26 leaned right, 354 leaned left.\23\ Politics could not be determined for 219 of the 599 recipients.\24\ Moreover, of 380 scholars with political affiliations, 93% were ``affiliated'' with left leaning politics.\25\

<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Frederica S. Wilson, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark Takano, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Summer L. Lee, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: The College Fix's analysis is plagued by many of the same assumptions made by AEI. In many of the years of its decades of analysis, the number of scholars whose politics could not be determined was greater than the number of liberal and conservative coded scholars combined.\26\ While they claimed to see liberal scholars everywhere, the College Fix also seemed to go out of its way to deny that conservative scholars existed. In describing one member of the 2021 cohort, they said, ``One of the award winners, an economics student at Michigan State, interned at the conservative American Enterprise Institute and interned with the White House Council of Economic Advisors during the Donald Trump administration, but his political affiliation remains unclear.''\27\ In 2022, a year the website said the Truman cohort was ``dominated'' by Democrats and progressives, 5 scholars had worked in Democratic offices, 3 had worked in Republican offices.\28\

The Majority's oversight of the Truman Foundation is a continuation of its narrative alleging there is a conservative bias on campus. Further, the Committee's Oversight of the Truman Foundation relies heavily on the purported ability to ``code'' certain topics of study as ``conservative'' or ``liberal''. This approach assumes the rhetorical lines politicians use to debate issues in Washington are transferrable to the academic disciplines researchers work in. In many instances, that is simply not the case. There is ``unequivocal'' scientific data that show global surface temperatures have been rising since the mid 1970s.\36\ Similarly there is a near universal consensus among climate scientists that human activity is largely responsible for driving this rise.\37\ So for highly motivated postgraduate scientists looking to continue research in their field towards the end of public service, i.e. Truman Scholars, climate change is likely not a political debate between conservatives and liberals, but instead an established problem that needs addressing by our best and brightest minds, their political beliefs notwithstanding.\38\

H.R. 7894 INFUSES POLITICS INTO THE TRUMAN SCHOLARSHIP
After decrying the problem of the politicization of the Truman Scholarship, H.R. 7894 makes significant changes throughout Truman Scholarship's authorizing statute that will infuse more politics into the program. Section 2 of H.R. 7894 creates a definition of ``affiliated with'' to refine requirements in current law that certain members of the Scholarship's Board of Trustees be ``from each political party''.\39\ The bill also inserts political party affiliation requirements into the Regional Review Panels, the bodies that interview all finalists for the scholarship and recommend candidates from each state to be scholars to the Foundation.\40\ The ideological background of members of these review panels was an issue that the Majority raised in hearing, despite the fact that the Scholarship's regulations state that a panels' recommendations are based on the Finalist's application, and their evaluation of the Finalist's ``leadership potential and communication skills, likelihood of ``making a difference'' in public service, and intellectual strength, analytical abilities, and prospects of performing well in graduate school''.\41\ By intentionally politicizing the panels, it will call into question whether scholars are selected per the regulations, or selected for their politics.
\39\20 U.S.C. Sec.  2004(A)-(C).
\40\20 U.S.C. Sec. 2006(b); 42 CFR 1801, Supbart C--The Competition.
\41\45 C.F.R. 1801.17, 22-23.
Section 3 of the bill changes the statutory composition of the Foundation's Board of Trustees. Some of these changes are cosmetic, others are not. For example, eight of the 13 Board members would still be nominated by the President, and require Senate confirmation; the Secretary of Education, or her designee would still serve ex officio. However, the bill re-words the requirements for the four Congressionally-appointed members of the Board. Under current law, the House and Senate-appointed members of the Board are Members of the House and Senate respectively. Under H.R. 7894, the Congressionally-appointed Board members are just nominated by the Speaker and Minority leader of the House, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate--there is no requirement the nominees are Members of the House or Senate. In further revisions, Board members would now be term limited to two six-year terms and the bill enshrines that seven members of the Board shall constitute a quorum. The bill then mandates that within 90 days of the date of enactment of the Act (in this case the date of President's signature), the entire current Board would be dissolved and current Members terminated. This would allow President Trump to immediately appoint eight new members to the Board. While the bill does provide those appointments to be staggered--only two of the eight Presidential appointments to the new Board will serve six year terms--it would vest quorum proof control of the Board in the hands of Trump appointed nominees for two years.

Grijalva>: This is extremely concerning considering the damage to institutions that the President has been able to hand select Board majorities, particularly the Kennedy Center and the U.S. Peace Institute.\42\ Based on these real-world examples, it is not beyond the pale to hypothesize that a Trump-led Board would not hesitate to rename this the Trump/Truman--or just Trump-- Foundation Program.\43\ Based on concerns raised by these provisions, Ranking Member Scott offered two amendments that would seek to prevent the President and his handpicked board for exerting undue influence. The first amendment would delay the effective date of this act until after President Trump left office. The amendment also made clear the Board members would not have the power to rename the Foundation or to award scholarships in the name of anyone besides President Truman. The amendment was defeated on a party line vote. The second amendment recognized the reality that the sponsor of H.R. 7894, the bill that would dissolve the Board, is a current Member of the Board. The amendment would prohibit any Member of Congress who supported the dissolution of the current Board of Trustees would not be allowed to serve as a Trustee constituted under this bill if it was made law. This seemed to prevent what would be rather inherent conflict of interest a Member might have to vote to create vacancies they could then fill. This amendment was also defeated on a party line vote.

Section 4 of the bill amends the portion of law that determines how Truman Scholars are selected. Like section 3, some edits are non-controversial such as re-wording of requirements currently found in regulation.\44\ But the bill includes new statutory dictates on how the Regional Review Panels are composed, requiring the Foundation to ensure party parity among the members of these panels. Further, the bill would prohibit a scholar from having been a ``leader, officer, director, or organizers'' of a student organization that was suspended or expelled from campus. This is an obvious attempt to disqualify certain students affiliated with campus groups that were suspended or expelled from their schools in the wake of post-Oct. 7 protests in such a way that would not allow these students to explain or distinguish themselves in fairly important ways.\45\ Finally, section 4 prohibits the Scholarship from disfavoring candidates who intend to pursue a Masters of Business Administration (MBA) degree. The Truman Scholarship program is designed to award scholars who intend to pursue a career in public service.\46\ Regulations that govern the program require that ``Scholars must include in their submission to the Foundation a statement of interest in a career in public service that specifies in detail how their graduate program and their overall educational and work experience plans will realistically prepare them for their chosen career goal in government or elsewhere in public service.''\47\ The Foundation has found that in general MBA degree programs will not meet this threshold, and admittedly the Foundation has not gone out of its way to demonstrate that this is not a hard-and-fast rule.\48\ But there are many scholars with MBA degrees. Recognizing that this disfavor is not an accurate description of how the Foundation handles MD or MBA applicants, Ranking Member Scott offered an amendment striking these provisions as unnecessary. The amendment was defeated on a party-line vote.

The bill makes further changes that will infuse politics into the program. Section 6 would revise the selection of the Foundation's Executive Secretary, and just as Section 3 dissolved the current Board, section 6 would remove the current Executive Secretary in the bill's efforts to ``clean house.'' This action is taken with no suggestion of improper actions by the current holder of the position and would allow \2/3\ of the board to elect a new Executive Secretary. Again, as the President appoints eight members to the Board and the Secretary of Education sits ex officio, this would allow for an Executive Secretary hand-picked by the President's hand-picked Board.
Section 7 would require the Foundation to maintain press releases, program announcements, biographies of scholarship recipients on their website. This is based on the fact that the Foundation put these documents behind a password-protected wall after AEI and The College Fix used these documents as ``evidence'' in their ``analysis'' of Truman scholars. As the Right has already shown a willingness to dox and misconstrue this data to give impressions of bias, section 7 would only make this easier, and likely have a chilling effect on certain students from applying to be scholars in the first place. Section 8 establishes effective dates of the bill and holds harmless previous the awards of previous Truman Scholars.

CONCLUSION
Based on dubious research from conservative-leaning foundations and publications, this Committee has engaged in politically charged oversight of the Truman Foundation. At a time when Americans are finding it harder to afford a higher education, the Majority has written multiple letters, held hearings, and marked up a bill based on a program that serves approximately 60 students annually. This is not a judicious use of this Committee's time and resources. bill_title: PBM Kickback Prohibition Act
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 7895, the PBM Kickback Prohibition Act, amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act\1\ (ERISA) to prohibit pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) from paying referral fees to brokers, consultants, and similar entities. In doing so, the legislation takes a modest step to address inappropriate compensation arrangements and potential conflicts of interest between brokers and consultants and PBMs that raise costs for both workers and employers alike. In previous congresses, the Committee on Education and Workforce (Committee) worked in a bipartisan manner to develop meaningful legislation that addresses related challenges that employer-sponsored health plans confront when working with PBMs. However, rather than engage in such a process in developing and advancing H.R. 7895, the Majority chose to proceed through a rushed, partisan approach that dismisses Democratic suggestions for improvements to this legislation. As a result, both the introduced and reported versions of H.R. 7895 are inadequate to address the scope of the problem the bill seeks to address. Instead, the bill serves primarily as a partisan talking point to promote President Trump's so-called ``Great Healthcare Plan.''\2\ Committee Democrats supported the legislation because it is a small step toward addressing misaligned incentives in health care. However, moving forward, the legislation should be improved to ensure that it meaningfully addresses the full scope of conflicts of interest among health plan service providers such as insurance companies, third party administrators, and other middlemen.
\1\Pub. L. No. 93-406 (1974).
\2\The Great Healthcare Plan, The White House (Jan. 2026), https:// www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/The-Great-Healthcare- Plan.pdf.
RISING COSTS INCREASINGLY MAKE HEALTH CARE UNAFFORDABLE FOR CONSUMERS
High health care costs represent an urgent issue for American consumers, who increasingly face unaffordable health insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs. In 2024, total national health expenditures in the United States reached $5.3 trillion or 18.0 percent of gross domestic product.\3\ Americans' per capita health care spending has risen to $14,775, approximately double the average amount spent per capita in peer countries.\4\ These expenditures are heavily driven by high prescription drug prices and the rates charged by hospitals, physicians, and other providers.\5\ Additionally, growing health care spending is also directly correlated with rising administrative costs associated with middlemen, particularly for individuals with private health coverage.\6\
\3\Ctrs. for Medicare & Medicaid Servs., National Health Expenditures 2024 Highlights 1 (2026), https://www.cms.gov/files/ document/highlights.pdf.
\4\Imani Telesford et al., How Does Health Spending in the U.S. Compare to Other Countries?, Peterson-KFF Health Sys. Tracker (Mar. 11, 2026), https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/chart-collection/health-spending-u-s-compare-countries/.
\5\See Cong. Budget Off., The Prices That Commercial Health Insurers and Medicare Pay for Hospitals' and Physicians' Services (Jan. 2022), https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57778.
\6\See Linda J. Blumberg et al., Untangling the Complex Web: Summary of a New Expert Perspective, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Nov. 19, 2025), https://chir.georgetown.edu/untangling-the-complex-web-summary-of-a-new-expert-perspective/.
Approximately 181 million people in the United States receive health coverage through an employment-based plan.\7\ Although individuals with job-based health benefits generally express satisfaction with their plans,\8\ rising health care costs present a substantial affordability challenge for millions of workers and their families. Since 2015, the average annual premium in an employer-sponsored family plan has risen 53 percent, reaching $26,993 in 2025.\9\ The average general annual deductible for single coverage in the employer market has increased 42.9 percent over the last decade, growing from $1,320 in 2015 to $1,886 in 2025.\10\ These rising costs continue to squeeze workers and their families, and addressing the drivers of these costs should be a top priority for Congress.
\7\Lisa N. Bunch & Halelujha Ketema, Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2024 2 (Sept. 2025), https://www2.census.gov/ library/publications/2025/demo/p60-288.pdf.
\8\What Leads to Greater Satisfaction With Health Plan Coverage?, Emp. Benefits Rsch. Inst. 1 (Apr. 6, 2023), https://www.ebri.org/docs/ default-source/fast-facts/ff-463-cehcs7-6 apr23.pdf?sfvrsn=c599392f_2.
\9\2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey 35, KFF (Oct. 22, 2025), https://files.kff.org/ attachment/Employer-Health-Benefits-Survey-2025-Annual-Survey.pdf.
\10\Id. at 101.
HEALTH PLAN SERVICE PROVIDERS OFTEN HAVE CONFLICTS OF INTEREST THAT
HARM CONSUMERS
Employers who sponsor health plans often rely on a range of service providers to assist in administering and managing their plans. While many such service providers play a valuable role in delivering benefits, their business models have also been described as ``a complex web of common ownership, contracting arrangements, and financial deals which create an array of conflicts of interests and hidden flows of money.''\11\ These business models can have an inflationary effect on health care spending, ultimately at the expense of consumers who must shoulder rising premiums and cost-sharing.\12\
\11\Blumberg et al., supra note 6.
\12\Id.
PBMs, which are the primary focus of H.R. 7895, are one such type of service provider. They contract with health plans to perform a number of services related to the administration of prescription drug benefits, including developing and maintaining lists of covered drugs (formularies), negotiating prices and rebates with drug manufacturers, and reimbursing pharmacies for drugs dispensed to plan participants.\13\ The opaqueness of PBM practices has received substantial scrutiny in recent years, resulting in major legislative reforms enacted by Congress in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026\14\ and a proposed rule issued by the U.S. Department of Labor earlier this year.\15\
\13\Christopher J. Sroka, Pharmacy Benefit Managers, Cong. Rsch. Serv. (Nov. 29, 2000), https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/ 20001129_RL30754_ae8115ed5c22ac5d657bb297e78f9a 8b62bd060f.pdf.
\14\Pub. L. No. 119-75, div. J, tit. VII (2026).
\15\Improving Transparency Into Pharmacy Benefit Manager Fee Disclosure, 91 Fed. Reg. 4,348 (Jan. 30, 2026), https:// www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-30/pdf/2026-01907.pdf.
However, PBMs are just one component of the ``complex web'' of middlemen whose business models harm consumers and employers alike. For example, the majority of workers with job-based health benefits are covered through a self-insured plan, in which the employer bears the financial risk, rather than an insurer.\16\ Due to the complexity of administering such plans, employers generally contract with third party administrators (TPAs) to perform critical functions with respect to the plans.\17\ These TPAs are often owned by commercial insurers that, in turn, often own hospitals and physician groups, creating structural conflicts of interest that misalign incentives to the detriment of both plan sponsors and workers.\18\
\16\Christine Monahan, Questionable Conduct: Allegations Against Insurers Acting as Third-Party Administrators, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Mar. 24, 2023), https://chir.georgetown.edu/ questionable-conduct-allegations-insurers-acting-third-party-administrators/.
\17\Karen Handorf et al., Third-Party Administrators--The Middlemen of Self-Funded Health Insurance, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (May 28, 2025), https://chir.georgetown.edu/third-party-administrators-the-middlemen-of-self-funded-health-insurance/.
\18\Id.
Payments from these service providers to brokers and consultants are one such example of potential conflict of interest. A 2023 article in Stat investigated the fees paid by PBMs to certain brokers and consultants who encouraged their clients to contract with PBMs from whom they received such payments.\19\ However, this article highlights just one instance of such fees steering plans toward favored service providers. In 2019, for example, ProPublica found that insurers frequently pay commissions to brokers based on the number of employers they enroll in coverage.\20\ These fees are substantial, often between three to six percent of the plans' premiums, creating an incentive to further drive up health care spending.\21\ Similar compensation arrangements, regardless of whether the payments are made by PBMs or any other service provider, steer health plans toward service providers who generate profits for brokers and consultants but may not be the best choice for employers and workers.
\19\Bob Herman, It's Beyond unethical' Opaque Conflicts of Interest Permeate Prescription Drug Benefits, Stat (June 23, 2023), https:// www.statnews.com/2023/06/20/pbms-consulting-firms-investigation/.
\20\Marshall Allen, Behind the Scenes, Health Insurers Use Cash and Gifts to Sway Which Benefits Employers Choose, ProPublica (Feb. 20, 2019), https://www.propublica.org/article/health-insurance-brokers-cost-commissions-bonuses.
\21\Id.
THE COMMITTEE HAS PREVIOUSLY WORKED IN A BIPARTISAN MANNER TO IMPROVE
TRANSPARENCY
The Committee has a long history of working in a bipartisan manner to address problems in employer-sponsored health plans. These efforts have resulted in meaningful reforms that increase transparency and have protected consumers from the rising costs of health care.
During the 116th Congress, the Committee negotiated and advanced H.R. 5800, the Ban Surprise Billing Act,\22\ introduced by Rep. Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott (D-VA) and Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC). This legislation addressed the pernicious issue of surprise medical billing by out-of-network health care providers and relied on a benchmark payment rate that would help keep prices down. Additionally, it shined a light on excessive fees and conflicts of interest among service providers such as brokers, consultants, PBMs, and TPAs by requiring disclosure of direct and indirect compensation to plan fiduciaries. Several provisions of the ConsolidatedAppropriations Act, 2021 (CAA 2021)\23\ incorporated the Committee's efforts, including groundbreaking service provider disclosure requirements added to section 408(b)(2) of ERISA.\24\
\23\See Pub. L. No. 116-260, div. BB (2020).
\24\See 29 U.S.C. Sec. 1108(b)(2)(B).
\22\H. Rept. No. 116-615 at 49 (2020).
In the 118th Congress, the Committee took a number of additional actions to reduce costs and address conflicts of interest, including the markup of a package of bills relating to transparency. These bills included H.R. 2401, the Hidden Fee Disclosure Act, introduced by Rep. Joe Courtney (D-CT) and Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN), which strengthened the 408(b)(2) disclosure requirements to ensure that plan fiduciaries have information needed to responsibly monitor TPAs and PBMs for conflicts of interest. Additionally, H.R. 4507, the Transparency in Coverage Act, introduced by Rep. Bob Good (R- VA) and Rep. Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA), improved transparency by, among other reforms, requiring PBMs to disclose their rebates, fees, alternative discounts, and other remuneration. This bipartisan work contributed to the enactment of similar reforms in the 119th Congress as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA 2026),\25\ including similar PBM reporting requirements and a clarification of which service providers must fully disclose their direct and indirect compensation under section 408(b)(2).\26\
\25\Pub. L. No. 119-75 (2026).
\26\29 U.S.C. Sec. 1108(b)(2)(B)(ii)(bb).
THE MAJORITY'S PARTISAN APPROACH TO H.R. 7895 HAS RESULTED IN
INADEQUATE LEGISLATION
