committee_name: House Committee on Ways and Means
bill_title: Stopping Foreign Influence in Elections Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Richard E. Neal>: Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 9771, Stopping Foreign Influence in Elections Act of 2026. This bill does nothing to address the affordability crisis or bring relief to families struggling under the weight of higher health care bills, pain at the pump, or rising grocery costs. The Majority would rather manufacture problems involving charities and unions than stand up to the President, root out corruption, and lower costs for constituents. The Committee could have marked up legislation to revoke his tax immunity agreement, dissolve the ballroom project, or turn off the President's trade-related price hikes, if only the Majority would stiffen their spines.
This bill is the Majority's direct attack on charities and unions. This bill is redundant, overly broad, and onerous. We all agree that protecting American elections from foreign influence is imperative. However, this bill requires ``specified'' tax-exempt organizations--i.e., organizations that file Form 990--that make a ``disqualified political committee contribution'' to pay a penalty equal to two times the amount of the contribution. A ``disqualified political committee contribution'' is any contribution made by such organization to a ``political entity'' if the tax-exempt organization received any contribution or gift from a foreign national during the two-year period ending on the date of the contribution. The bill defines ``political entity'' as a political committee or any organization described in Section 501(c)(4) (e.g., a social welfare organization).
H.R. 9771 is overly broad in its application to organizations. It applies to any tax-exempt organization described in Section 501(c) that files a Form 990, including unions, civil rights organizations, food banks, community health centers, business leagues, and trade associations. Committee Democrats offered an amendment to exclude unions from this bill, which was defeated on a party-line vote. It is unclear if union dues count as ``contributions'' for purposes of the bill. If ``contribution'' in the context of a labor union were to be interpreted to mean union dues, then any time an employer hires a guestworker or a person with temporary protected status, and that worker exercises their fundamental right to join the union and pay dues, the union would be disqualified from donating to a political action committee (PAC) or a Section 501(c)(4) or face dire tax consequences.
Labor unions take the workforce as an employer employs it and represent all the workers in a bargaining unit. A represented employer could hire one foreign national into the bargaining unit. That foreign national could be fully authorized to work in this country. Once the employer places that foreign national into the bargaining unit, the union is obligated to represent them, and they are entitled to participate. When they pay their dues to the union and any portion of those dues is considered a contribution under H.R. 9771, the union's right to fully participate in the political process is restricted by the bill. As a result, the bill forces one of two consequences: knocking unions out of the political process or dividing the workforce and weakening unions. Both consequences are plainly to the detriment of U.S. workers.
Additionally, H.R. 9771 is overly broad in its definition of ``political entity.'' It subjects Section 501(c) organizations to penalties (including possible loss of tax exemption for two years) for contributions made to any Section 501(c)(4) organization. The penalties also apply regardless of whether the social welfare organization engages in political activities or the contribution was made for a permissible charitable purpose. Under this bill, a Section 501(c)(3) charitable nonprofit receiving a single foreign contribution would face penalties for contributing to Section 501(c)(4) organizations for any number of reasons unrelated to political campaigns. Section 501(c)(4) organizations should not be included in the definition of ``political entity.''
Furthermore, the bill also is onerous. It places an undue risk on Section 501(c) organizations that receive contributions from foreign nationals. It effectively forces them to learn the nationality of their donors, even donors contributing small amounts of cash (there is not a de minimis threshold in the bill). Currently, nonprofits do not collect this information with respect to donations. Expanding the list of questions nonprofits must ask and the information they must keep and/or report could damage relationships with their donors and community, chilling charitable giving and hurting the communities these nonprofits support.
For these reasons, we oppose this bill.
Sincerely,
Richard E. Neal,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Enhancing Geothermal Production on Federal Lands Act
content:
<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 5576 would amend the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 by designating certain geothermal exploration projects as non-major federal actions, thereby exempting these activities from review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). The bill would also direct the Interior Secretary to designate areas of federal land for priority geothermal leasing. After the initial designations, the Secretary is also directed to prepare programmatic environmental impact statements (PEISs) for geothermal leasing. No additional NEPA analysis would be necessary for a lease sale of lands covered by such a PEIS for at least 10 years.
There are two primary concerns with this legislation.
First, rather than expediting permitting through a well-considered administrative NEPA categorical exclusion (CE), this bill would waive all NEPA review for certain exploration activities. It is far more appropriate for federal agencies to develop CEs rather than for members of Congress to create legislative exemptions to NEPA. Agencies use their technical expertise to ensure a proposed categorical exclusion has little to no environmental impact, and agencies may incorporate public feedback and define site-specific conditions where the CE may not apply.
In the final months of the Biden administration, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) finalized and adopted several CEs for geothermal exploration that preserve key safeguards that this legislation would eliminate, and the geothermal industry is utilizing these CEs effectively.
In contrast, the waiver in this legislation is highly specific--limited to test wells with a diameter of 13\3/8\ inches, a number that has changed each Congress as versions of this legislation have been introduced. Directing BLM to develop a more general CE would allow far more flexibility and offer essential protection in extraordinary circumstances.
Second, while Committee Democrats support efforts to identify priority areas for geothermal leasing and to conduct thorough programmatic environmental reviews, there are concerns about waiving all NEPA requirements for geothermal leasing following a PEIS. Eliminating lease-sale-level NEPA analysis would short-circuit the way PEISs work. Committee Democrats strongly support PEISs, as they take a broad look at an activity's impacts and can streamline more specific analysis at the lease-sale level. Lease sale-level analysis can draw on PEIS-level analysis and build upon it as needed to incorporate site-specific information and ensure decisions are legally and scientifically defensible.
Last Congress, this provision of the bill said, ``If the Secretary determines that the designation of a geothermal leasing priority area has been sufficiently analyzed by a programmatic environmental impact statement, the Secretary shall not prepare any additional analysis under [NEPA]'' for a specific area.
Now, the bill text says that the Secretary ``shall not prepare any additional analysis under [NEPA]'' for a specific area ``unless the Secretary determines there are substantial new circumstances or information'' about adverse effects (emphasis added). This change would establish a presumption against lease-sale analysis in many cases, even when site-specific risks, conflicts, or new information warrant it.
Democrats made several suggestions to amend the legislation to secure unanimous consent, but the majority declined to negotiate.
I oppose the legislation as written.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Rural Jobs and Hydropower Expansion Act
content:
<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 7487, the Rural Jobs and Hydropower Expansion Act, would amend the Reclamation Project Act of 1939, authorizing all non-federal hydropower development projects associated with Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) facilities to utilize the Department of the Interior's Lease of Power Privilege (LOPP) permitting process in lieu of the permitting and licensing process used by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).
Congress tasked FERC with overseeing most non-federal hydropower development in the United States and designed the Federal Power Act (FPA) licensing process to balance energy production with other important public interests, including the protection of Tribal reservations, federal public lands, and fish and wildlife resources. The Interior Department's hydropower permitting process does not provide clear equivalents to the FPA in statute. Under current law, the development of hydropower by non-federal entities on Reclamation projects is permitted by both Reclamation and FERC. Jurisdiction is defined under Memorandums of Understanding, with Reclamation maintaining exclusive jurisdiction over Reclamation facilities authorized by Congress for federal hydropower purposes, while FERC is responsible for permitting at Reclamation facilities not originally authorized for federal hydropower development.
H.R. 7487 would significantly expand the use of the Interior Department's statutorily less protective permitting process for non-federal hydropower development at Reclamation water facilities, including many projects that would otherwise be licensed by FERC under the FPA. Specifically, FPA section 4(e) requires FERC, before licensing or relicensing a hydropower project affecting a federal reservation--including Tribal trust lands and many federal public lands--to determine that a project will not interfere or be inconsistent with the purposes for which a federal reservation was created. FERC is also required to include hydropower license conditions prescribed by the federal agency with jurisdiction over that reservation to ensure its adequate protection and use. FPA section 18 also gives the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the National Marine Fisheries Service authority to prescribe mandatory fishway conditions for projects that would affect fish passage. FPA section 10(j) also requires FERC to include license conditions to protect, mitigate damage to, and enhance fish and wildlife affected by a licensed hydropower project, based on recommendations from federal and state fish and wildlife agencies, unless FERC determines those recommendations are inconsistent with the FPA or other law. Together, these provisions give Tribes, federal land managers, and resource agencies enforceable tools to protect Tribal rights and resources, federal reservations, fish passage, recreation and other environmental resources during the hydropower licensing process.
While Reclamation regulations may incorporate similar protections into the permitting process, the Reclamation Project Act of 1939 does not provide the same protection as the FPA. H.R. 7487 would remove many non-federal hydropower projects from the enforceable statutory protections of the FPA and place them under the Interior Department's less protective permitting process without requiring similar safeguards.
Congress can support hydropower development and improve the licensing process without weakening major existing safeguards for Tribes, public lands, and our native fish and wildlife. In an effort to work with the Majority, the Minority offered an amendment that would preserve existing FPA safeguards for non-federal hydropower development projects affecting Tribes, treaty rights, fish and wildlife and other public resources, while still allowing the bill to consolidate licensing at the Interior Department. Unfortunately, our amendment was not adopted. For these reasons, I oppose this legislation.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Ways and Means
bill_title: Fair Treatment of Religious Organizations Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Richard E. Neal>: Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 9722, Fair Treatment of Religious Organizations Act of 2026. This bill does nothing to address the affordability crisis or bring relief to families struggling under the weight of higher health care bills, pain at the pump, or rising grocery costs. The Majority would rather manufacture problems involving charities and unions than stand up to the President, root out corruption, and lower costs for constituents. The Committee could have marked up legislation to revoke his tax immunity agreement, dissolve the ballroom project, or turn off the President's trade-related price hikes, if only the Majority would stiffen their spines.
Religious freedom is an American bedrock value that all of us support and is protected by the First Amendment. However, this bill would allow religious tax-exempt organizations to obtain and preserve federal tax benefits while espousing deeply harmful or discriminatory beliefs. This bill prohibits the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) from denying tax-exempt status to a religious organization even if its beliefs or practices on marriage, sexuality, or gender identity are inconsistent with law or public policy. It also provides that a belief cannot fail to be a religious purpose simply because it is not central or compelled by a particular religion.
This bill would permanently exempt religious organizations from the Section 501(c)(3) public policy requirement when it comes to their practices concerning marriage, sexuality, and gender identity--no matter how egregious those actions are. For instance, this would apply to practices related to same-sex marriage, interracial marriage, polygamous marriage, and child marriages. This bill would prevent the IRS from withholding tax-exempt status to a group that invents a belief tomorrow purely to discriminate, with no grounding in religious tradition.
This bill is essentially repealing the Supreme Court case, Bob Jones University v. United States, 461 U.S. 574 (1983). Over 40 years ago, the Supreme Court affirmed that Americans should not be forced to subsidize an organization whose core practices violate fundamental public policy or promote illegal conduct. In Bob Jones University, the organization claimed that its religious beliefs permitted it to reject any student who is married to a person of a different race. The Supreme Court held that the organization was entitled to its religious belief, but it is not entitled to require taxpayers to subsidize a practice contrary to law or public policy.
By exempting practices concerning sexuality from the public policy test, this bill would force the IRS to approve tax-exempt status for a church whose tenets support child pornography or sex between children and adults. In 2010, the United States Tax Court affirmed the IRS's decision denying tax exempt status to an organization whose stated purpose was to decriminalize sex between adults and children and eviscerate our child pornography laws because the purpose was contrary to public policy and promoted criminal conduct. This bill inhibits the public policy doctrine and strips this tool away for anything labeled as a religious belief about sexuality, giving bad actors a roadmap for wrongdoing.
Committee Democrats offered several commonsense amendments to exempt conduct contrary to law and public policy from the bill:
• An amendment to exclude from the bill any
``belief or practice'' that discriminates against same-
sex marriage, promotes polygamy or marriage to minors,
promotes exploitation or endangerment of children, or
discriminates based on gender identity or sexual
orientation. Failed on party-line vote.
• An amendment to exclude from the bill any
``belief or practice'' that promotes the marriage of
children under 18. Failed on party-line vote.
• An amendment to exclude from the bill any
``belief or practice'' that promotes female genital
mutilation. Failed on party-line vote.
This bill would set a dangerous precedent. It would provide a permanent taxpayer-funded license to discriminate or act against law and public policy.
For these reasons, we oppose this bill.
Sincerely,
Richard E. Neal,
Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. John W. Mannion, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 2555, the Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act, introduced by Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN), amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA) to prohibit institutions of higher education (IHEs) that receive funding under title IV of HEA (Title IV) from preventing students from forming or applying to join a single-sex social organization. The bill also prohibits IHEs from taking adverse actions against students based solely on their membership in a single-sex organization. The Committee has considered legislation similar to H.R. 2555 over several Democratic and Republican-led Congresses. However, the markup of H.R. 2555 needlessly inserted a poison pill (specifically language to discriminate against transgender individuals) into an otherwise bipartisan bill. Until these provisions are removed, Committee Democrats cannot support this bill.
STUDENTS' RIGHTS TO FREELY ASSOCIATE HAVE BIPARTISAN SUPPORT
As introduced, H.R. 2555 stood for a simple proposition: institutions of higher education should not be able to take adverse actions against students simply for their decision to join fraternities, sororities, or other single-sex organizations. Language to amend HEA for this very purpose was included in comprehensive bills reauthorizing the HEA led by Republicans in the 115th Congress, and Democrats in the 116th Congress.\1\ Committee Democrats support the rights of college students to join fraternities, sororities, and other student organizations. Many Members of Congress are members of such organizations and some continue to participate as alumni members of such organizations.
\1\H.R. 4508 Sec. 119, 115th Cong. (2017); H.R. 4672 Sec. 1020, 116th Cong. (2019). In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic the Committee did not consider a comprehensive HEA reauthorization in the 117th Congress, and in the 118th Congress, the Committee considered a non-comprehensive reauthorization bill focused on the cost of college.
TRANS-EXCLUSIONARY POLICIES ARE A MAJORITY POISON PILL
As introduced, H.R. 2555 was a bipartisan bill likely to garner widespread (if not unanimous) Committee support. However, the amendment in the nature of a substitute (ANS) offered during consideration of H.R. 2555 needlessly inserted partisan poison pills into the bill related to the exclusion of transgender students. Specifically, the ANS added definitions of ``sex'', ``male'', ``female'', and ``single-sex organization'' to the bill, denying the right to of transgender students to be protected under the bill.\2\ Based on the language of the ANS, single-sex organizations would be defined as groups composed of students based on their sex as assigned at birth, and would bar transgender students from joining single-sex organizations consistent with their gender identity.\3\
\2\The ANS' definitions are an attempt to limit the definition of ``sex'' in this section to mean biological sex at birth. However, the Supreme Court held in 2020 that, even when interpreting ``sex'' to mean biological sex at birth, certain instances of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity require a prerequisite discrimination on the basis of biological sex at birth and as such are illegal under certain sex discrimination statutes. Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644, 660. Recent analysis by the Court, specifically in the Title IX context suggests this interpretation is still valid. See West Virginia v. B.P.J., 609 U.S. ___ (Gorsuch J. conc.) (``Bostock v. Clayton County supports, not undermines, the Court's conclusion.'') (internal citations omitted).
\3\Compare H.R. 2555, 119th Cong. (2025) (as introduced) (``Any student (or group of students) enrolled in an institution of higher education shall--(1) be able to form or apply to join any recognized or unrecognized social organization, including any single-sex social organization;'') with H.R. 2555, 119th Cong. (2025) (Amdt. in the Nature of a Substitute) (``Any student (or group of students) enrolled in an institution of higher education . . . shall--`(1) be able to form, apply to join, join, participate in, or lead a single-sex social organization of the student's sex . . .'') (emphasis added).
Prior to the ANS, there was no language in H.R. 2555 related to single-sex organizations and gender identity. Such language was not present in past iterations of the Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act considered as part of HEA reauthorizations by the Committee, or in the standalone version of the bill from previous Congresses introduced by Republican Members of the Committee.\4\ The narrow focus of the bill from its inception up until this markup was protecting students' rights to associate from university intrusion. Instead, the bill, as reported out of Committee, removes university intrusion but replaces it with congressional intrusion into students' rights to associate among themselves. Committee Democrats have seen nothing to suggest that the fraternal and sororal organizations that advocated for H.R. 2555 asked for this language to be added to the bill. This is consistent with the Majority's continued insistence on moving legislation through Committee that denies the existence of transgender students.
\4\See H.R. 4508 Sec. 119, 115th Cong. (2017); H.R. 4672 Sec. 1020, 116th Cong. (2019); H.R. 7488, 117th Cong. (2022).
The ANS essentially undermines H.R. 2555's entire rationale. Students either have the right to freely associate among themselves or they do not. By definition, part of that right involves letting students freely make decisions about the makeup of their organizations on their own.
During the markup, the Majority made mention of a sorority being sued based on its membership policy limiting its membership to cisgender women. It is clear there will be emerging legal questions regarding the right of single sex organizations to make membership decisions based on their member's sex assigned at birth. It is also clear that those questions will likely not be as clear cut as the Majority would like us to believe.\5\ Regardless, those questions are fundamentally different than and extraneous to the legal question the Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act was written to answer.
\5\See West Virginia v. B.P.J., 609 U.S. ___ (Gorsuch, J., conc.) (``Bostock v. Clayton County supports, not undermines, the Court's conclusion.'') (internal citations omitted); West Virginia v. B.P.J., 609 U.S. ____ (Op. of Sotomayor, J.,) (``Yet there are plenty of contexts outside of athletics in which Title IX applies and does not allow sex distinctions like this one to be drawn. Title IX does not allow schools, for example, to institute mandatory sex-segregated classes or extracurricular activities like chess club, theater, and student government.'')
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 2555
At markup, Ranking Member Robert C. Bobby Scott (D-VA) put forward an amendment to strip the trans-exclusionary language from the bill. The amendment was defeated on a party-line vote.
Amdt.                         Offered By              Description              Action Taken
#2...................................  Mr. Scott..............  Removed trans-           Defeated
exclusionary language
from the bill.
CONCLUSION
As introduced, H.R. 2555 had two bipartisan original co-sponsors. As a result of the adoption of the ANS, the lead Democrat co-sponsoring the bill, removed his support for the bill.\6\ It is clear from the ANS' adoption that Majority's obsession with making the world harder for transgender students wherever possible is more important than delivering long-sought bipartisan policy solutions. For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present opposed H.R. 2555 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on June 25, 2026. Unless the trans-exclusionary language is removed from the bill, we urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
\6\172 Cong. Rec. 107, H4252 (June 25, 2026) (statement of Rep. Garcia of California).
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Mark DeSaulnier,
John W. Mannion,
Adelita Grijalva,
Members of Congress.

bill_title: Protecting Investors’ Personally Identifiable Information Act
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Cleo Fields>: This bill prohibits securities exchanges and members of exchanges from collecting or providing personally identifiable information (``PII'') data when complying with the Consolidated Audit Trail or ``CAT.'' The CAT was born partially out of the 2010 ``Flash Crash'' when markets plunged and then recovered inside the space of an hour, due primarily to aggressive selling orders executed by high-frequency trading algorithms that triggered a massive decline in market prices, temporarily erasing almost $1 trillion in market value. In the aftermath of this crash, the SEC adopted Rule 613 to create the CAT so that regulators would have a means to efficiently and accurately track activity throughout U.S. securities markets, and to ensure that regulators would be able to quickly access data they need to analyze market activity in response to major market events. According to Rule 613, the CAT's primary purpose is to expand the data available for regulators to reconstruct market animalities (such as the Flash Crash) and perform surveillance and investigations for illegal activities such as insider trading, wash sales, or manipulative practices. Rule 613 was finalized in 2012, and after nearly a decade of consideration of the plans put forth by SROs, the CAT database was largely implemented in 2021.
Since its implementation, the CAT has enabled SEC staff to better understand the variables that lead to market volatility and investor harm, and the use of PII helps it to more quickly detect wrongdoing. PII also helps the agency to identify bad actors that the agency can then levy civil and administrative actions against, which in turn can reimburse investors for their losses. It is important to also note that this information is already routinely collected by registered broker-dealers, so the collection of this data is not new or onerous. The SEC has sophisticated systems and procedures in place to limit access to secure the sensitive data in CAT and significantly restricts the staff that may access this data.
The CAT is now needed more than ever, especially given the multiple market manipulative actions of the President\20\ and his decision to sell his market moving announcements through Truth Social to those who could use it to front-run investors and further manipulate the market.\21\ CAT will be critical, if not the only, tool at the hands of the SEC to deter, investigate, detect, and punish fraud including fraud related to the President's actions.
The scope of PII included in CAT has been narrowed significantly since implementation. In 2020, the SEC excluded from CAT the use of actual social security numbers (SSNs), Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITINs), and full birth dates. In 2025, the SEC issued an exemptive order further restricting the use of names, addresses, and birth years for U.S. persons. This bill would not only make the exemptive order permanent, it would extend the prohibition to all PII, including widely available information, such as that typically listed in a phone book (name, address, phone number), as well as valuable, anonymized information like IP addresses. This bill would therefore effectively eliminate CAT as a tool for identifying insider trading and market manipulation at the SEC. It would force the SEC to rely solely on piecemeal investigatory methods, such as subpoenas. Because the SEC already has in place means to limit access to sensitive PII, and because this data is already collected by registered broker-dealers, this bill does not effectively balance investors' privacy with the crucial need of the SEC to maintain safe and orderly markets and to safeguard them from manipulation and insider trading.
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 1483.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Brad Sherman,
Stephen F. Lynch,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Cleo Fields,
Members of Congress.

bill_title: Credit Access and Inclusion Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Cleo Fields>: H.R. 5402 would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) and is designed to promote the expanded use of alternative data--specifically with respect to rent, cell phone, and utility payments--in the credit reporting system. However, which such reporting is already permitted by the FCRA and is happening to a certain degree, the legislation would preempt a number of state-level consumer protections. Instead of expanding access to credit through consumer-permissioned standards or promoting better alternative data options that have emerged in recent years, like cash flow underwriting, H.R. 5402 would make it harder for consumers to not only get credit, but also get an apartment or job, which is why we oppose this anti-consumer bill.
Credit scores and credit reports are increasingly relied upon by lenders, employers, housing providers, insurers, and even law enforcement, and now serve as a critical gatekeeper to many aspects of economic opportunity. The U.S. credit reporting system is unique because it relies on consumer data for use and profit by private companies. However, it is a system riddled with errors and shortcomings, resulting in it being a perennial top concern for consumers.<SUP>3</SUP> A recent study found that almost half of consumers who participated had mistakes in their credit reports, with more than a quarter having serious errors that damaged their credit scores.<SUP>4</SUP> Moreover, in 2017, Equifax experienced a cybersecurity breach so massive that it affected approximately 148 million consumers. In addition to releasing the personally identifiable information of approximately half of all Americans, this breach also highlighted deficiencies in the credit reporting system, including the lack of an effective dispute process for consumers who find errors in their credit reports.<SUP>5</SUP>
Meanwhile, more than two decades have passed since Congress passed comprehensive reform of the consumer reporting system.<SUP>6</SUP> And many have argued for comprehensive reforms to make the system more equitable and more accountable to consumers.<SUP>7</SUP> During the Biden Administration, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) sought to hold credit bureaus accountable and improve the credit reporting process, including by seeking to eliminate the inclusion of misleading medical debt in consumers' credit files.<SUP>8</SUP> Committee Democrats convened hearings with the major credit bureaus and advanced a number of bills to overhaul the credit reporting system, including several to promote the use of alternative data.<SUP>9</SUP>
In contrast, the Trump Administration and Congressional Republicans have prioritized efforts to undermine the CFPB, including by slashing the agency's budget by nearly half, attempting to fire most of the staff, and halting the supervision of large credit bureaus and other major financial companies for compliance with consumer protection laws. Some estimates show that with all their CFPB rollbacks, in just a year, the Trump Administration has already cost consumers at least $19 billion.<SUP>10</SUP> Additionally, the Trump Administration recently made it harder for consumers to file complaints through CFPB's complaint database, particularly regarding problems they have with consumer credit reporting.<SUP>11</SUP> They did this after such consumer complaints exploded under their watch. In 2020, the CFPB handled about 542,300 complaints, with more than 58% of those complaints regarding credit and consumer reporting representing the most complaints received about any consumer product or service during that time.<SUP>12</SUP> Five years later, in 2025, the CFPB received a record 6.6 million complaints as Trump shutdown the CFPB, while the vast majority--5.8 million of those complaints (88%)--were about credit reporting.<SUP>13</SUP>
The House previously passed a version of this measure eight years ago in the 115th Congress.<SUP>14</SUP> Back then, the Committee was seeking to promote the use of alternative data-- like the reporting of rental, cell phone, and utility bill payments--but a lot has changed since then. Back then, even in a Republican Administration, we had a functioning CFPB and didn't see the kind of radical and unlawful shutdown of the agency that we've seen in Trump's second term. Furthermore, alternative data has been increasingly reported and included in various types of credit scores. The Committee later held a hearing on a revised Democratic draft that would address consumer advocate concerns,<SUP>15</SUP> including not preempting state protections and empowering consumers to opt-in to sharing such data. Negating state protections, as H.R. 5402 would do, after undermining the operations of the Federal agency with authority to supervise and enforce FCRA, would leave consumers worse off.
At a time when consumer data is increasingly used throughout the economy, an opt-in provision would give consumers more control over their own data, an approach that gained bipartisan support when this Congress curbed abusive trigger leads in 2025.<SUP>16</SUP> To that end, Rep. Janelle Bynum (D-OR) offered an amendment to add an opt-in requirement to allow consumers to decide if their information is shared with credit bureaus. This amendment also would eliminate the bill's sweeping preemption of protections for consumers available at the state level. Ranking Member Waters (D-CA) offered an amendment to restore CFPB funding and staffing for purposes of supervising and enforcing to ensure adequate oversight of credit bureaus and the credit reporting system. Unfortunately, Republicans rejected both amendments and instead further harmed consumers by removing a provision that would have allowed a consumer to opt-out from having their information shared with credit bureaus.
Consumer groups are strongly opposed to H.R. 5402 and have warned the bill would reduce a consumer's control over their own data; override state law protections for renters from tenant screening abuses; make it harder for consumers to obtain rental housing; and undermine other state consumer protections.<SUP>17</SUP> They also note there is a range of better alternatives to expand the use of alternative data, like cash flow underwriting.<SUP>18</SUP> Specifically, 70 consumer, housing, civil rights, utility rights, and advocacy groups are opposed to H.R. 5402, including the following national organizations: National Consumer Law Center (on behalf of its low-income clients), 20/20 Vision, Accountable.US/ Accountable.NOW, Americans for Financial Reform (AFR), Center for Digital Democracy, Center for Economic Justice, Consumer Action, Consumer Federation of America, Consumer Reports, National Association of Consumer Advocates, National Association of State Utility Consumer Advocates (NASUCA), National Consumers League, National Fair Housing Alliance, National Housing Law Project, and Public Citizen. The bill was also opposed by the following state and local organizations: Center for Economic Integrity (AZ), William E. Morris Institute for Justice (AZ), Arkansas Community Organizations, Community Legal Services in East Palo Alto (CA), Center for Accessible Technology (CA), Disability Rights California, Housing and Economic Rights Advocates (CA), The Academy of Financial Education (CA), TURN-The Utility Reform Network (CA), Watsonville Law Center (CA), Western Center on Law & Poverty (CA), Colorado Poverty Law Project, Connecticut Legal Services, Inc., Legal Aid DC, Jacksonville Area Legal Aid (FL), Florida Legal Services, Inc., Georgia Watch, Legal Action Chicago, Citizens Action Coalition of IN, Legal Key Partnership for Health and Justice (MA/RI), Coastal Enterprises, Inc. (ME), Maine People's Alliance, Economic Action Maryland Fund, Low- Income Energy Affordability Network (LEAN)(MA), Public Justice Center (MD), Michigan Poverty Law Program, Housing Justice Center (MN), Legal Aid Center of Southern Nevada, Nevada Coalition of Legal Service Providers, Legal Services of New Jersey, New Jersey Appleseed Public Interest Law Center, New Jersey Citizen Action, New Jersey Institute for Social Justice, New Economy Project (NY), New Yorkers for Responsible Lending, Western New York Law Center, Inc., Legal Aid Society of Southwest Ohio, Oregon Consumer Justice, Oregon Consumer League, HELP: MLP (PA), Philadelphia Solar Energy Association, Pennsylvania Utility Law Project (on behalf of its low- income clients), Community Legal Services of Philadelphia, George Wiley Center (RI), South Carolina Appleseed Legal Justice Center, Texas Utility Law Project, Texas Appleseed, Legal Aid Justice Center (VA), Vermont Legal Aid, Virginia Citizens Consumer Council, Virginia Organizing, Hopelink (WA), Byrd Barr Place (WA), El Centro de la Raza (WA), and Washington State Community Action Partnership.<SUP>19</SUP>
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 5402.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Stephen F. Lynch,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,

bill_title: Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: H.R. 9330, the Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act establishes a disclosure framework for so called ``Earned Wage Access'' advances but does not appropriately include consumer protections to protect the users of such products from abuse, such as any caps on the associated costs. Among other issues, this legislation excludes EWA advances from traditional caps on credit, like state usury caps. Furthermore, any limits on the access to earned wages requested by customers, including the amount of earned wages a consumer can access, how many times a consumer can access their earned wages, and associated fees and tips for accessing earned wages, would be determined by the EWA providers themselves. Moreover, the bill does not address the lack of federal oversight of consumer laws presently, as the Trump Administration continues to try to shutter the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
EWA advances offer individuals access to a portion of their earned income, prior to being issued their paycheck at the end of the standard pay period.\22\ EWA providers have varied business models, fee structures, and repayment methods and do not have standardized practices across the industry.\23\ Two major EWA models consist of the direct-to-consumer (D2C) model and the employer-integrated model, also called employer-partnered model.\24\ D2C EWA providers utilize their own funds to execute the advance for the user and typically recover funds by debiting users' checking accounts.\25\ Employer-integrated models are directly connected to the employer's payroll data, which provides information on the user's wages, pay period, and related data.\26\ In various EWA business models, EWA providers can charge workers one or more of the following fees: ``a monthly membership fee, [expedited access fees] for instant access or same-day [deposits,] fee per withdrawal (some EWA apps equate this to an ATM fee), fee per bank transfer, and/or an optional `tip' after each transaction.''\27\ Depending on the EWA product, particularly those that are structured as a subscription service, EWA products could result in consumers ending up in a cycle of consistently accessing their wages before they are actually paid, and accumulating fees and interest in the process. A Harvard study ``found that 40% of the people who had access to an EWA program through their employer were using it at least once a week . . . The survey further found that 60% of respondents had used a business-to-consumer (B2C) EWA app--often more expensive than an employer-sponsored EWA program--and the vast majority of those had used more than one, employing 2.45 apps on average.''\28\ The variety of business models and fee structures used by different EWA providers demonstrates the range of risks consumers may confront in the EWA marketplace, none of which are adequately addressed by this legislation.
EWA risks to consumers are especially heightened with a weakened Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and the agency's drastically scaled back oversight under the Trump Administration. In fact, this bill restricts the enforcement and oversight of the EWA ecosystem by placing the oversight of EWA providers under the CFPB while ignoring Trump's attempted shutdown of CFPB. The bill does not increase CFPB funding, proscribe CFPB supervision of EWA providers, and nor authorize expanded state authorities or new private rights of action to hold EWA providers accountable.
In addition to not including any meaningful limits or caps on the charges associated with EWA products, this legislation ensures EWA advances are not considered credit, that EWA providers are not considered creditors or lenders, and that fees or tips are not considered interest or finance charges under federal law. Through this language, EWA advances would be exempted from being regulated as credit-like products, and EWA users would not have the range of consumer protections encompassed in the extension of credit. For example, under this legislation, service members would no longer benefit from the Military Lending Act (MLA) 36% rate cap relating to fees and tips they pay for EWA products. This language stands in contrast to court rulings that have concluded that EWA products are, in fact, a form of credit.
Furthermore, as written, Republicans have carved out EWA providers from having to comply with federal civil rights laws and fair lending laws like the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)--a critical legal protection that addresses systemic discrimination in consumers' access to credit. Republicans have also failed to include any robust protections of users' data in this legislation, although EWA services amass vast consumer financial data, sometimes including worker geolocation data. To make matters worse, while this bill purports to establish rules around tipping, it includes language that would still allow EWA companies to request a tip and encourage users to tip under certain conditions. In the same way that it would be widely considered inappropriate if a banking app were to solicit tips, it is inappropriate for EWA companies to do the same.\29\
During the markup, Democrats offered two amendments aimed at alleviating the deficiencies within the legislation, but both were rejected by Republicans.\30\
• Ranking Member Waters' amendment establishes
a monthly $10 limit on fees and tips that an EWA
provider can charge or solicit from a consumer in
connection with EWA services.
• Rep. Pressley's amendment would ensure that
this bill does not preempt the consumer protections and
other provisions of State laws governing EWA services.
H.R. 9330 is opposed by 226 labor, consumer, civil rights, and community organizations.\31\ For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 9330.
Sincerely,
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Brad Sherman,
Stephen F. Lynch,
Bill Foster,
Joyce Beatty,
Rashida Tlaib,
Sylvia R. Garcia,
Members of Congress.

bill_title: SEC Reform and Restructuring Act
content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Cleo Fields>: This bill would restrict and harm the SEC's mission of investor protection and capital formation. Among its provisions, this bill makes it harder for the SEC to help market participants comply with the law by requiring staff guidance and interpretive releases to meet the heightened procedural requirements of formal rulemakings, including by requiring staff to conduct cost-benefit analyses and notice-and-comment. For formal rulemakings, this bill adds an onerous step to the rulemaking process by requiring the SEC to continuously evaluate the cumulative impact of new regulations, diverting scarce resources to rules that have already been promulgated and inhibiting the ability of the SEC to consider and finalize new rules. The bill also dismantles, and moves the functions of, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) to the SEC, exposing what have traditionally been nonpartisan audit, ethics, and quality control standards to the political whims of the Commission.
Democrats offered two amendments during mark-up of this bill. Ranking Member Waters offered an amendment to remove the problematic provisions of the bill that harm SEC's ability to protect investors, narrowing the bill to: require the SEC Chair testify semiannually; require GAO to audit SEC's IT infrastructure and data handling practices; and requiring 60-day notice-and-comment periods for most SEC rulemakings and an expedited 30-day comment period if the SEC determines risk of imminent investor harm. Rep. Lynch offered an amendment that would require SEC staff, when conducting cost-benefit analysis, to consider the impact a proposal would have on digital asset market infrastructure as well as financial market participants that use AI. Additionally, it would also require any cost-benefit analysis to look at a proposal's effects on investors and market integrity caused by the use of AI. Republicans rejected both amendments.
The bill is opposed by Americans for Financial Reform, Consumer Federation of America, and Public Citizen.
For these reasons, we oppose H.R. 9329.

Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: Title IX Clarification Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 8781, the Title IX Clarification Act of 2026, introduced by Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX), amends title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 (Title IX) to ``clarify'' the definition of ``sex'' and to add definitions of ``female'' and ``male'' to the statute. The Majority claims this bill is needed to provide clarity in the face of legal ambiguity. Such ambiguity as to the definition of sex does not exist as a legal matter, as attested by recent Supreme Court decisions.\1\ H.R. 8781 is instead an attempt to write transgender students out of the law and deny them protection from discrimination based on their gender identity.
\1\Infra text accompanying notes 14-16.
TRANS-EXCLUSIONARY POLICIES ARE THE COIN OF THE MAJORITY'S REALM
Less than one percent of the U.S. population identifies as transgender.\2\ However, so far in the 119th Congress, the Committee has had no less than six hearings where the subject of gender identity in education has been discussed.\3\ H.R. 8781 is at least the sixth bill the Committee has either marked up or managed on the House floor of this Congress that involves gender identity in some fashion.\4\ This fixation comes at the expense of many issues in the Committee's jurisdiction that Americans want Congress to address such as ensuring that employers pay wages that keep up with the cost of basic necessities, expanding access to affordable child care, or expanding access to paid family and medical leave.\5\
\2\E.g., George Petras, How many Americans now identify as transgender? Many are age 13-17, USA Today (Aug. 23, 2025), https:// www.usatoday.com/story/graphics/2025/08/23/how-many-americans-identify-as-transgender/85737062007/.
\3\The State of American Education Hearing Before the H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, 119th Cong. (2025); Safeguarding Student Privacy and Parental Rights: A Review of FERPA and PPRA Hearing Before the Subcomm. on Early Childhood, Elementary and Secondary Educ. of the H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, 119th Cong. (2025); Defending Faith and Families Against Government Overreach: Mahmoud v. Taylor Hearing Before the Subcomm. on Early Childhood, Elementary and Secondary Educ. of the H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, 119th Cong. (2026); Speech or Silence? The Future of the First Amendment in Higher Education Hearing Before the Subcomm. on Higher Educ. & Workforce Development of the H. Comm. on Education & Workforce, 119th Cong. (2026); Breaking Trust: Attacks on Parental Rights, Inappropriate Content, and Legal Abuses in America's Schools Hearing Before the H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, 119th Cong.
(2025); Training Activists not Physicians: The Impact of DEI on Medical Schools Hearing Before the H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce (2026).
\4\H.R. 28, 119th Cong. (2025) (prohibiting transgender women and girls from participating on athletic teams consistent with their gender identity); H.R. 2617, 119th Cong. (2025) (prohibiting the advancement of ``concepts related to gender identity''); H.R. 2616, 119th Cong.
(2025) (requiring schools to obtain parental consent before changing a minor's gender markers, pronouns, or preferred name on any school form or sex-based accommodations, including locker rooms or bathrooms); H.R. 7661, 119th Cong. (2025) (defining any material that ``involves gender dysphoria or transgenderism'' as sexually oriented material); H.R. 8705, 119th Cong. (2026) (preventing the use of federal funds to teach ``gender ideology extremism'' as defined in Pres. Trump's Executive Order 14168); H.R. 8781, 119th Cong. (2026).
\5\LaShonda Brenson, Building a More Inclusive Agenda: A Survey of Congressional Priorities Across Race, Joint Ctr. for Pol. & Econ. Studies, Sept. 27, 2023, https://jointcenter.org/ congressional-top-priorities-passing-legislation-to-ensure-americans-have-the-right-to-vote-is-respondents-top-priority/.
H.R. 8781 MARS TITLE IX'S ANTI-DISCRIMINATORY LEGACY
Title IX states ``No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance ...''\6\ It is hard to overstate the transformational effect Title IX has had on American society. In its over 50-year history, Title IX has created opportunities for millions of women and girls to participate in sports at the high school and college levels. By 2016, two in every five girls in the United States played sports.\7\ Further, while the public may recognize the law's impact on sports primarily, Title IX prohibits sex discrimination in all vestiges of education; it has helped secure advancements for women in academic and career fields traditionally dominated by men and provided procedural and substantive rights for victims of sex discrimination, sex harassment and sexual assault in educational settings, irrespective of their gender.\8\
\6\20 U.S.C. Sec.  1681(a).
\7\Women's Sport Foundation, Title IX and the Rise of Female Athletes in America, (Sept. 2, 2016) https:// www.womenssportsfoundation.org/education/title-ix-and-the-rise-of-female-athletes-in-america/.
\8\Women's Sports Foundation, 50 Years of Title IX: We're Not Done Yet 7, 2021 https://www.womenssportsfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/ 2022/05/Title-IX-at-50-Report-FINALC-v2-.pdf (``Pathways once closed or significantly inaccessible to women have opened as Title IX created greater access to academic pursuits leading to careers in an array of occupations for women, including but not limited to astronauts, athletes, carpenters, chief executive officers, construction workers, doctors, engineers, entrepreneurs, farmers, filmmakers, firefighters, football coaches, investors, journalists, lawyers, musicians, police officers, military personnel, rock stars, Supreme Court justices, and television news anchors.''); U.S. Dep't of Educ., Title IX and Sex Discrimination, last reviewed Jan. 30, 2026, https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/civil-rights-laws/title-ix-and-sex-discrimination.
In recent years, Title IX has been discussed in the context of the right of transgender women to participate in sports consistent with their gender identity. The question as to whether ``sex'' in the context of Title IX includes sexual orientation and/or gender identity has been the subject of court cases, federal legislation, and administrative regulation. A version of these questions came before the Supreme Court this year in two cases heard concurrently, B.P.J. v. West Virginia, and Little v. Hecox. The very specific questions before the Court were whether, under Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, schools may maintain women's and girls' sports teams for cisgender females, i.e., whether schools can determine eligibility for female sports based on sex assigned at birth.\9\
\9\B.P.J. v. West Virginia No. 24-43, slip op. at 2 (U.S., June 30, 2026).
The Court held 9-0 that Title IX allows schools to provide separate women's and men's sports teams defined by biological sex, and a state can limit participation based on biological sex at birth.\10\ Title IX and the Javits Amendment\11\ create a regulatory scheme that provides for separate teams for men and women because of the biological differences between the sexes. Title IX regulations authorize, ``separate women's and girls' teams in sports when the teams are `based upon competitive skill or the activity involved is a contact sport.'''\12\ The Court concluded it was reasonable at the time of Title IX's passage to separate sports teams based on ``sex'', which all parties before the Court agreed at the time of the law's writing, meant biological sex at birth. Because the law and amendments recognize in the sports context a reasonable distinction between the biological sexes, the Court held it is not discrimination on the basis of sex under Title IX to limit participation on sports teams based on biological sex at birth.\13\
\10\Id. at 9-12. When describing the Court's holding and rationale or quoting from H.R. 8781, we use the term the Court and the bill use-- biological sex--rather than the preferred ``sex assigned at birth''. National SOGIE Ctr., Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity & Expression Glossary of Terms, https://sogiecenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ SOGIE-Glossary-Final.pdf (last visited Aug. 30, 2026).
\11\Much of the impact of Title IX in sports comes not from the law itself but the regulations promulgated under it. These were the result of the Javits Amendment, which directed the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (the predecessor to the Department of Education) to promulgate ``reasonable (regulatory) provisions considering the nature of particular sports''' in intercollegiate athletics.'' U.S. Dep't of Educ., Policy Interpretation: Title IX and Intercollegiate Athletics, https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/civil-rights-laws/ federal-register-notices-and-regulations/policy-interpretation-title-ix-and-intercollegiate-athletics.
\12\B.P.J. v. West Virginia No. 24-43, slip op. at 10 (U.S., June 30, 2026).
\13\Id. at 9-12.
H.R. 8781 IS UNNECESSARY TO ``PROTECT'' ATHLETICS
H.R. 8781 would clarify that under Title IX ``sex'' means ``biological'' sex at birth and would also add definitions of ``female'' and ``male'' based on biological sex at birth to Title IX. At first glance, this seems very unnecessary: both the B.P.J. majority opinion written by Justice Kavanaugh and leading dissent written by Justice Sotomayor make clear that all parties in these cases agreed that ``sex'' in Title IX should be interpreted to mean sex assigned at birth.\14\ This was also the interpretation of ``sex'' in the Bostock case which recognized discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity as sex discrimination under title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.\15\ The brief concurrence by Justice Gorsuch suggests his Bostock analysis is still good law: many instances of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity are outgrowths of underlying discrimination on the basis of sex.\16\
\14\Id. at 10-11; Id. at 30-31 (Sotomayor, J., dissenting).
\15\Id. at 2 (Gorsuch, J., concurring) (``Bostock v. Clayton County supports, not undermines, the Court's conclusion.'') (internal citations omitted); Bostock v. Clayton County, 590 U.S. 644, 660.
\16\Id.
Both the Kavanaugh opinion and Sotomayor dissent provide additional clues as to why the Majority is now advancing H.R. 8781. Justice Kavanaugh, writing for the majority, made two prominent caveats that bookend his opinion. First, very early on, he states that this case does not ``present the distinct question of whether, under Title IX and the equal Protection Clause, schools may allow biological males who identify as female to participate on girls' and women's sports teams. . . . Nothing in this opinion is intended to decide that question.''\17\ He makes it clear the Court in this decision is not stopping a state from allowing or requiring girls' and women's teams to allow transgender girls and women to play. Committee Republicans claim H.R. 8781 is necessary to prevent states and localities from doing just what the Court said it was not outruling: interpreting Title IX to require schools to allow transgender athletes to play on teams consistent with their gender identity. As such, H.R. 8781 seems to contradict the supposed overarching education policy goal of the Majority on this Committee--to return education to the states. The Supreme Court made clear nothing in the B.P.J. ruling prevents a state or locality from recognizing a transgender student's right to be free from discrimination on the basis of their gender identity. In response, the Majority has offered H.R. 8781, nationwide legislation to overrule such an interpretation and take decision-making authority in education away from the states.
\17\B.P.J. v. West Virginia No. 24-43, slip op. at 3 (U.S., June 30, 2026) (n.1).

bill_title: Title IX Clarification Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: Second, Justice Kavanaugh closes out his opinion with a long argument for why this decision is needed in the context of sports. He suggests the nature of competition, the spirit of fair play, and the country's deep obsession with sports all require this opinion.\18\ Although he does not explicitly state it, the strong suggestion is that the B.P.J. interpretation of Title IX is limited to the world of sports. The Sotomayor dissent takes the baton from the Kavanaugh opinion and makes this contextual interpretation more explicit:
\18\Id. at 27-29.
[T]here are plenty of contexts outside of athletics in
which Title IX applies and does not allow sex
distinctions like this one to be drawn. . . I do not
understand the majority to suggest, for instance, that
schools could expressly bar transgender students from
participating in certain classes or extracurricular
activities entirely, or on the more extreme end, that
schools could expel transgender students because they
are transgender, and that those actions would not
violate Title IX. Such actions would qualify as sex
discrimination. . .\19\
\19\Id. at 32-33 (Sotomayor, J., dissenting).
Both Justice Kavanaugh (implicitly) and Justice Sotomayor
(explicitly) suggest in the Title IX context, B.P.J. is strictly limited to sports. The opinions leave little doubt that a Title IX case arguing discrimination on the basis of gender identity in an educational context other than sports would be easily distinguishable from B.P.J.
It is the Court's suggestion that its decision is limited to sports that is the more insidious rationale for H.R. 8781. Had the Supreme Court held that Title IX offered no protection from discrimination on the basis of gender identity whatsoever, we doubt the Committee would have considered this bill. But, by inferring its decision in B.P.J. was limited to the context of sports, and by not striking down the holding of Bostock, the Court did not limit transgender rights consistent with the Majority's desires, making H.R. 8781 necessary. Reading the bill in the context of Justice Sotomayor's dissent, it is clear that the Majority would like to prevent Title IX from offering protections to transgender students in those other ``contexts outside of athletics'' she mentioned. This is consistent with the President's Executive Order on Gender Ideology Extremism, which seeks to eliminate transgender individuals from consideration in federal law.\20\ The Majority has justified spending valuable Committee and House Floor time over the last two Congresses on anti-transgender legislation because they needed to protect women's and girls' sports from transgender athletes. Now that the Supreme Court has done just that, H.R. 8781 makes clear the real goal all along was to ensure civil rights law did not protect transgender students on the basis of their gender identity.
\20\Exec. Order 14168, 90 Fed. Reg. 8615 (Jan. 30, 2025).
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 8781
Committee Democrats offered no Amendments to H.R. 8781.
CONCLUSION
The Majority's obsession with making the world harder for transgender students wherever possible appears to be the most important policy goal for this Committee. To achieve this, H.R. 8781 takes legal interpretive power from states and localities, in an attempt to unilaterally mandate a position the Supreme Court did not take, namely that Title IX does not protect students from discrimination on the basis of their gender identity. We disagree. For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present opposed H.R. 8781 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on July 21, 2026. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Mark DeSaulnier,
Adelita Grijalva,
Members of Congress.

content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 9203, the Student Protection and University Accountability Act, amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA), adding requirements related to compliance with title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VI) to the Provisional Participation Agreement (PPA) institutions of higher education (IHEs) enter into in order to receive access to Federal Student Aid. The bill also makes changes to the process by which the U.S. Department of Education (Department or ED) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) handles Title VI claims. While we appreciate the spirit in which the bill is offered, we have concerns about specific provisions in the bill that may increase the backlog of cases at OCR and could result in inequitable outcomes between complaints based in Title VI and other education civil rights cases.
In evaluating a substantially similar bill last Congress, the Civil Rights Protection Act,\1\ our Minority Views focused on the actions of the Committee in relation to Title VI in the 118th Congress.\2\ Committee Democrats remain concerned the Majority has taken a narrow view of the scope of Title VI in its choice of hearings and oversight activity this Congress.\3\ However, the Committee's actions have been greatly overshadowed by the Administration's actions in education civil rights generally, Title VI specifically. Taken in total, these actions suggest that this administration cannot be given any additional authority over Title VI from Congress until substantial oversight has been conducted on how it has wielded, and surpassed its authority so far.
\1\H.R. 8648, 118th Cong., (2024).
\2\H.R. Rep. No. 118-593 at 38-43 (``We fervently hope that the Committee is able to get answers from schools to the allegations of antisemitism on their campuses that it has requested. There is no justification for threats, violence, harassment, or intimidation against any student on campus, especially if such threats are the result of their shared ancestry, national origin, or ethnic characteristics. The Committee's failure to address any such accusation of threats, violence, harassment, or intimidation against any Muslim student on any campus in America in the wake of October 7th does not change this hope, but it does raise significant concern. We fear this oversight failure on the Committee's part will solidify the impression that this Committee is not interested in ensuring that all students have safe, nurturing learning environments.'').
\3\E.g. From Playground to Classroom: The Spread of Antisemitism in K-12 Schools Hearing Before the Subcomm. on Early Childhood, Elementary & Secondary Educ. of the H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, 119th Cong.
(2025) (statement of Ranking Member Rep. Suzanne Bonamici) (``Instead of offering any real solutions, Republicans use antisemitism as an excuse to turn our nation's civil rights laws upside down and undermine public education. We have seen this most prominently with higher education, and it is clear the committee is now seeking to do the same thing to our local public elementary, middle, and high schools. The reality is that the Trump Administration and Congressional Republicans are using the real plight of Jewish students experiencing antisemitism to destabilize institutions they don't approve of, whether institutions of higher education or teachers' unions.'').
H.R. 9203 IGNORES THE DISMANTLING OF ED OCR AND CIVIL RIGHTS
ENFORCEMENT
President Trump ran for re-election in part on a promise to shut down the U.S. Department of Education.\4\ A bi-partisan consensus of legal scholars agrees this is an act the President does not have the power to do.\5\ Nevertheless, his Administration is attempting to abolish the Department, with little apparent regard for the statutory duties Congress has placed on the Department and its offices. This is nowhere more obvious or impactful than in the Department's Office for Civil Rights.
\4\E.g., Graham Kates, Can Trump Dismantle the Department of Education? It Won't be Easy, Experts Say, CBS News (Feb. 4, 2025), https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-dismantle-education-department/; Time Staff, Read the Full Transcript of Donald Trump's 2024 Person of the Year Interview with TIME, TIME (Dec. 12, 2024), https://time.com/6972022/donald-trump-transcript-2024-election/.
\5\E.g., Laura Mannweiler, Can Trump Really Dissolve A Government Agency?, USNews, Feb. 11, 2025, https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/ articles/2025-02-11/can-trump-really-dissolve-a-government-agency-like-usaid-or-the-department-of-education.
OCR is the specific office charged in statute with enforcing Title VI education cases.\6\ OCR was one of the offices that lost the most employees (in both number and percentage) as a result of the Department's reduction-in-force in 2025.\7\ The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) documented how the Department paid OCR employees as much as $38 million to not work last year.\8\ The Senate HELP Committee Minority Staff recently reported that in 2025, OCR had lowest rate of resolved cases in over a decade, including zero resolution agreements in cases of racial harassment and discriminatory school discipline.\9\ The same Chairman that called up H.R. 9203 for consideration recently championed the interagency agreement (IAA) that sent the majority of OCR's investigatory work to the Department of Justice.\10\ It remains puzzling that this majority purports to champion civil rights enforcement while simultaneously supporting the destruction of the office charged with enforcing educational civil rights.
\6\Department of Education Organization Act, Pub. L. No. 96-88
Sec.  203, 93 Stat. 669 (1979).
\7\See U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. of the Inspector Gen., FLASH REPORT Review of U.S. Department of Education Changes in Staffing and Operations 5, June 2026, https://www.oversight.gov/sites/default/files/ documents/reports/2026-06/FY26%20F25DC0245%20%286.22.26%29v100_508_ SECURED.pdf (showing OCR lost a total number of employees second only to the Office of Federal Student Aid, and ranked 6th out of the 16 ED offices affected by the reduction in force by percentage of employees lost).
\8\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-26-108320, Department of Education: Full Costs and Savings Estimate Needed for Reduction-in- Force and Restructuring of the Office for Civil Rights 2 (2026), https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-26-108320.pdf.
\9\S. Comm. on Health, Educ., Lab., & Pensions, Minority Staff, Justice Denied: How Trump's Office for Civil Rights Reached a 12-Year Low in Protecting Students from Discrimination, (Apr. 28, 2026), https://www.sanders.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/ 04.24.26-Justice-Denied-How-Trumps-Office-for-Civil-Rights-Reached-a- 12-Year-Low-in-Protecting-Students-from- Discrimination_FINAL.pdf.
\10\Press Release, H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, Chairman Walberg Praises Trump for Putting Students First, Cutting Bureaucracy (June 16, 2026), https://edworkforce.house.gov/news/ documentsingle.aspx?DocumentID=413416.
Concurrent with this slowdown in complaint and case management, OCR has refocused its reduced capacity on a few key, politicized areas: Title IX cases where schools and colleges allow transgender students access to facilities or sports teams consistent with their gender identity; Title VI cases involving programming related to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI); and Title VI cases involving allegations of antisemitism.\11\ This is consistent with the warped approach to Title VI that has been embraced across Departments by this Administration.
\11\Rachel M. Perera, How the US Department of Education Has Turned Civil Rights Enforcement into a Discriminatory Tool, BROOKINGS, Feb. 20, 2026, https://www.brookings.edu/ articles/how-the-us-department-of-education-has-turned-civil-rights-enforcement-into-a-discriminatory-tool/.
H.R. 9203 IGNORES THE WARPING OF TITLE VI FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES
The administration hit the ground running on February 14, 2025, when the Department promulgated guidance in the form of a Dear Colleague Letter (DCL) that threatened to take away funding from any school that went beyond what they believed were the bounds of the Supreme Court's decision in Students for Fair Admissions (SFFA).\12\ In that case,the Court ruled against Harvard University's and the University of North Carolina's admissions processes that used race as one of many factors in college admissions decisions, saying they violated Title VI.\13\ The Court noted the decision was narrowly tailored to the controversy before it.\14\ However, in its guidance to schools, ED claimed that the SFFA decision went beyond admissions touching any consideration of race, including DEI, in education generally.\15\ Further, ED would have required schools to certify that they were complying with the viewpoints expressed in the guidance, leaving them liable to litigation if they were found to have certified falsely.\16\
\12\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. for C.R., Dear Colleague Letter: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act in Light of Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (Feb. 14, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/media/ document/dear-colleague-letter-sffa-v-harvard-109506.pdf; Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181 (2023).
\13\Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181, 230
(2023).
\14\600 U.S. at 208 (``These cases involve whether a university may make admissions decisions that turn on an applicant's race.''); 600 U.S. at 343 (``Answering the question whether Harvard's and UNC's policies survive strict scrutiny under settled law is straightforward, both because of the procedural posture of these cases and because of the narrow scope of the issues presented by petitioner Students for Fair Admissions, Inc.'') (Sotomayor, J., dissenting).
\15\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. for C.R., Dear Colleague Letter: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act in Light of Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard (Feb. 14, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/media/ document/dear-colleague-letter-sffa-v-harvard-109506.pdf (``Although SFFA addressed admissions decisions, the Supreme Court's holding applies more broadly. At its core, the test is simple: If an educational institution treats a person of one race differently than it treats another person because of that person's race, the educational institution violates the law.'').
\16\Id.; U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. for C.R., Reminder of Legal Obligations Undertaken in Exchange for Receiving Federal Financial Assistance and Request for Certification Under Title VI and SFFA v. Harvard (April 3, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/media/document/reminder-of-legal-obligations-undertaken-exchange-receiving-federal-financial-assistance-and-request-certification-under-title-vi-and-sffa-v-harvard-april- 3.pdf.

Regulatory actions at the General Services Administration and the Office of Management and Budget have both attempted to force recipients of federal assistance to certify their adherence to the Administrations' interpretations of Title VI and civil rights more broadly.\19\
