The Administration's radical interpretation of Title VI is most apparent in its ``investigations'' into antisemitism at prominent colleges and research universities. These investigations were used as justification to cancel hundreds of millions of dollars in federal grants and contracts at Columbia University, Harvard University, Brown University, the University of California, Los Angeles, and other schools.\20\ Resembling less a standard civil rights investigation and more of a ``shakedown'', many schools reached agreements with the Administration, desperate to restore needed funding.\21\ In the instances where schools pushed back, we have seen courts recognize these institutions were compliant with Title VI, and should not have had their funding cut.\22\ Further, recent whistleblower allegations suggest that some of these investigations were based not on factual or legal analysis but political priorities, with punishments in some cases being determined before investigations were even completed.\23\
\20\Ben Unglesbee, Tracking the Trump administration's deals with colleges, Higher Ed Dive https://www.highereddive.com/news/tracking-the-trump-administrations-deals-with-colleges/803434/ (last updated Dec. 2, 2025).
\21\Am. Ass'n of Univ. Professors, Extorted Compliance: A Threat to Institutional Autonomy, Academic Freedom, and Shared Governance, July 2026, https://www.aaup.org/reports-publications/aaup-policies-reports/topical-reports/extorted-compliance-threat-institutional.
\22\ President & Fellows of Havard College v. Dep't of Health & Hum. Svcs., 1:25-cv-10910-ADB (D. Mass., Sept. 3, 2025) (``That said, there is, in reality, little connection between the research affected by the grant terminations and antisemitism. In fact, a review of the administrative record makes it difficult to conclude anything other than that Defendants used antisemitism as a smokescreen for a targeted, ideologically-motivated assault on this country's premier universities, and did so in a way that runs afoul of the APA, the First Amendment and Title VI.'').
\23\Letter to The Hon. Chuck Grassley, et al, from Dana L. Gold et al., Gov't Accountability Project (Aug. 17, 2026), https://democrats-judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/democrats-judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/08.17.26-title-vi-whistleblower-disclosure-for-congress.pdf (``The disclosure presents information she reasonably believes evidences violations of law, rule, or regulation; gross mismanagement; gross waste of funds; and abuse of authority in connection with DOJ and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) leadership's handling of Title VI investigations concerning alleged antisemitic discrimination and harassment at Columbia, Brown, and Harvard Universities.'').
H.R. 9203 IGNORES THE ABANDONING OF DISPARATE IMPACT ANALYSIS TO FIGHT
RACIAL DISCRIMINATION
Data show that robust enforcement of compliance with Title VI's protections by programs receiving federal funds from the Department is necessary to achieve equity of educational opportunity.\24\ Remedies achieved through individual challenges under Title VI to discriminatory policies and practices were once an essential tool to bring about this robust enforcement, especially during periods of demonstrated hostility to proactive federal enforcement.\25\ Because racial discrimination is rarely explicit, identifying potential cases of discrimination by analyzing their impact--rather than just their motive--was critical to the enforcement of civil rights protections. Disparate impact theory was used for decades by private individuals in education settings, challenging practices that while facially race neutral, had an obvious disparate effect on Americans of different races or national origins.\26\ President Kennedy most eloquently explained the need for civil rights law to find violations linked to effect and not just to intent:
\24\U.S. Comm'n on Civil Rights, Are Rights a Reality? Evaluating Federal Civil Rights Enforcement 511, Nov. 2019, available at https:// www.usccr.gov/pubs/2019/11-21-Are-Rights-a- Reality.pdf.
\25\See Alexander v. Sandoval, 532U.S.275, 301-303(2001) (Stevens, J., dissenting).
\26\E.g. Lau v. Nichols, 414 U.S. 563 (1974).
``Simple justice requires that public funds, to which
all taxpayers of all races contribute, not be spent in
any fashion which encourages, entrenches, subsidizes,
or results in racial discrimination. Direct
discrimination by Federal, State, or local governments
is prohibited by the Constitution. But indirect
discrimination, through the use of Federal funds, is
just as invidious; and it should not be necessary to
resort to the courts to prevent each individual
violation.''\27\
\27\See H.R. Misc. Doc. No. 124, 88th Cong., 1st Sess. 3, 12
(1963).
In Alexander v. Sandoval,\28\ the Court overturned four decades of statutory protection against discrimination by removing the private right of action of individuals to bring cases based upon disparate impact, leaving federal agencies as the only entities that can enforce disparate impact regulations. Since 2001, private citizens may have their civil rights violated under Title VI in a way that can only be proven via a disparate impact test, but if the government is not willing to take administrative action on their behalf, they have no remedy.
\28\532 U.S. 275 (2001).
On April 25, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14281, denouncing disparate impact theory and directing the Attorney General ``to initiate appropriate action to repeal or amend the implementing regulations for Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 for all agencies to the extent they contemplate disparate-impact liability.''\29\ The Department of Education rescinded its Title VI regulations via a Final rule on July 24, 2026 without warning or opportunity for public comment.\30\ Following its regulatory retreat, the Department has also rescinded guidance related to school discipline--an area where studies have consistently found that Black and Brown students are disproportionately subject to exclusionary discipline (suspensions and exclusions) than similarly situated White students.\31\
\29\Exec. Order No. 14281, 90 Fed. Reg. 17537 (Apr. 28, 2025) (``It is the policy of the United States to eliminate the use of disparate-impact liability in all contexts to the maximum degree possible to avoid violating the Constitution, Federal civil rights laws, and basic American ideals.'').
\30\Rescinding Portions of the Department of Education Title VI Regulations To Align With the Statutory Text and Conform to Executive Order 14281, 90 Fed. Reg. 46733 (July 23, 2026).
\31\Press Release, U.S. Department of Education Directs Schools to Stop Racial Balancing in Student Discipline Policies, Investigates Two School Districts, Aug. 18, 2026, https://www.ed. gov/about/news/press-release/us-department-of-education-directs-schools-stop-racial-balancing-student-discipline-policies-investigates-two-school-districts; See Cory Turner, When Is Suspending Students Discrimination? Education Department Renews An Old Fight, Nat'l Pub. Radio, Aug. 25, 2025, https://www.npr.org/2026/08/25/nx-s1-5936474/discrimination-school-discipline-suspension-race-education-department-civil-rights, (``Multiple federal investigations have found that discrimination still plagues America's schools, even as it's been illegal for decades, thanks to federal civil rights law . . . . In late 2018, OCR reachedan agreement with Wake County Public School System in North Carolina after finding that, among other things, Black students being disciplined for their first offense were more likely to be suspended than similarly situated white students.'').
These are some, but not all of the actions taken by the Trump Administration that strongly suggest they are either unwilling or unable to enforce Title VI in a fair and equitable manner. They continue to try and turn Title VI on its head in an effort to turn the clock back on civil rights.
SUMMARY OF CONCERNS ON H.R. 9203
While it is not a fatal flaw, we are perplexed that H.R. 9203 places new requirements on compliance with Title VI, without amending Title VI itself. The decision to place requirements and penalties related to Title VI compliance in HEA was likely made to avoid amendment of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Such amendment would likely implicate the jurisdiction of the Committee on the Judiciary. But this is something the Committee has considered in the past and successfully overcome.
In 2019, then-Chairman Bobby Scott (D-VA) first introduced the Equity and Inclusion Enforcement Act (EIEA) in the 116th Congress.\32\ In addition to restoring the private right of action for disparate impact liability, the bill requires all recipients of federal funds under Title VI (K-12 schools and IHEs) to have Title VI Monitors, nearly identical to those required under Title IX, and similar to what is required under H.R. 9203. Unlike H.R. 9203, EIEA includes provisions that amend the Civil Rights Act of 1964--squarely in the jurisdiction of the Committee on the Judiciary--and provisions related to requirements of staffing at the Department of Education, squarely in the Committee on Education and Workforce's jurisdiction. In 2019, as the bill had been referred to both Committees, after our Committee marked the bill up, we were able to reach an agreement with the Judiciary Committee regarding a discharge of their consideration and the bill went to the floor and was passed.\33\ The Majority in this instance could have done the same thing with H.R. 9203 but chose not to. By choosing to limit the operative clauses to the HEA, the compliance provisions of H.R. 9203 do not apply to all educational settings receiving federal assistance, but just colleges and universities that participate in the Federal Student Aid program. K-12 schools and IHEs that do not participate in federal student aid, are not bound by H.R. 9203's requirements. The Majority should work with its counterparts on the Committee on the Judiciary to settle any lingering issues so that the scope of H.R. 9203 eventually mirrors that of Title VI itself, that is, all educational programs receiving federal assistance.
\32\Equity and Inclusion Enforcement Act, H.R. 2574, 116th Cong.
(2019); H.R. 3606, 119th Cong. (2025).
\33\166 Cong. Rec. H4473-74 (2020).
H.R. 9203 OCR Reforms are Unworkable and Inequitable

<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: In addition to the compliance requirements of H.R. 9203, the bill allows several reforms to the process by which OCR handles complaints it receives. Under H.R. 9203, OCR would be prohibited from dismissing Title VI complaints due to the filing of a complaint involving the same allegations with another Federal, State, or local agency or a court. OCR would be prohibited from delaying or pausing an investigation due to the filing of a similar complaint with another Federal, State, or local agency. H.R. 9203 would only allow OCR to pause an investigation because of a court filing.
OCR handles complaints based on violations of all educational civil rights laws in accordance with their Case Processing Manual. That manual spells out numerous situations under which OCR may dismiss cases. These dismissals are justified based on considerations OCR makes, as documented in one instance in the manual:
The same or similar allegation(s) filed with OCR
involve the same operative facts currently pending
before another federal, state, or local civil rights
enforcement agency or through a recipient's internal
grievance procedures, including due process
proceedings, and OCR anticipates that the allegations
will be investigated and that there will be a
comparable resolution process pursuant to legal
standards that are acceptable to OCR. OCR will advise
the complainant that she or he may re-file within 60
days of the completion of the other entity's action.
Generally, OCR will not conduct its own investigation;
instead, OCR reviews the results of the other entity's
determination and decides whether the other entity
provided a comparable resolution process in which it
applied comparable legal standards.\34\
\34\Off. for Civ. Rts., U.S. Dep't of Educ., Case Processing Manual, (2025), https://www2.ed.gov/about/offices/list/ocr/docs/ ocrcpm.pdf.
Based on the limited resources OCR has to investigate claims, and concerns about multiple investigations of the same situation by multiple agencies or courts potentially reaching different conclusions, OCR's current practice regarding cases that are pending with other agencies or courts makes sense. In 2024, the Department expressed concerns that this provision could make the case management at OCR harder, and it seems logical that such a rule could increase the overall number of complaints OCR has to investigate. Further, as drafted H.R. 9203 would create equity concerns. These new prohibitions would apply to Title VI cases only, situating them differently than all other cases at OCR. Further, as these prohibitions would not apply retroactively, H.R. 9203 would situate Title VI cases opened after the bill's passage differently than any Title VI cases opened prior to its passage. There are currently 959 records of complaints of Title VI racial harassment open at OCR,\35\ some stretching back to as far as 2012. Committee Democrats cannot support any bill that would somehow situate new cases more favorably than ones that have been waiting over a decade for resolution.
\35\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Off. for C.R., Pending Cases Currently Under Investigation and Elementary-Secondary and Post-Secondary Schools, https://ocrcas.ed.gov/open-investigations? (last updated Jan. 14, 2025). This does not include current open Title VI cases at OCR alleging violations relating to admissions policies, assignment of students, general compliance, denial of benefits, discipline, resource comparability, or retaliation. It also does not include the approximately 75 shared ancestry and national origin cases opened since October 7. 2023 Id. And, since the Trump Administration has not updated this web page since the taking office in January of 2025, the number is a rough estimate at best. Id.
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING CONSIDERATION
OF H.R. 9203
The concerns Committee Democrats have expressed around the OCR process reforms proposed in H.R. 9203 could be allayed somewhat if H.R. 9203 authorized sufficient funding to OCR to do its job and required the work of OCR actually be done at the Department. The Department has noted that from fiscal year (FY) 2013 to FY 2023, the number of complaints OCR has received rose by 93 percent, yet the number of investigative staff at OCR decreased slightly during that same period of time.\36\ This was before the dismantling actions that reduced OCR to a shell of its former self. Leading civil rights groups have suggested that OCR needs double the funding it received in FY 2024 to be effective.\37\ As such, Rep. Scott offered an amendment that would authorize $280 million for OCR. Such funding could help the Office address the backlog of current investigations and ensure that institutions receiving federal financial assistance follow civil rights laws that are enforced by the agency.
\36\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Fiscal Year 2025 Congressional Justification Office for Civil Rights, 13-14 (2024) https:// www2.ed.gov/about/overview/budget/budget25/justifications/dd-ocr.pdf (``As shown in the chart above, OCR continues to receive an unprecedented number of total complaints, which has increased 883% since 1983, more than tripled compared to 2003, and nearly doubled in the past decade.'').
\37\Letter from 92 Civil Rights Groups to President Joe Biden, (Feb. 14, 2024), https://civilrights.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ Double-the-Funding-for-ED-OCR.pdf.
This amendment was merely an authorization of funds, and not an appropriation--such an appropriation would not have been in order. But as we enter appropriations season on the floor, the amendment could have sent a bipartisan message to our colleagues on the Labor-HHS Appropriations Subcommittee that our Committee supports OCR and its work, and wants to provide it with the resources necessary to ensure it can do the work it is being tasked with. The amendment was defeated on a party line vote.
Recognizing the Administration has sought to effectively shutter OCR, Rep. Scott also offered an amendment requiring that any work OCR was required to do in H.R. 9203 be performed by the actual office. The amendment would prevent the Secretary of Education from using an Interagency Agreement or any other authority to accomplish this work outside of the Department of Education. The amendment was defeated on a party line vote.
CONCLUSION
We are concerned that the Committee does not recognize the importance of Title VI compliance. We must realize our responsibility to afford the protections of civil rights law to all students. As such, Committee Democrats cannot support reforms to OCR's case management process that could result in inequitable or unworkable situations within the office. Further, the Committee and this Administration have not lived up to their duty to ensure that hatred based on shared ancestry and ethnic characteristics, whether it be antisemitic, anti- Muslim, Islamophobic, anti-Palestinian, or against any other class protected in our civil rights law, is identified and rooted out of our higher education system. Congress must engage in rigorous oversight of the Administration to ensure that Jewish students and all their peers--regardless of their race, nationality, sexual orientation, or any other characteristic-- feel safe and welcome in their learning environments. It is our hope that the Committee will take such oversight action in the near future. But due to the current Administration's approach to civil rights, even if Committee Democrats were supportive of H.R. 9203, giving this administration additional tools they could use to increase racial discrimination would be unconscionable. As such, we cannot support H.R. 9203, and we would urge the House to oppose it as well.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Mark DeSaulnier,
Adelita Grijalva,
Members of Congress.

content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: Introduction
H.R. 5267, the American Franchise Act, creates a new narrow definition of joint employment under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) and National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) for franchisors and franchisees, thereby creating numerous carveouts and safe harbors to protect large franchisors from any liability for NLRA and FLSA violations their franchisees may make based on the franchisor's standards, policies, and direction. This bill risks allowing franchisors to coerce their franchisees into adopting potentially unlawful policies and practices while shielding those very franchisors from liability, leaving franchisees solely liable and workers without full access to justice. Congress should not be in the business of incentivizing unlawful behavior by large corporate franchisors or shielding them from accountability at the expense of workers and small business franchisees.
H.R. 5267 is opposed by the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO); Actors' Equity Association; American Federation of Teachers (AFT); Alliance for Retired Americans; Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU); American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE); American Federation of Musicians (AFM); American Federation of School Administrators (AFSA); American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees (AFSCME); Association of Flight Attendants-CWA; Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers and Grain Millers (BCTGM) International Union; Communications Workers of America (CWA); Department for Professional Employees, AFL-CIO (DPE); International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (IATSE); International Association of Bridge, Structural, and Ornamental Iron Workers (IW); International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM); International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers (SMART); International Brotherhood of Boilermakers; International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE); International Organization of Masters, Mates and Pilots (MM&P); International Union of Bricklayers and Allied Craftworkers (BAC); International Union of Elevator Constructors (IUEC); International Union of Painters and Allied Trades (IUPAT); International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW); Major League Baseball Players Association (MLBPA); Metal Trades Department, AFL-CIO; National Association of Letter Carriers (NALC); National Federation of Federal Employees (NFFE-IAM); National Nurses United (NNU); SAG-AFTRA; Seafarers International Union of North America; Service Employees International Union (SEIU); SMART Transportation Division; Transportation Communications Union/IAM; Union Veterans Council, AFL-CIO; UNITE HERE; United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW); United Mine Workers of America (UMWA); United Steelworkers (USW); USL Players Association; and the Utility Workers Union of America (UWUA).
Background
Labor and employment laws have long held that, where more than one entity controls terms and conditions of employment, an employee may have multiple employers. This is referred to as ``joint employment.'' Under both the FLSA and NLRA, determining joint employment relies on determining the degree of control an entity exercises over a worker, regardless of whether it is direct, indirect, or reserved control.\1\ A narrower definition of joint employment would make it easier for low-road businesses to evade liability for obligations under and violations of the NLRA and FLSA. H.R. 5267 does exactly that for franchisors.
\1\``Reserved control'' is the right an employer retains to exert control over an employee, even if it is not being currently exercised. As summarized by the Supreme Court in the common law context, ``the relation of master and servant exists whenever the employer retains the right to direct the manner in which the business shall be done, as well as the result to be accomplished, or, in other words, `not only what shall be done, but how it shall be done.''' Singer Mfg. Co. v. Rahn, 132 U.S. 518, 523 (1889) (quoting Railroad Co. v. Hanning, 82 U.S. 649, 657 (1872)).
THE FLSA AND JOINT EMPLOYMENT
Joint employment under the FLSA arises not only out of the definition of employer, which ``includes any person acting directly or indirectly in the interest of an employer in relation to an employee,''\2\ but also out of the broad ``suffer or permit'' definition of ``employ,'' which Congress borrowed from the early state child labor laws of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.\3\ State authorities used this broad language to hold businesses accountable for child labor violations despite arrangements such as the ``inside shop,'' where a manufacturer might subdivide the departments of the business into shops contracted out to other business operators, who all nevertheless contributed to the manufacturer's enterprise.\4\
\2\See 29 U.S.C. Sec. 203(d) (emphasis added).
\3\Bruce Goldstein et al., Enforcing Fair Labor Standards in the Modern American Sweatshop: Rediscovering the Statutory Definition of Employment, 46 UCLA L. Rev. 983, 991 (1999).
\4\Id. at 1057-58.
The Supreme Court first examined FLSA joint employment in the 1947 case Rutherford Food.\5\ In that case, a slaughterhouse operator retained an independent contractor to provide labor for a deboning process, and the deboning contractor directly hired workers to perform that work.\6\ The employees worked on the meatpacking company's premises, received cattle carcasses from the meatpacking company's employees, deboned the cattle using the meatpacking company's tools and equipment, and then conveyed the deboned cattle along an overhead rail to another room where the meatpacking company's employees continued processing the carcasses into food products.\7\ During this work, the deboning contractor's employees were supervised by one of the meatpacking company's ``managing official[s].''\8\ Taking account of ``the circumstances of the whole activity,'' the Court agreed with the U.S. Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division that the deboning employees constituted ``a part of the integrated unit of production under such circumstances that the workers performing the task were employees of the establishment.''\9\
\5\Rutherford Food Corp. v. McComb, 331 U.S. 722 (1947).
\6\Id. at 724-25.
\7\Id. at 726, 730.
\8\Id. at 730.
\9\Id. at 729-730.
More recently, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit advised that scrutiny of potential joint employer liability should focus less on the relationship between business and worker and more on the interrelationships of the businesses themselves.\10\ In Salinas, the Fourth Circuit considered wage theft allegations brought by workers employed by a drywall and framing subcontractor, which almost exclusively worked on jobs for a construction contractor that specialized in finishing interiors.\11\ Among other things, the contractor assessed the final work product of the subcontractor's employees and required the subcontractor to order re-execution of work the contractor deemed insufficient; mandated that the subcontractor's employees wear the contractor's logo and hold themselves out as employees of the contractor; and periodically instructed the subcontractor to dispatch workers to meet the contractor's needs.\12\ Finding that the contractor was indeed jointly liable with the subcontractor for FLSA violations, the Salinas court clarified that joint employment inquiry ``requires courts to determine whether the putative joint employers are not wholly disassociated or, put differently, share or codetermine the essential terms and conditions of a worker's employment.''\13\
\10\Salinas v. Commercial Interiors, Inc., 848 F.3d 125 (4th Cir. 2017).
\11\Id.
\12\Id. at 145-46.
\13\Id. at 139.
Joint employment is not a major factor in FLSA cases. The National Employment Law Project (NELP) reviewed FLSA enforcement and litigation in 2019 and found:
there are not very many joint employer cases overall,
as compared to other FLSA cases, despite the [business
community's] pronouncements that the joint employer
question is harming business . . . . NELP's research
and case compendium of joint employer cases shows that
the majority arise in FLSA cases brought by
agricultural workers, and over half of all cases do not
result in a finding of joint and several liability.\14\
\14\Christine Owens et al., Nat'l Emp. L. Proj., Comments on RIN 1235-AA26: Joint Employer Status Under the Fair Labor Standards Act 3 n.1 (June 25, 2019), https://s27147.pcdn.co/app/uploads/2019/06/ Comments-USDOL-Joint-Employer-Status-FLSA.pdf.
In sum, establishing joint employment liability under the FLSA is a comprehensive, case-by-case, and fact-specific process that requires flexibility to ensure that in the cases where joint employment liability is appropriate, workers can receive the justice to which they are entitled.
THE NLRA AND JOINT EMPLOYMENT
The NLRA's definition of ``employer'' contemplates that there can be joint employers in an employment relationship. Under Section 2(2) of the Act, the term ``employer'' includes ``any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly.''\15\ Likewise, the term ``employee'' is not limited to the employees of a particular employer. Section 2(3) of the Act states: ``The term `employee' shall include any employee, and shall not be limited to the employees of a particular employer, unless [the Act] explicitly states otherwise.''\16\
\15\See 29 U.S.C. Sec. 152(2) (emphasis added).
\16\See id. Sec. 152(3).
For most of the time since the 1935 enactment of the NLRA, the NLRB has held that an entity may be liable to bargain with the employees of a subcontractor as a joint employer even if its control over terms and conditions of employment was indirect, such as exercised through an intermediary, or reserved but not yet exercised.\17\ This traditional standard is consistent with the Supreme Court's requirement\18\ that the NLRB interpret the NLRA's definition of employer as consistent with the common law regarding the principles that govern ``master'' and ``servant'' relationships and that liability is determined by the degree of control the ``master'' has over the ``servant.''\19\ The NLRA's joint employment standard is also consistent with the legislative history of the NLRA's 1947 amendments, which explicitly aligned the NLRA's statutory definition of employee with the common law standard.\20\
\17\See, e.g., Floyd Epperson, 202 NLRB 23, 23 (1973) (finding proof of joint employment where client employer had ``some indirect control over [employees'] wages'' and ``some control, albeit indirect, over [employee] discipline''), enforced 491 F.2d 1390 (6th Cir. 1974); Franklin Stores Corp., 199 NLRB 52, 53 (1972) (upholding ALJ finding of joint employment where one employer, ``by virtue of the lease arrangement with'' the other employer, ``has the right to veto the employment of employees by'' the other ``and to insist on the discharge of employees by'' the other).
\18\See NLRB v. United Ins. Co. of America, 390 U.S. 254, 256
(1968) (requiring the Board to ``apply general agency principles in distinguishing between employees and independent contractors under the Act'').
\19\See Restatement (First) of Agency Sec. Sec. 2, 220, Am. Law Inst. (1933).
\20\See H.R. Rep. No. 80-510, at 32-33 (1947) (Conf. Rep.), reprinted in 1 Legislative History of the Labor Management Relations Act, 1947, at 536-37 (1948) (explaining the exclusion of independent contractors from the definition of employee in order to overturn a Supreme Court decision that ``held that ordinary tests of the law of agency could be ignored by the Board'' in determining the existence of employment relationships).
JOINT EMPLOYMENT AND THE FISSURED WORKPLACE

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: American Franchise Act
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: Joint employment is a flashpoint in labor and employment law because of the recent trend toward ``fissuring,'' or the disintegration of the firm through the use of overlapping arrangements of contracting, subcontracting, franchising, and temping.\21\ Fissuring is increasingly common in low wage industries, including but not limited to logistics,\22\ food service, retail, and janitorial services.\23\ Today, there are nearly 9 million Americans working at over 800,000 individual franchises.\24\ Fissured work arrangements are associated with increased incidence of a host of workplace violations.\25\
\21\See generally David Weil, The Fissured Workplace: Why Work Became So Bad for So Many and What Can Be Done to Improve It (2014).
\22\See, e.g., Stacy Mitchell & Olivia LaVecchia, Amazon's Stranglehold: How the Company's Tightening Grip Is Stifling Competition, Eroding Jobs, and Threatening Communities (Nov. 2016), https://ilsr.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/ ILSR_AmazonReport_final.pdf.
\23\See Catherine Ruckelshaus et al., Who's the Boss: Restoring Accountability for Labor Standards in Outsourced Work, Nat'l Emp. Law Proj. (May 7, 2014), https://www.nelp.org/app/uploads/2015/02/Whos-the- Boss-Restoring-Accountability-Labor-Standards-Outsourced-Work- Report.pdf.
\24\Franchising Economic Outlook, Int'l Franchise Ass'n (2026), https://indd.adobe.com/view/c09364f3-8c80-4b2f-bbcc-56414924ae67.
\25\Weil, supra note 21.
The rise of the ``fissured workplace'' makes FLSA enforcement challenging. For example, it can be difficult for workers experiencing wage theft at the bottom of a chain of contracts to collect stolen wages when the nominal employer is a fly-by-night staffing company. In such a case, the joint employer theory allows workers to seek their stolen wages from a larger company further up that chain, if that larger company shares power over the terms of employment.
Fissuring can also weaken workers' bargaining power. Absent the joint employment doctrine, workers hired by an intermediary firm but laboring for a larger, more powerful firm with actual control over their working conditions and wages will find it difficult to bargain meaningfully.
THE FRANCHISE MODEL AND JOINT EMPLOYMENT
In the franchise business model, the corporate parent or ``franchisor'' allows an independent business owner, or franchisee, to use its branding, business model, and other intellectual property. In return, the franchisee agrees to pay an upfront franchise fee, ongoing royalties, and is subject to the terms of the franchise agreement that sets operating, performance, and management standards for the franchisee.\26\
\26\Introduction to the Franchise Business Model, Int'l Franchise Ass'n, https://www.franchise.org/franchising-overview/introduction-to-the-franchise-business-model/ (last visited Aug. 19, 2026).
Despite claims that franchisees operate as independent small businesses, corporate franchisors can and do exercise significant amount of control over their franchisees. Through franchise agreements, brand standards, and operational requirements, franchisors often set operating hours, mandate staffing levels, require specific scheduling or payroll software, establish detailed rules for how work must be performed, and restrict who may work under a franchise agreement. For example, some fast-food franchisors provide their franchises with extensive operation manuals that set franchise requirements on everything from workers' training, dress, and appearance to approved food and merchandise suppliers to participation in advertising, sales promotions, and required computer systems.\27\
\27\Andrew Elmore, The Future of Fast Food Governance, Univ. of Pennsylvania Law Rev. Online (May 24, 2017), https://papers.ssrn.com/ sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2903691.
Franchisees are under immense pressure to conform with franchisor standards and directives and risk losing their businesses if they do not. This level of control and supervision meaningfully constrains and directs how franchisees conduct their day-to-day business and worker supervision. Adding to franchisees' constrictions, the American Franchise Act explicitly shields franchisors from any sort of liability for these sorts of practices when determining joint employment liability.
A Narrow Joint Employment Standard Will Harm Workers and Small
Businesses and Benefit Low-Road Employers
The American Franchise Act seeks to radically rewrite longstanding law by amending the FLSA and NLRA to dramatically narrow the standard for finding joint employer liability for franchisors and franchisees. The bill would limit the finding of joint employment liability to a franchisor's possession and exercise of ``substantial direct and immediate control'' over their franchisees' workers' terms and conditions of employment, such as their pay, hiring, firing, and scheduling. While this extremely narrow standard is problematic enough, the bill goes a step further by also creating explicit safe harbors in which certain actions that could normally be considered ``direct and immediate control, are carved out from being indicators of joint employment.
The bill would weaken enforcement under the FLSA, which also governs federal wage theft and child labor laws. By limiting FLSA liability only to franchisors that exercise ``substantial direct and immediate control,'' the American Franchise Act would allow franchisors to evade liability for unlawful business practices and technology requirements that could result in wage theft and child labor violations. Instead, the franchisee, who may be obligated to follow these unlawful practices if it wishes to comply with its franchise agreement, is left fully liable for any damages and other consequences caused by the franchisor.
This bill would also severely limit how unionized workers could effectively bargain over all of the terms and conditions of their employment under the NLRA, which provides private-sector workers the right to organize a union and collectively bargain with their employer.\28\ Under common law, the employer does not need to exercise substantial direct and immediate control in order to determine the essential terms and conditions of employment because a joint employer can limit the wages and benefits paid by the employees' direct employers through contractual arrangements, such as salary caps. By narrowing joint employment liability to only franchisors that exercise ``substantial direct and immediate control,'' workers for the franchisee would be unable to bargain with the franchisor that determines wages and other conditions, and the franchisee would be unable to meaningfully bargain with its employees on its own.
\28\See generally 29 U.S.C. Sec. 151-169.
The American Franchise Act would also create a safe harbor for franchisors to engage in worker retaliation. The bill allows franchisors to supervise a franchisee's workers--so long as it is not ``consistently and directly''\29\ exercised--and inform the franchisee of their ``opinions'' on the performance of employees, and whether they meet acceptable standards. Through this safe harbor, a franchisor could strongly encourage a franchisee to terminate a worker engaged in union organizing activity or who raises concerns about unlawful actions in the workplace and face zero consequences.
\29\The bill does not provide a definition of ``consistently and directly'' and instead only lists examples of supervision that would not constitute consistent and direct control, leaving a large degree of uncertainty regarding what qualifies as consistent and direct control. See American Franchise Act, H.R. 5267, 119th Cong. Sec. 20(a)(G)
(2025).
In sum, the American Franchise Act is bad for workers, bad for small business franchisees, and writes a blank check to big businesses to bully and control small businesses and their workers without any accountability.
Democratic Amendments Offered During the Markup of
H.R. 5267
Committee Democrats proffered two amendments to improve H.R. 5267. The first amendment would have struck the joint employment definition under the FLSA created by H.R. 5267 and replaced the joint employment definition under the NLRA with the more equitable and worker-friendly definition from the text of H.R. 20, the Protecting the Right to Organize Act.\30\ The second amendment would have established the right for franchisees to sue franchisors for damages if the franchisee is found liable for NLRA or FLSA violations due to franchisor-mandated policies or guidance. Committee Republicans rejected both amendments.
