content:
<Rep. Richard E. Neal>: Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 7972, the Taxpayer Workforce Modernization Act. This bill is not a serious modernization strategy for the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). It also does nothing to help taxpayers, efficiently administer the tax laws, lower costs, or address the affordability crisis.
This bill creates a new fellowship program to recruit 10 data scientists from the private sector at salaries of no less than a GS-15 and up to $400,000 (equivalent to the President's salary) to identify complex, new, or emerging tax issues. The data scientists are handpicked by the Commissioner and work at his direction. He also has authority to hire them at the conclusion of their fellowship.
The IRS already has a division dedicated to exactly that work, the Research, Applied Analytics and Statistics (RAAS) Division. The RAAS Division employs data scientists and technical experts who develop advanced tools to detect tax evasion, estimate the tax gap, and strengthen tax compliance. Ten data scientists cannot replace the tens of thousands of IRS employees no longer with the agency. The Trump Administration cut the IRS workforce by 27% (27,600 employees) and that includes a 27% cut to the RAAS Division. If the Majority is serious about hiring data scientists, it should restore full funding to the RAAS Division and hire them through the competitive hiring process.
Furthermore, this bill duplicates existing responsibilities while ignoring the real issue. We are against the pretense that a handful of data scientists can backfill the skilled and dedicated employees fired by the Trump Administration. The IRS has been stripped of its skilled personnel and the funding that it needs to do its job. This is not modernization but demolition.
We should be looking for real ways to help make the IRS more efficient, more effective, and better equipped to serve all taxpayers. Democrats invested $80 billion in the IRS through the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), but Republicans clawed back 90% of that funding. Modernization is an important goal and we support responsible innovation. Thus, we should fully restore the IRS budget, including the IRA investment.
For these reasons, we oppose this bill.
Sincerely,
Richard E. Neal,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Northern Nevada Economic Development and Conservation Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 2317, the Northern Nevada Economic Development and Conservation Act, is an extensive legislative package aimed at addressing a range of public land issues in Northern Nevada. In total, the bill, as ordered reported, proposes the conveyance of at least 9,500 acres of federal land for various public purposes and would direct the sale or exchange of up to approximately 356,100 acres. In addition to authorizing numerous conveyances and land sales, the bill would designate nearly 150,000 acres of wilderness and release approximately 50,000 acres from wilderness study areas in Douglas and Pershing counties.
Balancing conservation with development on U.S. public lands is a complex challenge that requires careful consideration of both environmental protection and economic growth. Public lands are valuable assets owned by all Americans, and their responsible management involves safeguarding essential ecosystems, wildlife habitats, and cultural heritage, while also encouraging sustainable development that benefits local communities and economies. H.R. 2317 is a genuine effort to strike this balance in Northern Nevada. That is why the bill has received significant local support.
However, H.R. 2317 will significantly impact public lands in northern Nevada, and there are lingering questions about the intent and design of certain details in the version of the bill that the Committee marked up. Most notably, Title V of the bill would authorize the sale of thousands of acres of public lands.
Sec. 512 would even authorize the sale of certain encumbered land to ``the owner of a mining claim, millsite, or tunnel site located on a portion of the encumbered land,'' effectively greenlighting the sale of public land directly to mining companies operating in the area. This would facilitate a broad expansion of mining activity without any federal review or a guarantee of a fair return for the American taxpayer.
The House Committee on Natural Resources plays a critical role in ensuring that federal lands are managed in a fair and equitable manner. Americans do not support the sale or transfer of public lands, and the Committee has a responsibility to fully vet these sweeping land disposals through the regular legislative process, ensure a fair return for taxpayers, and restore a genuine balance between economic development and permanent conservation.\1\ H.R. 2317 should not be an exception this rule. The House should accordingly consider further revisions to the bill or the possibility of advancing the bill as part of a larger, balanced agreement that reflects the interests of the full Nevada delegation.
\1\Vast Majority of Americans Oppose Selling or Closing Public Lands, New Poll and Report Reveal, Trust for Public Land (Apr. 16, 2025), Available online: https://www.tpl.org/media-room/vast-majority-of-americans-oppose-selling-or-closing-public-lands-new-poll-and-report-reveal.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: Health DATA Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 9228, the Health Data Access, Transparency, and Affordability (Health DATA) Act of 2026, amends the Employee Retirement Income Security Act\1\ (ERISA) to increase access to data by fiduciaries of employer-sponsored health benefit plans. Although this legislation seeks to address the shared, bipartisan goal of improving health care transparency, it lacks needed safeguards that would ensure data is used appropriately and that workers and their families are protected from discrimination and retaliation based on their health information and medical records. Committee Democrats are therefore unable to support this legislation in its current form.
\1\Pub. L. No. 93-406 (1974).
The Majority's decision to advance H.R. 9228 in a partisan manner is a regrettable departure from past collaborations between Committee Democrats and Republicans on similar issues. During the 118th Congress, the Committee on Education and Workforce (Committee) worked in a bipartisan manner to develop similar legislation, also entitled the Health Data Access, Transparency, and Affordability (DATA) Act (H.R. 4527), introduced by Reps. Lori Chavez-DeRemer (R-OR), Kathy Manning (D-NC), and Mark Takano (D-CA). The bill was reported favorably to the House of Representatives by the Committee on July 12, 2023,\2\ but was not ultimately enacted prior to the conclusion of the 118th Congress. Rather than continuing this collaborative process during the 119th Congress, the Majority instead chose to develop H.R. 9228 on a partisan basis without even conferring with any Committee Democrats, including one of the original bill's co-authors, Rep. Takano. As a result of this unusual and unnecessarily partisan process, the legislation appropriated the name, but not the substance, of the bill from the 118th Congress, and it contains serious flaws that jeopardize the privacy of workers and their families.
\2\H. Rept. 118-260 (2023).
CONGRESS SHOULD FOCUS ON RISING HEALTH CARE COSTS, INCLUDING WASTEFUL
SERVICE PROVIDER FEES AND CONFLICTS OF INTERESTS
High health care costs represent an urgent issue for consumers across America, who increasingly face unaffordable health insurance premiums and out-of-pocket expenses. In 2024, total national health expenditures in the United States reached $5.3 trillion or 18.0 percent of gross domestic product.\3\ Individuals' per capita health care spending has risen to $14,775, approximately double the average amount spent per capita in peer countries.\4\ These expenditures are heavily driven by high prescription drug prices and the rates charged by hospitals, physicians, and other health care practitioners.\5\ Additionally, this growing health care spending is also directly correlated with rising administrative costs associated with service providers, particularly for individuals with private health coverage.\6\
\3\Ctrs. for Medicare & Medicaid Servs., National Health Expenditures 2024 Highlights 1 (2026), https://www.cms.gov/files/ document/highlights.pdf.
\4\Imani Telesford et al., How Does Health Spending in the U.S. Compare to Other Countries?, Peterson-KFF Health Sys. Tracker (Mar. 11, 2026), https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/chart-collection/health-spending-u-s-compare-countries/.
\5\See Cong. Budget Off., The Prices That Commercial Health Insurers and Medicare Pay for Hospitals' and Physicians' Services (Jan. 2022), https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57778.
\6\See Linda J. Blumberg et al., Untangling the Complex Web: Summary of a New Expert Perspective, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Nov. 19, 2025), https://chir.georgetown.edu/untangling-the-complex-web-summary-of-a-new-expert-perspective/.
Employers who sponsor health plans often rely on a range of outside vendors who assist in administering and managing their plans. While many such service providers play a valuable role in delivering benefits, they can also be described as middlemen who create ``a complex web of common ownership, contracting arrangements, and financial deals which create an array of conflicts of interests and hidden flows of money.''\7\ These business models can have an inflationary effect on health care spending, ultimately at the expense of consumers who must shoulder rising premiums and cost-sharing.\8\ In 2019, for example, ProPublica found that insurers frequently pay commissions to brokerage service providers based on the number of employers they enroll in coverage.\9\ These fees are substantial, often between three to six percent of the plans' premiums, creating an incentive to further drive up health care spending.\10\
\7\Id.
\8\Id.
\9\Marshall Allen, Behind the Scenes, Health Insurers Use Cash and Gifts to Sway Which Benefits Employers Choose, ProPublica (Feb. 20, 2019), https://www.propublica.org/article/health-insurance-brokers-cost-commissions-bonuses.
\10\Id.
Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are one such service provider. PBMs contract with health plans to perform a number of services related to the administration of prescription drug benefits, including developing and maintaining lists of covered drugs (formularies), negotiating prices and rebates with drug manufacturers, and reimbursing pharmacies for drugs dispensed to plan participants.\11\ The opaqueness of PBM practices has received substantial scrutiny, resulting in major legislative reforms enacted by Congress in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026\12\ (CAA 2026) and a proposed rule issued by the U.S. Department of Labor earlier this year.\13\
\11\Christopher J. Sroka, Pharmacy Benefit Managers, Cong. Rsch. Serv. (Nov. 29, 2000), https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/20001129-- RL30754--ae8115ed5c22ac5d657bb297e78f9a8b62bd060f.pdf.
\12\Pub. L. No. 119-75, div. J, tit. VII (2026).
\13\Improving Transparency Into Pharmacy Benefit Manager Fee Disclosure, 91 Fed. Reg. 4,348 (Jan. 30, 2026), https:// www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-30/pdf/2026-01907.pdf.
Additionally, the majority of workers with job-based health benefits are covered through a self-insured plan, in which the employer bears the financial risk, rather than an insurer.\14\ Due to the complexity of administering such plans, employers generally contract with third party administrators (TPAs) to perform critical functions with respect to the plans.\15\ These TPAs are often owned by commercial insurers that, in turn, often own hospitals and physician groups, reflecting structural conflicts of interest that create misaligned incentives to the detriment of both plan sponsors and workers.\16\
\14\Christine Monahan, Questionable Conduct: Allegations Against Insurers Acting as Third-Party Administrators, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (Mar. 24, 2023), https://chir.georgetown.edu/questionable-conduct-allegations-insurers-acting-third-party-administrators/.
\15\Karen Handorf et al., Third-Party Administrators--The Middlemen of Self-Funded Health Insurance, Georgetown Ctr. on Health Ins. Reforms (May 28, 2025), https://chir.georgetown.edu/third-party-administrators-the-middlemen-of-self-funded-health-insurance/.
\16\Id.
THE COMMITTEE PREVIOUSLY WORKED IN A BIPARTISAN MANNER ON SIMILAR
LEGISLATION TO INCREASE SERVICE PROVIDER TRANSPARENCY
Despite the partisan nature of H.R. 9228, the Committee has a history of working in a bipartisan manner on similar legislation, namely, H.R. 4527, the Health DATA Act of 2023. The development of H.R. 4527 was a collaborative process that resulted in consensus legislation supported by both Committee Democrats and Republicans. The bill addressed ``gag clauses'' that prevent fiduciaries of group health plans from performing necessary oversight of their service providers, such as PBMs and TPAs. Congress initially attempted to prohibit such gag clauses in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021\17\ (CAA 2021), but that prohibition proved ineffective in practice.\18\ To address this issue, H.R. 4527 enhanced the CAA 2021 gag clause prohibition by:
\17\Pub. L. No. 116-260 (2020).
\18\See Sara Hansard, Employers Still Struggle to Access Insurers' Health Cost Data, Bloomberg Law (Feb. 22, 2024), https:// news.bloomberglaw.com/daily-labor-report/employers-still-struggle-to-access-insurers-health-cost-data.
• Prohibiting additional contract terms that
prevent group health plan fiduciaries from auditing
data held by plan service providers;
• Providing authority to the Secretary of
Labor to impose civil monetary penalties to ensure that
entities that are responsible for violations of the gag
clause prohibition are held liable, while clarifying
that PBMs may be penalized for violations;
• Voiding contract provisions that violate the
gag clause prohibition;
• Modifying the attestation process for
ensuring compliance; and
• Requiring the Department of Labor to provide
a report to Congress regarding the potential treatment
of data as a ``plan asset'' under ERISA.
H.R. 4527 was a carefully negotiated product introduced by a bipartisan group of Committee Members. It balanced the important interests of increasing transparency and ensuring data would be used for the appropriate purpose of auditing service providers to identify conflicts of interest and excessive fees. It ultimately passed the House as part of H.R. 5378, the Lower Costs, More Transparency Act of 2023,\19\ but was not enacted prior to the conclusion of the 118th Congress.
\19\H.R. 5378, 118th Cong. (2023).
H.R. 9228 FAILS TO ADEQUATELY PROTECT PRIVACY AND ENSURE DATA IS USED
PROPERLY
Although the subject matter of H.R. 9228 is generally similar to H.R. 4527, H.R. 9228 fails to strike the proper balance between transparency and privacy. H.R. 9228 would amend ERISA to increase the ability of group health plan fiduciaries to conduct oversight of plan service providers. Specifically, it would:
• Prohibit a number of contract terms between
group health plans and other entities that limit an
employer's access to health claim and encounter data
and any documentation supporting claim payment,
including patient medical records;
• Specify in detail the exact format in which
disclosures must be provided to group health plans,
including stating that such information must contain
``unmodified data;''
• Void contract terms that contain prohibited
gag clauses or other violations of ERISA, as well as
terms that indemnify certain individuals from liability
for penalties;
• Establish penalties for violations of the
existing gag clause prohibition; and
• Modify the attestation requirement for
ensuring compliance.
Unfortunately, as written, several of these provisions raise serious implementation and privacy concerns. Section 2(a) of H.R. 9228 amends section 408(b)(2) of ERISA to provide that data held by a service provider must be available to the responsible plan fiduciary of a group health plan for certain purposes. However, the scope of data subject to this provision extends far beyond the de-identified claims and encounter data contemplated in H.R. 4527 because H.R. 9228 includes ``any documentation, including medical records and policy documents, supporting claim payments.'' Additionally, the entities with whom such data can be shared under H.R. 9228 is vastly expanded to include not just the responsible plan fiduciary, but also ``the designated agent,'' a term not defined in either the legislation or current law. There are no explicit requirements that data provided contain any limitations on personal health information (PHI), either by restricting data to summary health information or fully de-identifying it in a manner consistent with regulations under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA).\20\
\20\45 C.F.R. Sec. 164.514.

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: Health DATA Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier>: This approach is troubling for privacy. There is no clear policy rationale for granting broad access to health data that has essentially no direct link to payment of plan benefits, such as medical records, in order to perform oversight of plan service provider compensation. Additionally, the vagueness of the legislation's reference to ``other supporting documentation'' suggests that sensitive personal information other than medical records could also be shared under this provision, potentially including PHI. It is not difficult to imagine how this kind of data disclosure could negatively impact workers. For example, medical records could contain specific information about behavioral health conditions, such as mental health issues.
The categories of individuals with whom health data must be shared under the bill is also broader than needed for performing fiduciary oversight of plan service providers. ``Designated agent'' is not defined in either the legislation or current law, but the bill notes that the term includes, at a minimum, ``the plan sponsor, the plan administrator, or a business associate.'' Under ERISA, the plan sponsor is generally the employer in the majority of plans, who may be performing settlor, rather than fiduciary, functions under ERISA.\21\ Other entities that characterize themselves as designated agents purportedly entitled to access this data could include outside vendors who may or may not be performing a fiduciary function. The authors of this legislation have failed to articulate any reason why this expansion is necessary and have neglected to place any guardrails on what specific purposes the data may be used for.
\21\See, e.g., Norman P. Stein and Dana M. Muir, Two Hats, One Head, No Heart: The Anatomy of the ERISA Settlor/Fiduciary Distinction
(2014), https://scholarship.law.ua.edu/fac_working_papers/155.
Although H.R. 9228 acknowledges that individuals described must comply with existing regulations under HIPAA, this offers little additional protection for privacy. Because this bill requires the sharing of plan data by service providers, it may be considered a ``disclosure required by law'' under HIPAA, which is an exception that allows the disclosure of PHI when it would otherwise be impermissible.\22\ Without additional protections that ensure only limited, necessary data is shared with appropriate entities, the bill's privacy provisions simply restate current law and provide little additional assurance for workers and their families.
\22\45 C.F.R. Sec. 164.512(a).
COMMITTEE DEMOCRATS OFFERED AN AMENDMENT TO IMPROVE THE BILL AND
RESTORE THE PREVIOUSLY BIPARTISAN PROCESS
During the markup of H.R. 9228, Rep. Takano offered an amendment that would have restored the bipartisan work that began in 2023 while taking additional steps to strengthen the bill. His amendment, which has since been introduced as standalone legislation, H.R. 9486, the Health DATA Act of 2026,\23\ largely reflected the approach taken in the bipartisan 2023 legislation while making several additional improvements.
\23\H.R. 9486, 119th Cong. (2026).
Critically, the amendment would have limited the scope of data to that which is currently described in the existing statutory gag clause prohibition.\24\ Unlike H.R. 9228, the amendment would not have provided an open-ended grant of authority to access medical records and other documents, and any information shared would have been required to be fully de-identified in a manner consistent with HIPAA regulations at 45 C.F.R. Sec. 164.514. Additionally, such data would have been available for the specific, limited purpose of conducting audits of service providers to ensure compliance with title I of ERISA or the terms of the plan and to identify unreasonable compensation.
\24\29 U.S.C. Sec. 1185m(a)(1).
The amendment would also have clarified that individuals with any authority over plan data must handle that data in a manner consistent with ERISA's fiduciary standards. While plans and service providers should already behave in this manner, it is unclear the extent to which they do so. Clarification that ERISA's fiduciary standard applies to any entities exercising any control over plan data, including PBMs and TPAs, would have ensured that service providers can be held accountable for charging excessive fees or engaging in self-dealing. It would also have ensured that data is handled prudently, including through appropriate actions to protect privacy and implementing best practices with respect to cybersecurity.
Finally, the amendment would have provided strong protection for workers and their families against discrimination and retaliation based on plan data. It would have expressly prohibited employers, plan sponsors, administrators, or fiduciaries from using health plan data to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or discriminate against participants or beneficiaries. This prohibition would have been enforced by the Department of Labor through a civil monetary penalty and a private right of action with appropriate remedies to ensure individuals are made whole.
During debate on the amendment, Committee Republicans failed to offer a meaningful justification for their position and incorrectly described the policy effect of H.R. 9228. When offering his amendment, Rep. Takano correctly stated that under H.R. 9228, employers would be granted direct access to employee medical records. Rep. Robert Onder (R-MO) disputed this fact, stating: ``Nothing in this bill would give employers access to medical records. It gives employers much needed access to claims data.''\25\ Ranking Member Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott (D- VA) corrected the record, reading directly from the legislation:
\25\Comm. on Educ. and Workforce Democrats, Markup: H.R. 8476, 4795, 9203, 2555, H.R. 5505, 2332, 4122, 8822, 8823, 9381, and 9228, 3:29:30, YouTube (June 25, 2026), https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=zwlZN-WEo58.
The Gentleman from California said all that needed to
be said except for--[on] the question of medical
records--on page 2 it says on line 22, ``No contract or
arrangement for services [. . . .] is reasonable within
the meaning of this paragraph unless such contract . .
. . allows . . . . access to . . . . any documentation,
including medical records.'' So, it looks like you can
get people's medical records under the bill. That's
what the gentleman from California is trying to
fix.\26\
\26\Id. at 3:31:35.
The Majority did not provide any response to Ranking Member Scott on this point. Following the conclusion of debate, the amendment was rejected and the legislation was reported favorably by the Committee on a party-line vote of 18 yeas and 15 nays.
CONCLUSION
Although Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 9228 in its current form, we share the Majority's goal of improving health care transparency. As Congress moves forward with legislation to increase health care transparency, it must do so in a manner that properly balances the equities of improving transparency with the imperative of ensuring proper management of health data. To that end, the Majority should return to the bipartisan process begun in 2023 while working to ensure proper guardrails are in place to protect workers and their families.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Mark DeSaulnier,
Members of Congress.

bill_title: CRUISE Act
content:
<Rep. Mark Takano>: Ranking Member Takano and Committee Democrats echo the Majority's frustrations with the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA's) inability to process Adaptive Automobile Equipment (AAE) invoices in a timely manner. Failure to do so puts stress on the businesses providing these necessary adaptations to veterans and risks these businesses leaving the veteran vehicle adaptation space. The Committee must address this issue; however, H.R. 7083 falls short of adequately doing so. Background
AAE claims are fairly unique in VA in that two separate agencies within VA are required to process each claim (the Veterans Health Administration [VHA] and the Veterans Benefits Administration [VBA].) Within VHA, the claims are organized at the Medical Center (VAMC) level (170 nationwide), while at VBA they are processed at Regional Offices (ROs, generally one per state with a few in territories/overseas and a couple states having multiple.) To pass claims and information between the agencies, there is not a dedicated IT system. Assigned claims processors scan and email documents back and forth.
At VAMCs, the claims processors can have multiple duties and tend not to stay in the position for long. This means that an employee receiving an AAE claim may need training to properly process it and that claims can easily be lost/delayed because they are emailed to an employee no longer in the position or with the agency. Companies have often expressed frustration due to an inability to reach a point of contact to find out the status of a claim or determine corrections that need to be made.
At ROs, a variety of VA related claims are processed (VA education, Veteran Readiness & Employment, Disability, etc.) AAE claims are a very small portion of the overall number of claims that ROs receive, and AAE claims require specific expertise to process correctly. ROs tend to have a small handful of people trained on AAE claims, but not enough come in for those employees to only work on AAE claims or maintain proficiency. AAE claims are also not tracked in the same systems as the rest of VBA claims. They are received via email from VHA and then must be input into VBA systems for processing/payment. If errors or missing information are identified, the claims processor must come out of the system and email the VHA representative to email the company to send a correction back by email to VHA, who then has to send it back to VBA. It is easy to see how claims can be lost, delayed, or stuck in limbo with so many single points of failure.
Companies that make the AAE adaptations and are attempting to get paid by the VA are often frustrated that the process seems to change depending on which VAMC they are working with. Businesses are also rightly upset that processing times can be ridiculously long because claims packets get lost in the email back and forth or due to employees swapping out, with no one able to track down where the packet is in the process or the issue causing the delay. Addressing the Problems
The VA needs strong leadership from the Department level to direct and oversee the cross-agency collaboration needed to process these claims. The responsible program offices at VHA and VBA need to be held accountable to standardize the process. Positions need to be staffed, and knowledge management processes must be implemented to ensure claims reach completion and issues with individual claims can be remedied.
VBA should be encouraged to centralize processing at several ROs. This is a common practice at VBA for types of claims that require specialization to process correctly or do not have enough volume at individual ROs to keep employees engaged full time. (VBA does this for VA education, Agent Orange, Blue Water Navy, and Military Sexual Trauma claims, to name a few.) Committee Democrats would recommend against reducing it to one RO (as this bill does) as VBA best practices have found that having between 2-5 ROs with specialty teams helps mitigate issues like time zones, weather/facilities closures, and regional specific issues.
VA also needs an IT solution processing these claims. Emailing scanned documents back and forth between agencies only invites delays and failure into this process. Having the claims documents in one database that can be uploaded to/accessed by the claimant, VHA, and VBA would simplify and speed up the process. It would allow proper oversight, standardize the process, identify where claims are stuck, and provide updates to the claimant about timeline for payment. It would also help identify who should be held responsible for failures to process claims in a timely and accurate manner. Shortfalls of the Bill as Written
While Committee Democrats appreciate the Majority taking up the issue, the legislation as written has several shortfalls. The bill directs VA to make payments promptly, but contains no resources to make that happen, no incentives to encourage VA leadership to focus on making it happen, and no penalties to motivate VA to correct itself when it fails to do so. VA is already required to make these payments in a timely manner, but has not prioritized doing so. This legislation does not meaningfully change the status quo.
The Majority's approach to legislating without oversight also falls short. Requiring VA to conduct frequent updates or meet with the Committee would drive faster change in the Department. Holding a hearing or series of hearings on the topic would have forced VA leadership to own the problem and focus on fixing it. The bill does not even create or designate an official to be held accountable for fixing the problem going forward. Attempting to legislate a solution a few months before the end of a Congress realistically means that any solution is likely punted to years in the future.
The legislation also requires no planning for an IT solution or set aside funding for creating one. It is unlikely VA starts planning one under its own volition for a variety of reasons, so Congress failing to direct them to do so means that veterans, companies, and claims processors will be stuck in the status quo of emailing documents back and forth.
Minority Democrats are glad some of the more destructive ideas from the Majority's first drafts were removed, but this version is still lacking. If this bill becomes law as written, this Committee and Congress will likely be trying to address this issue yet again in a future Congress.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.

committee_name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
bill_title: Equal Campus Access Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Lucy McBath, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 5505, the Equal Campus Access Act of 2026, prohibits federal funding to public institutions of higher education (IHEs) that deny religious student organizations any benefit that is afforded to other student organizations because of the religious student organization's beliefs, practices, speech, leadership standards, or standards of conduct.\1\ Supporters of H.R. 5505 claim that the legislation will give religious groups the same rights as other student organizations.\2\ In reality, H.R. 5505 would give special treatment to religious student organizations by exempting them from rules that apply to all other officially authorized student clubs, if those rules conflict with the religious practices, standards, etc. of the religious student organization. It also advances the rights of religious student organizations at the expense of the rights of students who seek to participate in such student organizations.
\1\H.R. 5505 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2025).
\2\Press Release, Rep. Tim Walberg, WSJM: Walberg praises legislation seeking recognition of religious groups on college campuses (July 24, 2026), https://walberg.house.gov/media/in-the-news/wsjm-walberg-praises-legislation-seeking-recognition-religious-groups-college.
Public institutions of higher education are state actors and must already comply with First Amendment protections related to speech, religion and association.\3\ H.R. 5505 puts the religious liberty right of student organizations to discriminate over the right of public IHE students to be free from discrimination. Lastly, H.R. 5505 must be examined against the backdrop of actions by the Trump Administration to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education (ED or Department) and the failure of this Committee to address this Administration's illegal actions. The Committee has not held a single hearing addressing the dysfunction caused by the Trump Administration at the Office for Civil Rights and its failure to address discrimination against students whose rights have been violated under federal civil rights laws.\4\ Yet, Committee Republicans have repeatedly advanced legislation, including H.R. 5505, in the 119th Congress that add to the Department's responsibilities under federal education law; notwithstanding the fact, the Department cannot fulfill its current statutory responsibilities.\5\
\3\E.g. Healy v. James, 408 U.S. 169 (1972) (``[S]tate colleges and universities are not enclaves immune from the sweep of the First Amendment.'').
\4\Minority Staff Report of the S. Comm. on Health, Educ., Lab. & Pensions, Justice Denied: How Trump's Office for Civil Rights Reached a 12-Year Low in Protecting Students from Discrimination, (April 28, 2026), https://www.sanders.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/04.24.26- Justice-Denied-How-Trumps-Office-for-Civil-Rights-Reached-a-12-Year- Low-in-Protecting- Students-from-Discrimination_FINAL.pdf.
\5\See, e.g., H.R. Rep. No. 119-442 (2026) (H.R. 2617, Say No to Indoctrination Act); H.R. Rep. 119-460 (2026) (H.R. 6502, College Financial Aid Clarity Act of 2025); H.R. Rep. 119-461 (2026) (H.R. 6498, Student Financial Clarity Act of 2025); Student Protection and University Accountability Act, H.R. 9203, 119th Cong. (as reported by H. Comm. On Educ. and Workforce, June 25, 2026); and Protect Economic and Academic Freedom of 2025, H.R. 4795, 119th Cong. (as reported by H. Comm. Educ. and Workforce, June 25, 2026).
CONCERNS
H.R. 5505 undermines rules for student organizations to ensure they are
open to all students
If enacted, H.R. 5505 could undermine nondiscrimination rules adopted by public IHEs to ensure all students can fully participate in officially recognized student organizations. These organizations are an important part of campus life providing students with social, mental and academic benefits.\6\ The opportunity for students to both join and lead student groups is an essential part of the collegiate experience. Recognized student groups often receive funding collected from mandatory student activity fees and access to other school resources. Many colleges and universities adopt nondiscrimination policies that prohibit officially recognized student organizations from discriminating against students on protected characteristics, e.g., race, sex, etc. Some schools adopt all-comers policies which allow any student to join, participate in, and seek leadership in officially recognized groups.\7\ As public entities, public IHEs have an obvious interest in preventing their funds provided to student organizations from being used for discriminatory purposes.
\6\See e.g., Ricardo Montelongo, Student Participation in College Student Organizations: A Review of Literature, 2002 J. of the Indiana Univ. Student Pers. Ass'n 50-63.
\7\Christian Legal Soc'y v. Martinez, 561 U.S. 661, 671 (2010). Christian Legal Society (CLS) claimed that U.C. Hastings Law School's all-comers policy for official clubs interfered with its First Amendment rights to free speech, expressive association, and free exercise of religion. Hastings Law School has an open membership policy for all officially sanctioned student groups--all groups must accept any student who wishes to be a member, without regard to their personal beliefs or status. In lieu of official recognition, Hastings Law School offered CLS access to school facilities and other resources to conduct its meetings. See also Am. C.L. Union, What Does the United States Supreme Court's Decision in Christian Legal Society v. Martinez Tell Us about University Nondiscrimination Policies?, https://www.aclu.org/ sites/default/files/field_document/cls_fact_sheet_final.pdf (last visited July 29, 2026).
H.R. 5505 ignores this interest against discrimination and establishes a policy of special treatment for religious student organizations, over secular student organizations, as it pertains to an institution's rules. H.R. 5505 prohibits a public IHE from denying any benefit to a religious student organization ``because of the religious beliefs, practices, speech, leadership standards, or standards of conduct of the religious student organization.''\8\ What recourse then, would a female student interested in leading a campus religious student organization have in the circumstance where the organization has a stated practice, as a religious matter, that women cannot hold leadership positions within the organization?\9\
\8\H.R. 5505 Sec. 2, 119th Cong. (2025).
\9\As a condition of receiving federal financial assistance, institutions of higher education are prohibited from discriminating on the basis of sex in its programs or activities. 20 U.S.C. Sec. 1681 et. seq. Yet, under H.R. 5505, an institution also faces potentially having funds withheld from a failure to accommodate a religious student organization's practice that could discriminate on the basis of sex.
As a result, H.R. 5505 could threaten public IHE's federal funding under the HEA unless they exempt religious student organizations from nondiscrimination rules that apply to all other student organizations. H.R. 5505 directly conflicts with nondiscrimination and all-comer policies, some of which are required by state and local laws, that many public IHEs have enacted to ensure so all students may participate in and take advantage of the opportunities offered by student organizations.\10\ It could also sweep so broadly as to undermine nondiscrimination protections under federal civil rights laws.\11\ It would impose on institutions ``the daunting task of trying to determine whether a student organization cloaked prohibited status exclusion [discrimination] in belief-based garb.''\12\ Moreover, H.R. 5505 would hand the Trump Administration another tool in its enforcement arsenal to withhold HEA title IV (Title IV) student aid from institutions.
\10\Letter from Ted Mitchell, Pres., Am. Council on Educ., to the Hon. Miguel Cardona, Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Educ., commenting on Proposed Rescission of Religious Student Organizations Rule (Feb. 22, 2023), https://www.regulations.gov/comment/ED-2022-OPE-0157-42961 (``For some public institutions, the current regulations have forced them to choose between aligning with state and local non-discrimination laws and maintaining eligibility for federal grant funding. For those public colleges and universities that choose to comply with the regulations, they run the risk of a legal challenge grounded in state and local non-discrimination laws.'').
\11\Letter from Aditi Fruitwala & Heather L. Weaver, Am. C.L.Union, to Ashley Clark, U.S. Dep't of Educ., commenting on Proposed Rescission of Religious Student Organizations Rule (March 23, 2023), https:// www.regulations.gov/comment/ED-2022-OPE-0157-43795.
\12\Christian Legal Soc'y, supra note 7, at 664.
The Committee received a letter signed by 25 civil rights, faith, religious freedom, education, LGBTQ+, and women's rights organizations opposing H.R. 5505.\13\ The letter states, in part:
\13\Letter from 25 civil rights, faith, religious freedom, education, LGBTQ+, and women's rights organizations to Chair. Tim Walberg & Ranking Member Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott re: H.R. 5505 (June 25, 2026), on file with the Committee.
Schools would have to give funding and recognition to a
religious student group that turned away a student who
is gay or a single mother. This is wrong--
discrimination has no place on our public university
campuses. This bill is not required by the First
Amendment. Any student club can become a recognized
group and access funds if it adheres to its school's
nondiscrimination policy.\14\
\14\Id.
The language in H.R. 5505 is so broad that the bill can even be interpreted to potentially shield religious student organizations from an institution's standards of conduct barring student organizations from engaging in hazing and other harmful conduct. While most student organizations enrich campus life for students, they can also be a source of behaviors that are harmful to students. A landmark National Study on Student Hazing found that college students reported experiencing hazing in a wide variety of student clubs and organizations, including in religious student organizations.\15\ Some religious student organizations have been found engaging in harassing and other harmful behaviors towards students on campus.\16\ One such organization has previously been banned from more than 39 college campuses for harassing conduct.\17\ Under H.R. 5505, institutions may have no recourse against a religious student organization which violates institutional policies, if such conduct is represented as a part of a religious practice.
\15\Elizabeth J. Allan & Mary Madden, Hazing in View: College Students at Risk, StopHazing.org (March 11, 2008), https:// stophazing.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/hazing_ in_view_web1.pdf.
\16\Melanie Zelle, ``Afraid of Damnation'': Inside a Christian Campus Group's Controversial Past and Present, The Phoenix (April 25, 2025), https://swarthmorephoenix.com/2025/04/17/afraid-of-damnation-inside-a-christian-campus-groups-controversial-past-and-present/; and ASU reportedly disciplines church for hazing, stalking students, KTAR.com (July 18, 2017), https://ktar.com/arizona-news/asu-reportedly-disciplines-church-hazing-stalking-students/1661467/.
\17\Zelle, supra note 16.
H.R. 5505 elevates some student First Amendment rights above others
In the 2010 case Christian Legal Society v. Martinez,\18\ the Supreme Court held that Hastings Law School, a public IHE, did not violate the First Amendment by refusing to recognize a religious student organization that discriminated against LGBTQ+ students, non-Christian students, and any student that failed to adhere to the organization's statement of faith in violation of the school's all-comers policy for officially recognized clubs.\19\ Justice Ginsburg, writing for the majority said,
\18\Christian Legal Soc'y, supra note 7.

content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Lucy McBath, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: \19\Id. at 672. CLS's statement of faith would exclude from participation any student who engages in same-sex conduct and any student who holds different religious convictions than those established in the statement of faith. Id.
``[Christian Legal Society (CLS)], it bears emphasis,
seeks not parity with other organizations, but a
preferential exemption from Hastings' policy. The First
Amendment shields CLS against state prohibition of the
organization's expressive activity, however
exclusionary that activity may be. But CLS enjoys no
constitutional right to state subvention of its
selectivity.''\20\
\20\Id. at 669.
Though CLS refused to alter its policies to open its organization to all students to gain official recognition, Hastings Law School nonetheless offered CLS access to its facilities for meetings and activities.\21\ The Court noted that ``Hastings . . . is dangling the carrot of subsidy, not wielding the stick of prohibition'' in its implementing the all-comers policy for its official student organizations, which receive access to funding.\22\ In other words, Hastings was not barring CLS from campus for its choice to discriminate, it merely prevented it from becoming an official student group which receives funding paid for with fees collected from all students because it chose to discriminate. CLS could reverse course and welcome all students if it chose and receive funding.
\21\Id. at 673.
\22\Id. at 683.
H.R. 5505 would place the First Amendment rights of religious organizations above all other rights, as it could provide exemptions for religious student organizations when their practices conflict with the rules established for all other student organizations. In the end, students will be harmed. In fact, H.R. 5505 would in some cases require students--who must pay activity fees to fund student clubs-- subsidize groups that discriminate against them. As a result, H.R. 5505 would interfere with institutional policies that are permissible under the First Amendment and designed to maximize participation in officially recognized student organizations.\23\
\23\However, the First Amendment requires public IHEs to administer its policies for student organizations in an even-handed manner. Several recent lower court cases have affirmed religious student organizations' challenge to nondiscrimination policies due to the schools' uneven enforcement of its own nondiscrimination policies. See, e.g., InterVarsity Christian Fellowship v. Wayne State University, The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, https://becketfund.org/case/ intervarsity-christian-fellowship-v-wayne-state-university/ (last accessed July 30, 2026).
H.R. 5505 goes further than the 2020 Trump Administration Regulation
Supporters of H.R. 5505 claim that the legislation is intended to codify a regulation put in place by the first Trump Administration.\24\ In 2020, the Department finalized a rule (2020 Final Rule) to prohibit public IHEs from denying a religious student organization any benefits that are otherwise afforded to other student organizations because of the organization's ``beliefs, practices, policies, speech, membership standards, or leadership standards, which are informed by sincerely held religious beliefs.''\25\ The 2020 Final Rule applies to several grant programs under HEA, but it does not apply to funding associated with student financial aid.\26\ In contrast, H.R. 5505 applies to the entirety of funding for Title IV student financial aid.
\24\Press Release, Rep. Tim Walberg, Walberg, Lankford, Scott Introduce Equal Campus Access Act (Sept. 18, 2025), https:// walberg.house.gov/media/press-releases/walberg-lankford-scott-introduce-equal-campus-access-act.
\25\Direct Grant Programs, State Administered Formula Grant Programs, Non Discrimination on the Basis of Sex in Education Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance, Developing Hispanic Serving Institutions Program, Strengthening Institutions Program, Strengthening Historically Black Colleges and Universities Program, and Strengthening Historically Black Graduate Institutions Program, 85 Fed. Reg. 59916, 59943 (Sept. 23, 2020) (codified at 34 C.F.R. Sec. 75.500(d) and 34 C.F.R. 76.500(d) (hereinafter 2020 Final Rule).
\26\Id. at 59924.
Furthermore, the preamble to the 2020 Final Rule states that public institutions may still adopt ``all-comers'' policies under the rule, as long as religious student organizations are not treated any differently than other student organizations.''\27\ H.R. 5505 fails to provide the assurance found in the 2020 Final Rule, that all-comer policies would be permissible.\28\ It should be noted, however, there is nothing in the plain regulatory text\29\ in the 2020 Final Rule that could be read to allow IHEs to adopt all-comer policies and still be in compliance.\30\ As a result, H.R. 5505 will only add to the confusion for public IHEs in terms of what policies they will be able to apply to their official student organizations. Lost in this debate are the students who could be denied opportunities to join and seek leadership positions in officially recognized organizations that are funded by them with their mandatory student activity fees.
\27\Id. at 59966.
\28\In 2023, the Biden Administration proposed rescinding the 2020 Final Rule, reasoning, in part, that the 2020 Final Rule created confusion because it could be construed to require IHEs to afford preferential treatment and prohibit IHEs from applying neutral and generally applicable nondiscrimination policies. See Direct Grant Programs, State-Administered Formula Grant Program, 88 Fed. Reg. 10857 (Feb. 22, 2023) (proposed rescission of 34 C.F.R. Sec. 75.500(d) and 76.500(d)) (hereinafter Proposed 2020 Recission). On December 26, 2024, the Biden Administration withdrew the proposal to rescind the regulation citing in part to the upcoming change in administration. See Direct Grant Programs, State-Administered Formula Grant Programs; Withdrawal, 89 Fed. Reg. 104935 (Dec. 26, 2024) (withdrawal of proposed rescission of 34 C.F.R. Sec. Sec. 75.500(d) and 76.500(d)) (hereinafter 2020 Recission Withdrawal).
\29\See 34 C.F.R. Sec. 75.500(d); 34 C.F.R. Sec. 76.500(d).
\30\Proposed 2020 Recission, supra note 28, at 10860 (``There is nothing in the regulatory text that clarifies or guarantees that an institution may insist that such religious organizations comply with the same neutral and generally-applicable practices, policies, and membership and leadership standards that apply equally to nonreligious student organizations, including but not limited to nondiscrimination requirements.'').
In the end, H.R. 5505 would have the effect of codifying the 2020 Final Rule with a broader application to the entirety of HEA, including Title IV student financial aid. As a result, H.R. 5505 would enshrine in law a policy to give religious student organizations preferential treatment, exempting religious student clubs from nondiscrimination and potentially other requirements that apply to all other officially recognized student organizations.
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 5505
Committee Democrats put forward two amendments. The amendment offered by Rep. Lucy McBath (D-GA) would have ensured that public IHEs may deny privileges to student organizations, including religious student organizations, that violate institutional policies related to nondiscrimination and anti-hazing. The second amendment offered by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR) prohibited the use of interagency agreements related to enforcement of requirements for campus access for religious student organizations and requires the Secretary of Education to carry out enforcement of the provisions of H.R. 5505, as it amends HEA. Both amendments failed on party lines.

bill_title: Veteran Infection Prevention Act
content:
<Rep. Mark Takano>: Committee Democrats appreciated the opportunity to work with Committee Republicans prior to the May 14, 2026, full Committee markup to make technical corrections to the text of H.R. 8052 to improve the policy. Such changes included the provision of a scholarship to attain the certification required by H.R. 8052, as well as a two-year window for current VA staff to obtain such certification, so as to not make this requirement financially restrictive or have it serve as a barrier for an already hard to recruit and hard to retain position.
Despite these changes, Committee Democrats recommend additional amendments to the text to fully ensure that H.R. 8052 meets the needs of the current and future VA sterile processing workforce. For example, during the Subcommittee consideration of this text on March 25, 2026, Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee Members and witnesses discussed the existence of VA's internal certification course, the VA Certified Registered Medical Supply Technician (VA-CRMST) course. This course is designed with VA employees and workloads in mind and was developed to be completed during the workday with no individual expenses by the VA employee.
The text of H.R. 8052 does not include a definition for ``accredited institution'', nor does it delineate which courses must be included in the training program, or the standards it must train to. The text also does not include a reference to the specific accrediting body that would accredit such course or institution. As this text is currently drafted, it is unclear whether the VA-CRMST course is sufficient or if current and future sterile processing technicians must incur costs and obtain a certification through other means. Further, while some associations, like the Healthcare Sterile Processing Association (HPSA), one of the Majority's witnesses for the March 25, 2026, legislative hearing, offers the exam for only $140 after coursework is completed, while some courses offered by other organizations can exceed $5,000 or more.
For most rank-and-file VA sterile processing technicians, the career ladder is GS-3-GS-6. GS-3 is entry level, GS-4 and 5 are developmental levels, and GS-6 is the full performance level. For example, using Cleveland, Ohio, locality pay as the median for VA pay, rank-and-file employees in this occupation earn between $33,867 (GS-3, step 1) and $61,638 (GS-6, step 10). Costs related to required trainings envisioned by this bill could threaten to place current employees in financially precarious situations, especially if they are required to obtain their certification and complete coursework separate from the Department's own free training.
Additionally, while data specific to sterile processing technicians is not readily available in VA's public monthly workforce dashboards, reporting from the VA's Office of the Inspector General indicates that 1 in 4 VA facilities is currently facing a severe occupational staffing shortage within its sterile processing workforce. These numbers very well may be higher today than when they were last reported in August 2025, following the impact of the deferred resignation program, the use of the voluntary early retirement authority, and other attrition. This Committee must focus on the recruitment and retention of this critical workforce, not on adding additional barriers.
Lastly, Committee Democrats would point out that Representative Jen Kiggans' (R-VA) amendment in the nature of a substitute edits establishes this program as a two-year pilot, which would expire in September 2028, in order to save costs. Establishing this sunset date so soon after passage, which may very well occur within the two-year pilot timeframe, may result in additional confusion for current and future VA sterile processing technicians. For example, if a technician is brought on board in July of 2027 and they have two years to obtain their certification, will they still be required to acquire it if this authority expires in September 2028?
Similarly, if one employee hired within the two-year pilot timeframe is required to achieve the certification mandated in H.R. 8052 while another employee that performs the same role, but has joined VA outside of this timeframe does not, how does VA plan to rectify these differences to ensure fairness across its sterile processing technician workforce? VA has been highly concerned by potential inequities between employees performing the same work in other legislative proposals put forth by this Committee; this bill, as currently drafted, potentially opens the Department to additional conflicts and inconsistencies as it pertains to this workforce.
Committee Democrats remain committed to ensuring VA employees have the tools and support they need to provide world-class care to veterans, while rejecting policies that create unnecessary burdens or unfair barriers for the workforce veterans rely on every day.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.

content:
<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. John W. Mannion, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 4986, the Parents Opt-in Protection Act,\1\ would amend the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment\2\ (PPRA) to require schools to obtain written consent from parents for each individual survey covering certain topics, as defined by law. Under the guise of parents' rights, the bill would make it more difficult for schools and districts to conduct student surveys, including mental health surveys. Further, it would replace the balanced approach to parents' rights and gathering data using surveys under current law with an opt-in requirement for which schools would need to obtain written consent from parents for each individual survey covering certain topics. This will make it harder for schools to collect critical information on student mental health, school climate, and safety. H.R. 4986 does this while offering no new rights for parents. The National Women's Law Center Action Fund\3\ and the Human Rights Campaign\4\ expressed opposition to the legislation.
\1\Parents Opt-in Protection Act, H.R. 4986, 119th Cong. (2025).
\2\20 U.S.C. Sec.  1232h. PPRA regulations are found at 34 C.F.R. Part 98.
\3\Letter from National Women's Law Center Action Fund to the Honorable Tim Walberg, Chair, and the Honorable Robert ``Bobby'' Scott, Ranking Member, H. Comm. on Educ. & Workforce, regarding H.R. 4986, the Parents Opt-in Protection Act (July 21, 2026) (on file with Committee Democratic staff).
\4\Letter from the Human Rights Campaign to Members of Congress regarding H.R. 4986, the Parents Opt-in Protection Act (July 20, 2026) (on file with Committee Democratic staff).
BACKGROUND
Parents' Rights and Student Privacy Safeguards Are Enshrined in Statute
The General Education Provisions Act\5\ (GEPA), originally enacted as part of the Elementary and Secondary Amendments of 1967, includes ``statutory provisions that are applicable to the majority of federal education programs administered by the U.S. Department of Education (ED), as well as provisions related to the powers and responsibilities of ED.''\6\ In 1974, amendments to GEPA added the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act\7\ (FERPA), which guarantees parents and guardians access to their minor student's education records and limits the disclosure of such records to outside entities, and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment\8\ (PPRA), which provides parents the right to access instructional materials used in their student's curriculum as well as rights over the collection of their student's data.\9\
\5\20 U.S.C. Sec. Sec.  1221 et seq.
\6\Rebecca Skinner & Jody Feder, Cong. Rsch. Serv., R41119, General Education Provisions Act (GEPA): Overview and Issues (2010).
\7\Pub. L. No. 93-380, 88 Stat. 484 (codified as amended at 20 U.S.C. Sec.  1232g). FERPA regulations are found at 34 C.F.R. Part 99.
\8\Id. (codified as amended at 20 U.S.C. Sec.  1232h). PPRA regulations are found at 34 C.F.R. Part 98.
\9\Both FERPA and PPRA establish protections and provide rights over student data to parents and guardians of students under the age of 18; the protections and rights transfer directly to a student upon reaching the age of majority or attending a postsecondary institution. For the purposes of these Minority Views, we will refer to the protections and rights as belonging to parents (including guardians and emancipated and adult minors) in the context of K-12 education.
PPRA serves a number of important roles in protecting both parents' rights and student data. For example, PPRA provides parents the right to access instructional materials used in their student's curriculum.\10\ It also provides parents the right to access instructional materials that will be used as part of a survey, analysis, or evaluation\11\ as well as the right to inspect a survey itself.\12\ PPRA also recognizes eight sensitive topics that might be raised in questions that are part of a survey. The eight enumerated sensitive topics are:
\10\20 U.S.C. 1232h(c)(1)(C)(i). Additionally, Title I of ESEA requires that districts conduct outreach to parents and family members, and implement programs, activities, and procedures to involve parents and families in their child's education. 20 U.S.C. 6318(a)(1), (b),
(d); 20 U.S.C. 6311(d); 20 U.S.C. 6314(b). Under the law, each district that receives Title I funds must have a written parent and family engagement policy in place that, in part, provides parents with a description and explanation of the curriculum and assessments used in their child's school. 20 U.S.C. 6318(a)(1); 20 U.S.C. 6318(b), (d). Districts and schools must distribute this policy to parents and family members and hold at least one annual meeting with families to explain the policy and their right to be involved. 20 U.S.C. 6318.
\11\20 U.S.C. 1232(h)(a).
\12\20 U.S.C. 1232(h)(c)(1)(A) and (B). PPRA defines ``survey'' as including ``evaluation.'' 20 U.S.C. 1232(h)(c)(5)(G).
(1) political affiliations or beliefs of the student
or the student's parent; (2) mental or psychological
problems of the student or the student's family; (3)
sex behavior or attitudes; (4) illegal, anti-social,
self-incriminating, or demeaning behavior; (5) critical
appraisals of other individuals with whom respondents
have close family relationships; (6) legally recognized
privileged or analogous relationships, such as those of
lawyers, physicians, and ministers; (7) religious
practices, affiliations, or beliefs of the student or
student's parent; or (8) income (other than that
required by law to determine eligibility for
participation in a program or for receiving financial
assistance under such program).\13\
\13\20 U.S.C. 1232h(b) (when given ``as part of any applicable program''); 20 U.S.C. 1232(h)(c) (when given by ``a local educational agency that receives funds under any applicable program''); Cong. Rsch. Serv., General Education Provisions Act (GEPA): Overview and Issues (Mar. 18, 2010), https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/ 20100318_R41119_5a354cfda1d0c171d9b65ef88f95a 401330ab359.pdf.
The policies surrounding the administration of a survey involving any of these sensitive topics depend on whether the survey is given under a program administered by ED or whether it is not given as part of such a program but is nonetheless given by an LEA that receives federal funding. In either case, no student is ever required to take a survey that touches on one of these sensitive topics.
If a survey addresses one of the enumerated topics and is given as part of a program administered by ED, PPRA requires that parents provide prior written consent, which may be done as a single, annual consent for any such surveys; adult or emancipated students must also provide prior consent though it does not have to be in writing.\14\ If a survey is given not as part of a program administered by ED but by an LEA that receives federal funding from ED, PPRA requires that LEAs develop policies, in consultation with families, to protect student data privacy and govern the disclosure of student information.\15\ Further, PPRA identifies three types of activities for which parents: (1) must be given advance notice ``at least annually at the beginning of the school year,'' including ``specific or approximate dates'' when the activities are expected to occur;\16\ and (2) have the right to opt their child out of these activities.\17\ The activities include: instances in which their child's information may be used for marketing or sales; certain ``nonemergency, invasive physical examination[s] or screening[s]''; and any survey that addresses one or more of specifically enumerated topics.\18\
\14\20 U.S.C. 1232h(b).
\15\20 U.S.C. 1232h(c)(1).
\16\20 U.S.C. 1232h(c)(2)(B).
\17\20 U.S.C. 1232h(c)(2)(A)(ii).
\18\20 U.S.C. 1232h(c)(2)(C).
Thus, current law does not require students to participate in surveys that touch on these enumerated topics. But current law does require either written consent of a parent before a student may participate or parental notification with the option to opt out of such surveys. The GOP's Parental Rights Campaign
The discussion about the roles and rights of parents in their children's education has existed since the inception of formal education, and modern efforts in the U.S. are evidenced by the creation of the National Parent Teacher Association in 1897.\19\ Democrats agree that parental engagement is critical to student success. In 2024 the Biden-led U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated, ``Parental engagement in schools is closely linked to better student behavior, higher academic achievement, and enhanced social skills.''\20\ Moreover, the U.S. Supreme Court has declared ``the interest of parents in the care, custody, and control of their children is perhaps the oldest of the fundamental liberty interests recognized by this Court.''\21\
\19\National PTA, History, https://www.pta.org/home/About-National- Parent-Teacher-Association/ Mission-Values/National-PTA- History (last visited July 22, 2026).
\20\U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention, Parent Engagement in Schools (Nov. 22, 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-youth-parent-resources/parent-engagement/index.html#::text= Parent%20engagement%20is%20closely%20linked,as%20tobacco%20use%20or%20vi olence.
\21\See, e.g., Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) (striking down a Washington state law that granted a third party child visitation rights over parental objections because it interfered with parents' fundamental right to direct their child's upbringing).
However, the recent parents' rights campaign--involving book bans, demanding control of curricula from a narrow and whitewashed perspective, and targeting transgender students, among other efforts--``has become a staple of some conservative attacks on public education.''\22\ Many have noted the ways this debate turns schools into political battlegrounds, separates communities, and diverts teachers' and children's attention away from teaching and learning.\23\ These efforts claim to provide parents with additional control over their students' education despite the fact that many of the rights being proposed already exist in state and federal law.\24\
\22\Suzanne Nossel, Parents Should Have a Voice in Their Kids' Education But We've Gone Too Far, Time (Sept. 20, 2022), https:// time.com/6215119/parents-rights- education-gone-too-far/.
\23\Id.
\24\Aallyah Wright, Educators warn bills to give parents more power could push teachers out, Minnesota Reformer (Feb. 14, 2022), https:// minnesotareformer.com/2022/02/14/ educators-warn-bills- to-give-parents-more-power- could-push-teachers-out/.

<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. John W. Mannion, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: H.R. 4986, introduced by Rep. Mary Miller (R-IL), would amend PPRA to purportedly ``stand up for parental rights and create a barrier between our nation's schoolchildren and inappropriate influences from radical transgender ideology and Big Tech.''\25\ H.R. 4986 would require written consent before participation in each survey that touches on what Rep. Miller refers to as ``sexual orientation, gender identity, and woke politics,''\26\ and in so doing it changes participation in these surveys. For surveys given as part of a program administered by ED, it would eliminate the annual written consent and require repeated consent for each survey; for surveys not part of such a program but in an LEA that receives federal funds, it would change the survey from opt-out to opt-in.\27\ While the Majority claims this is to protect parents' rights because schools ``force sexual materials or political ideology upon children while keeping parents in the dark,''\28\ it is clear that is not how school surveys are conducted. Instead, H.R. 4986 is yet another attempt to scapegoat transgender students as an excuse to undermine public education. H.R. 4986 would harm all students by reducing school, district, and state awareness of school climate, mental health, and other issues and limit the ability of schools, districts, and states to support students in addressing their needs.
\25\Press Release, Rep. Miller Sponsors Legislation to Protect our Schoolchildren from Dangerous Influences from Radical Transgender Ideology and Big Tech, Office of Congresswoman Mary Miller (Feb. 15, 2023), https://marymiller.house.gov/media/press-releases/rep-miller-sponsors-legislation-protect-our-schoolchildren-dangerous.
\26\Id.
\27\See infra text accompanying notes 37 & 38.
\28\Press Release, supra note 25.
H.R. 4986 WILL HINDER STATES', DISTRICTS', AND SCHOOLS' ABILITIES TO
ASSESS AND ADDRESS SCHOOL CLIMATE AND YOUTH MENTAL HEALTH
Research shows that students who feel safe and supported at school have better educational outcomes. As the Learning Policy Institute highlighted, ``[p]ositive school climates are associated with increased academic achievement and attendance, higher graduation rates, improved behavior, and lower teacher attrition rates.''\29\ Over the years, the U.S. Department of Education has supported improving school climate.\30\ The National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) at the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) ``prioritized research about school climate and the use of such research to develop more effective policy and school practices,'' including publishing a series of school climate surveys for use by states, districts, and schools.\31\
\29\Learning Pol'y Inst., Using Data to Improve School Climate: Fact Sheet (Nov. 2024), https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/media/4488/ download?inline&file=Data_School_Climate_FACTSHEET.pdf.
\30\See, e.g., the School Climate Transformation Grant program, which provided grants to LEAs (https://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/ grants-birth-grade-12/safe-and-supportive-schools/school-climate-transformation-grant-local-educational-agency-lea-grants-program) and State Educational Agencies (SEAs) (https://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/grants-birth-grade-12/safe-and-supportive-schools/school-climate-transformation-grant-state-educational-agency-grants-program), the Safe and Supportive Schools (S3) grant program (https:// www.cde.ca.gov/ls/ss/se/safesupportive.asp), and the former National Center on Safe and Supportive Learning Environments (https:// www.air.org/project/school-climate-survey-compendium and https:// www.schoolsafety.gov/resource/national-center-safe-and-supportive-learning-environments), as well as other efforts of the Office of Safe and Supportive Schools (OSSS)_and its predecessor, the Office of Safe and Healthy Students (OSHS)_within the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education (OESE) (https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-offices/oese/ safe-and-supportive-schools).
\31\Nat'l Ctr. for Educ. Statistics, Inst. of Educ. Sciences, ED School Climate Surveys (EDSCLS), https://nces.ed.gov/use-work/ elementarysecondary/ed-school-climate-surveys-edscls (last visited July 22, 2026).
For surveys conducted as part of a program administered by ED, PPRA already requires that the annual parental notice and consent for surveys discussed above (that touch on one of the eight enumerated topics) be in writing, but it does not require the annual notice and consent by emancipated or adult students be in writing.\32\ H.R. 4986 would amend PPRA to require that both be in writing. In and of itself, this is not an objectionable amendment to the law. However, H.R. 4986 goes further by requiring that written consent be given for each survey rather than a general annual consent currently permitted under the law. H.R. 4986 would also require written consent for each such survey given by an LEA that receives federal funding (even if the survey is not given under a program administered by ED), changing the law from a parental opt-out provision to a parental opt-in provision.
In her own words, Rep. Miller stated that the bill was introduced to specifically target surveys related to sexual orientation and gender ideology.\33\ However, it is worth noting that nothing in H.R. 4986 limits its scope to surveys involving sexual orientation or gender identity. The effect of the bill would be much broader and could significantly reduce survey responses on state/district/school climate surveys and other surveys, including the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) voluntary, biennial Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS). The YRBS is part of the CDC's Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS) and has been conducted since 1991 using a sampling of 9th through 12th graders.\34\ It ``measures health-related behaviors and experiences that can lead to death and disability among youth and adults,'' the results of which can be used to ``help monitor health trends, identify emerging issues, and plan and evaluate programs that can help improve adolescent health.''\35\ The CDC uses the YRBS to understand health-related behaviors and also issues such as weight, obesity, and asthma.\36\ According to the CDC, requiring opting-in for the YRBS could have significant detrimental consequences:

\33\Supra note 25.
\34\Nancy D. Brener et al., Overview and Methods for the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System--United States, 2023 3, U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) (Oct. 10, 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/ volumes/73/su/pdfs/ su7304-H.pdf.
\35\U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention, Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS): About YRBSS (June 14, 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/about/index.html.
\36\Laura Kann, et al., Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance--United States, 2017 3, U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control and Prevention Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) (June 15, 2018), https:// www.cdc.gov/mmwr/ volumes/67/ss/pdfs/ss6708a1-H.pdf.

students who participate in the survey because of the
difficulty of both getting permission forms home to
parents and having forms returned to school. As a rule,
