\37\U.S. Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention, Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS): A Guide to Conducting Your Own Youth Risk Behavior Survey 3 (Sept. 2024), https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs/ media/pdf/ 2023/2023_yrbs_conducting_your_own.pdf.
In fact, opt-in requirements generally hinder participation in surveys in general, and they also affect who participates in the survey.\38\ For example, in a school setting, an opt-in requirement for each survey may make it less likely that working parents or parents who speak a different language submit the written consent.
\38\Yvonne de Man et al., Opt-In and Opt-Out Consent Procedures for the Reuse of Routinely Recorded Health Data in Scientific Research and Their Consequences for Consent Rate and Consent Bias: Systematic Review, 25 J. Med. Internet Res. 1, 18 (2023), https:// pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ articles/PMC10015347/pdf/ jmir_v25i1e42131.pdf (``[C]onsent rates are lower in studies using opt-in procedures. . . In addition, in studies using an opt-in procedure, consenters are more likely not to be representative of the study population compared with studies using an opt-out procedure.'').
Committee Democrats agree it is imperative that parents be aware of what is happening in their child's school. Current law strikes a reasonable balance between requiring both parental notification and annual written consent while permitting parents to opt their child out of these surveys on the one hand and the importance of conducting such surveys for the success of students on the other. Upsetting this balance and requiring parents to opt-in for each survey likely means that far fewer students may be participating in surveys for reasons other than the survey subject matter. This will hinder the collection of research used to understand the health, mental health, and safety of students and the development of programs and supports to benefit our nation's youth, with no material increase in parents' rights.
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 4986
Committee Democrats did not offer any amendments to H.R. 4986.
CONCLUSION
As described above, H.R. 4986 would make it more difficult for schools and districts to conduct surveys, including mental health surveys, under the guise of parents' rights and would replace the balanced approach to parents rights and gathering data using surveys under current law, making it harder for schools to collect critical information on student mental health, school climate, and safety while offering no new rights for parents. All Committee Democrats present at the markup opposed H.R. 4986 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on July 21, 2026. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Mark DeSaulnier,
John Mannion,
Adelita Grijalva,
Members of Congress.

bill_title: BEACON Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Mark Takano>: This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to establish two grant programs, which the bill's proponents claim will expand research and improve treatment for mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Committee Democrats and VA have numerous concerns about the bill and, to address these concerns, offered eight amendments at the subcommittee and full committee markups. However, all of these amendments were rejected by the majority.
We strongly oppose this legislation because, if sufficient funds are not appropriated, it would siphon funds away from existing VA mental health treatment and research programs, by requiring VA to use existing funds appropriated for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) research and general mental health services to fund these grant programs. Further, the bill creates an inappropriate structure to administer one of the grant programs, by requiring VA to contract with a third-party entity to perform the inherently governmental responsibilities of allocating and overseeing the expenditure of grant funds. Additionally, the bill does not contain sufficient or robust guardrails to provide oversight of the grantees. Many of these concerns were echoed by VA's testimony at a January 13, 2026, Health Subcommittee legislative hearing where this bill was considered.
In particular, we share VA's concerns that the methodologies and approaches to clinical trials funded by the grant programs established ``would not result in or contribute to actual clinical care; at most, they seem to be a preliminary step toward research that may eventually produce new treatment approaches. This uncertain return on investment of funds VA could otherwise use to provide evidence-based treatments for mTBI is inadvisable. Funds made available for clinical care should be used to deliver clinical care.''
The Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute (A.N.S.) to the bill considered and adopted at the Health Subcommittee markup held on April 16, 2026, made some changes requested by Committee Democrats, but it did not fully address all of our concerns with the bill. Specifically, the A.N.S. changed the grantee eligibility criteria for both grant programs, to require that they have demonstrated some ability to carry out clinical trials, but the amendment did not go far enough to prevent unqualified entities from receiving grants.
The A.N.S. adopted at the Subcommittee markup also included some language requiring grantees to better coordinate care and refer veterans back to VA services, but it didn't address our underlying concern that this legislation will divert care and funding from VA research and mental health services. While it added some new reporting requirements to ensure accountability for grantees, it did not go far enough to ensure that outcomes are properly evaluated or that adverse outcomes are required to be reported in a timely manner.
Finally, the A.N.S. struck language requiring the grant program to ``align'' their activities with the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Grant program. The original language raised serious concerns that the goal of the program was to increase the likelihood of existing Fox Grant grantees receiving these new grants. Committee Democrats appreciate this change, considering it did not make sense for a grant program that is primarily focused on research and clinical treatment to ``align'' with a grant program that is primarily focused on upstream factors of suicide risk, such as financial wellbeing, and not clinical treatment or research.
However, the most concerning provisions-the provisions that allow funds to be diverted from existing appropriated sources at VA in the absence of sufficient funding and the requirement for VA to contract with a third-party entity to administer the grant program in Section 3-were not addressed by the A.N.S. at the Subcommittee markup.
During consideration of the bill at the Health Subcommittee markup, Democratic members offered four amendments, all of which were rejected by Republican members.
Specifically, Representative Morrison offered an amendment that would have strengthened oversight requirements by requiring grantees to collect adverse event data during clinical trials, added requirements to use accepted clinical standards to evaluate the effectiveness of clinical trial outcomes, and expanded the reporting requirements to ensure Congress can perform robust oversight of the programs. The Majority opposed this amendment on grounds that made it clear they are not interested in oversight and would prefer the funding from these grant programs be provided with as few guardrails as possible.
Representative Conaway offered an amendment that would have lowered the maximum grant amount per grantee per fiscal year from $5 million to $2.5 million. The grant program only authorizes $10 million per fiscal year, so if VA awards the maximum amount, only two awards would be given each fiscal year. Given that clinical trial results are not guaranteed to be successful or usable for VA, Committee Democrats believe $5 million is too much funding to provide to any one grantee to be responsible stewards of taxpayer funding. Republicans rejected this amendment.
Representative Brownley offered an amendment that would have stricken provisions within Sec. 2 and Sec. 3 of the A.N.S. that would have directed VA to fund the two grant programs from appropriations for its National Center for PTSD and VA mental health services, if Congress failed to appropriate specific funds for the two grant programs. Because the A.N.S. included the authorization of appropriations, as well as a provision to pay for the legislation using home loan fees, it is very difficult to understand this funding structure--which Committee staff have yet to see in any other bill before now--as anything other than a drain on the resources that VA can use to advance the study and treatment of PTSD and provide direct mental health care to veterans who need it. The Majority rejected this amendment but did not explain how they would ensure that this bill does not divert funding from existing VA appropriations.
Representative Brownley offered another amendment that would have prohibited grantees from receiving grants under both programs during the same fiscal year. The A.N.S. made it possible for certain grantees to be eligible for both grant programs, which could lead to a single grantee receiving up to $6.5 million in a single fiscal year ($5 million under the first grant program and $1.5 million under the second). Republicans also rejected this amendment.
During the bill's consideration at a Full Committee markup on May 14, 2026, Committee Democrats offered further amendments to address their concerns.
Representative Morrison again offered the amendment to strengthen oversight requirements that she offered at the subcommittee markup, which was again rejected.
Representative Brownley again offered the amendment to strike the provisions that would require VA to fund the two grant programs with existing PTSD and general mental health services appropriations if specific funding is not appropriated. Republicans again rejected this amendment and again refused to explain why they refused to include any guardrails in the bill that would prevent diverting VA resources to pay for the grant programs.
Ranking Member Takano offered an amendment that would have required grantees to share with VA all clinical data from the clinical trials funded through the grants under section 2, to ensure coordination of efforts, as well as transparency into the reported outcomes of grantees' research. Any research to improve treatments for mTBI must include coordination with VA, including sharing clinical data that could allow VA's world-class research ecosystem to develop the next great breakthrough. If we are using public funds to conduct research outside VA, we must ensure Congress and VA can evaluate the return on our investment, validate findings, and build on the clinical data created with taxpayer funds. Republicans rejected this amendment as well and defended the interests of the private entities who could receive grant funding from having to provide full transparency to VA or Congress.
Finally, Representative Dexter offered an amendment to strike section 3, to address concerns about the lower standard of research for the second grant program and to remove a requirement that VA enter into an agreement with a third-party entity to administer the grant program. Despite the fact that VA also opposed this grant funding administration structure, Republicans also rejected this amendment.
While we certainly understand and agree with the need for expanding research and improving treatments for mTBI, we are concerned that this legislation will lead to greater fragmentation of research and treatment for veterans. For the reasons cited above, Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 6993.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Recognizing Community Organizations for Veteran Engagement and Recovery Act
content:
<Rep. Mark Takano>: This legislation would pilot a three-year, $20 million-a-year grant program for community providers to receive grants of up to $1.5 million per year to deliver mental healthcare services to veterans and establish new outpatient facilities. Committee Democrats and the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) have expressed significant concerns about this bill, which would drive more resources to community providers, with fewer strings attached and even less accountability than currently exists under VA's existing Veterans Community Care Program (VCCP).
My colleagues and I fundamentally disagree with the very premise of establishing a carveout grant program for community providers of mental health, and as such could not offer any amendments that would improve this legislation. These providers already can and do furnish care to veterans through VA's existing community care authorities. A grant structure is not, in our view--or in VA's view--the right way to expand veterans' access to mental health services. At the legislative hearing on H.R. 2283, on January 13, 2026, VA cited significant concerns about this.
In addition, concerns were raised by Democratic members, by VA's witnesses, and by the minority's witness about the risk that this grant program would lead providers to ``double dip'' or even ``triple dip.'' In addition to receiving a grant, grantees could also be billing the VCCP, Medicare, and other health plans for very same care for the very same veteran. While the majority's Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute (A.N.S.) offered at the April 16, 2026, Health Subcommittee markup added a provision prohibiting such behavior, it is completely unenforceable. Because this is a grant program, without any claims submitted to VA as veterans are receiving care, there is no way for VA or this Committee to confirm providers are not double- or triple-dipping.
Furthermore, the lack of claims also gives us less oversight into the quality and safety of care delivered by grantees--we will have no claims, no returned medical records, and no insight at all into whether veterans are actually receiving evidence-based treatments. We appreciate that the majority added provisions to the A.N.S. at the full Committee markup to require grantees to be accredited and to submit ``plans'' for at least one of their providers have completed ``continuing education in the diagnosis and treatment of mental health conditions specific to veterans.'' However, a plan, for one trained provider in an entire clinic, for a $1.5 million-dollar-a-year grant, is hardly a high enough bar.
Finally, under this legislation, grantees would be able to use funds not just for direct delivery of mental healthcare. They also would be able to use funds to establish new facilities, conduct outreach, pay for clinician training, and ``support activities of the program that are not billable, reimbursable, or otherwise authorized by law.'' We would effectively be handing out $1.5 million dollars per year to community providers to use far more freely than the dollars we are sending to VA's own medical facilities.
For the reasons cited above, Committee Democrats oppose H.R. 2283, which would create a carveout grant program to funnel VA dollars to community providers of mental health, rather than investing them in VA's direct care system.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: VA Fiscal Management Modernization Act
content:
<Rep. Mark Takano>: Committee Democrats appreciate that this bill is intended to address concerns regarding financial and budgetary management at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA); however, there are serious issues and risks with centralizing all budget and finance employees under the Chief Financial Officer (CFO).
Committee Democrats also warn this Committee against giving tacit approval to VA to consolidate financial, acquisition, and programmatic activities for VA within a single office. Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, the President's appointee and current CFO, Richard Topping, has begun consolidating financial, acquisition, and programmatic functions within his office without any accountability to Congress. This power consolidation creates a serious conflict of interest pertaining to the oversight and award of large sums of VA funding to outside entities. The conflict of interest is apparent as Mr. Topping has taken over one of VA's most significant procurement activities. The current CFO, and not VA healthcare or acquisition officials, is leading the Community Care Network Next Generation Contract award process--a nearly $1 trillion procurement rife with issues.
In May 2026, Committee staff were briefed by Mark Englebaum, the Assistant Secretary for the Office of Human Resources and Administration, that VA must start shifting to a more aggressive planning cycle for the Department's budget for staffing, infrastructure, and other resources. That type of planning requires stability, which is often provided by career VA staff, not political appointees. These career staff are often the ones who have spent years in the Department, and know the intricacies of VA's numerous programs, its governance structures, and its employees. This is the kind of knowledge base we should be encouraging in an office such as this. While political appointees may have a role in transmitting the President's wishes as it relates to the budget, the over-politicization of planning and financial management is concerning.
At the full Committee markup on May 14, 2026, Ranking Member Takano (D-CA) offered an amendment that would have supported Mr. Englebaum's goals by restricting the number of political appointees within the Legislative and Congressional Budget Information (LCBI) office that is established in H.R. 7683. Over the last nearly year and a half, there has been a rise in the number of political appointees serving in roles traditionally held by career staff, followed by a subsequent decrease in the accessibility of information to veterans, Congress, and the public. Limiting the number of political appointees serves as a protection of processes that should be nonpartisan, including VA fiscal management. Unfortunately, this amendment failed by a recorded vote, with 10 ayes and 12 noes.
Additionally, the text of this bill creates conflicts with another bill that the majority is moving forward, Representative Barrett's H.R. 6833, the Acquisition Review and Cost Assessment Act, or ARCA, which is a bipartisan Committee priority. If both bills were to become law, they will create conflicts that would make implementation difficult, if not impossible due to how each bill alters authorities for acquisition officials within the agency. During the Oversight and Investigation Subcommittee's consideration of H.R. 7683 on March 25, 2026, concerns were raised about reconciling this bill with H.R. 6833 before consideration of either bill proceeds. Ranking Member Delia Ramirez (D-IL) encouraged a bipartisan effort to work with the Senate sponsor of H.R. 6833, Senator Jerry Moran (R-KS), to deconflict the text. To date, those negotiations have not occurred.
Another amendment, which was offered by Representative Ramirez at the full Committee markup, would have required the Department to report to Congress facility-level attrition data that Committee Democrats have requested since early 2025. The report would have included, for each employee that separated with the Department between January 1, 2025, and the enactment of this bill:
<ctr-circle> Occupation;
<ctr-circle> Job title;
<ctr-circle> Grade level;
<ctr-circle> Name and location of facility;
<ctr-circle> Reason for separation;
<ctr-circle> Whether the employee was retirement-
eligible;
<ctr-circle> Whether the employee participated in the
Deferred Resignation Program (DRP);
<ctr-circle> Whether the employee was terminated; and
<ctr-circle> Whether the position that was vacated by
the employee was eliminated by any such agency action.
This information would provide Members of the Committee critical information about the current state of the challenges facilities are facing in terms of workforce, especially as veterans begin feeling the impacts of the deferred resignation program and the voluntary early retirement authority.
Chairman Bost's rebuttal that the CFO functions--the position under which this bill intends to consolidate much of VA's financial power--are not related to the state of VA's staffing reflects a concerning trend in the Committee's oversight of this administration. Staffing makes up a significant portion of VA's $448 billion budget. To assert that this Committee does not need to know detailed information regarding staffing at the second largest federal agency is dangerous and exhibits a blatant lack of understanding regarding the budgetary functions this bill seeks to codify. Committee Democrats further argued that as VA embarks on the trillion-dollar acquisition for the Community Care Next Generation contract under CFO Topping's leadership, it is critical that we understand how VA staffing levels may impact referrals to outside care and the ongoing Republican-led privatization of VA. This amendment failed by a recorded vote, with 10 ayes and 12 noes.
Finally, on May 29, 2026, the Office of Management and Budget issued a Notice of Proposed Rule Making (NPRM) for the Proposed Federal Financial Assistance Rule, which would list the VA CFO as the official-in-charge of implementing that rule, if it becomes final. This rule would give unprecedented power to political appointees, and ultimately to the VA CFO, a veto over any science that conflicts with the current administration's ideology. The expansion of CFO power authorized in H.R. 7683 and this proposed rulemaking are concerning and unprecedented, and Committee Democrats hold that any increase in authority must be coupled with heightened oversight and accountability measures, which this legislation lacks.
Committee Democrats will continue to advocate for improving VA's fiscal operations but will reject proposals that politicize the Department's financial decision-making. Rather than improving accountability, this legislation would concentrate more power in the hands of political appointees, inviting greater political interference in VA's fiscal stewardship at the expense of veterans.
Mark Takano,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Reshoring American Manufacturing Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: In May 2025, the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) launched the Make Onshoring Great Again Portal, a free tool designed to help small businesses identify U.S. manufacturers and producers. The database provides links to four private lists or directories, which are: IndustryNet, Thomasnet, Connex, and IQS directory.
• IndustryNet is an industrial marketplace
search engine operating since 1912 that lists more than
350,000 suppliers of machinery parts, supplies, and
services.\1\
\1\SBA Onshoring Portal, https://www.sba.gov/about-sba/priorities/ american-manufacturers/make-onshoring-great-again-portal/.
• Thomasnet is a longstanding industrial
platform operating for over 120 years that helps small
and medium businesses connect with more than 500,000
American manufacturers and suppliers by location and
company size.\2\ Some businesses have raised concerns
on Reddit that it operates as a pay-to-play model,
where they have to bid for viability, however, the
option on the SBA website is a free basic model.
\2\Id.
• CONNEX Marketplace connects U.S.
manufacturers and suppliers into a searchable supply
chain solution.\3\ NIST utilizes CONNEX Marketplace to
help regional Manufacturing Extension Partnership (MEP)
centers locate specific suppliers and fulfill
government supply chain requests. The Department of
Defense's Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation
utilizes customized versions of the platform to map
defense manufacturing capabilities and ensure national
security in military supply chains.
\3\Id.
• The IQS Directory is an online business-to-
business industrial directory, which was founded in
2000. It connects original equipment manufacturer (OEM)
buyers and engineers with industrial suppliers,
fabricators, and distributors across the U.S. and
Canada.\4\
\4\SBA Onshoring Portal Directory, https://www.iqsdirectory.com/ madeinamerica/.
The Committee noted several challenges with H.R. 9718 as introduced. The SBA currently has an onshoring platform on its website, however, the Committee has limited data regarding its utilization, effectiveness, and whether it is necessary for Congress to codify. While the Portal is relatively new, the underlying data is not. The SBA does not own or manage the databases, raising concerns that the information may become outdated or stale. Additionally, although access to the Portal is free, some of the third-party platforms it relies on offer higher-tier paid models. The Committee remains concerned about the SBA's reliance on the Office of Advocacy (Advocacy) for updates and improvements to the portal and feels that the legislation is blurring the lines of independence between the SBA and Advocacy. With that said, Advocacy, under the leadership of former Acting Administrator of the SBA, Mr. Everett Woodell (January-February 2025), indicated that it has no issues with the SBA seeking input from the Chief Counsel. Given these concerns the Committee has negotiated a compromise, which will be offered as an amendment in the nature of a substitute (ANS).
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Several nations are considered foreign adversaries by hawkish policymakers. These countries often include Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, and Venezuela. Most foreign adversaries are pariah states, either for their military aggression against neighbors or totalitarian dictatorships.
But one--the People's Republic of China--seeks to expand its global influence, entangling it into a growing economic, diplomatic, and military rivalry with the U.S. that foreign policy scholars label ``Thucydides's Trap.'' In this phenomenon, the rise of one power threatens a more established power, leading to competition, and potentially conflict, between them. Additionally, the Communist Party's tight control of the P.R.C. government and its nominal ideology drive fundamental differences between the political economies of the P.R.C. and the U.S. While the Party therefore has coercive influence over the decisions and activities of citizens and businesses, private property and markets exist in the P.R.C., complicating descriptions of it and the Party as strictly socialist entities.
Party-controlled firms, and companies affiliated with other foreign adversaries, sometimes employ business and competitive practices that are underhanded, illegal, and immoral. These tactics include intellectual property (IP) theft, counterfeit goods, predatory investment, and slavery.
When companies--especially in the P.R.C.--do not employ these practices, however, U.S. businesses of all sizes benefit tremendously from trade and collaboration. The P.R.C. has the world's second-largest economy after the U.S., with a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of almost $19.4 trillion, and has been a top U.S. trading partner since its accession to the World Trade Organization in 2001.\1\ Small businesses reap lower costs, greater innovation, and access to vast sales markets, from their trade and collaboration with P.R.C. partners--in areas outside of critical and military technology. Furthermore, the U.S. has attracted scores of P.R.C. scientists and engineers, leveraging their skills and expertise to serve U.S. national interests, instead of our competitor's. This net outflow of talent has created and reinforced a ``brain drain'' from top P.R.C. labs and companies.
\1\Karen M. Sutter, Cong. Rsch. Serv., IF11284, U.S.-China Trade Relations (Sep. 9, 2025).
On March 25, 2026, the full Committee held a hearing titled ``Defending Main Street: Combating CCP Threats to America's Small Businesses,'' at which Dr. Rush Doshi, the C.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, testified to the P.R.C.'s strategic ambitions and capacity to compete with the U.S., emphasizing that the key to successfully outcompeting the P.R.C. lies in greater volumes and coordination of domestic and allied scientific research, manufacturing, and capital access--not President Trump's tariffs, One Big Beautiful Bill Act, or racism. As part of its oversight duties, the Committee will closely monitor the implementation of this legislation, if enacted into law, to ensure that it is laser-focused on foreign conduct harming small businesses, and not on ethnicity or national origin.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Disaster Loan Outreach Consistency Act
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Federal disaster relief programs are subject to periodic regulatory changes. In June 2023, SBA published a direct final rule to expand options for disaster loan recipients and reflect cost increases from inflation by increasing home lending limits and extending the deferment period for repayment. Similarly, in January 2024, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) published an interim final rule amending its regulations governing Individual Assistance for major disasters, removing the requirement to apply for SBA disaster loans as a condition of eligibility for some types of assistance from FEMA.
On May 18, 2026, the Government Accountability Office issued a report that found that SBA's field operations centers did not consistently update SBA's disaster specific press releases or fact sheets to capture key components of the SBA's 2023 and FEMA's 2024 rules. According to SBA guidance, the field operations centers are responsible for outreach materials for declared disaster that affect localized areas which are the most common types of disasters. SBA relies on press releases and fact sheets to inform disaster survivors and the media about the program. While SBA has established a process for standardized outreach materials, GAO identified gaps in those controls.
When comparing outreach materials between east and west field operations centers, GAO found that While the Eastern Centers included increased limits and eligible uses for mitigation for all loans in most press releases, the Western Center did not. Similarly, the Eastern Center included information referencing FEMA's new rule in press releases, while the Western Center did not. Ensuring all potential borrowers have all relevant information when struck by a disaster is important to ensure all those that can be helped are helped. This bill requires the SBA to establish standard procedures to ensure disaster outreach materials are consistent across field operations centers, and ensure information is accurate and current.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Ensuring SBA Implementation of GAO Recommendations Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: On December 21, 2023, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) issued a report\1\ finding that the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) procedures for reporting on Veteran-owned businesses need improvement.
\1\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-24-106071, Small Business Administration: Procedures for Reporting on Veteran Owned Businesses Need Improvement (Dec. 21, 2023).
The SBA provides entrepreneurial training and education through Veterans Business Outreach Centers (VBOCs), mainly through the Boots to Business and Boots to Business Reboot programs. The SBA office responsible for overseeing the VBOC program is the Office of Veteran Business Development (OVBD). The Veterans Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development Act of 1999 requires the SBA to submit an annual report to the House and Senate Small Business and Veterans Affairs Committees on the needs of veteran-owned and service-disabled-veteran-owned businesses. This annual report must include information on: (1) the availability of SBA programs for such businesses and the degree of utilization by such businesses during the preceding 12-month period, including statistical information on such utilization compared to the small business community as a whole; (2) the percentage and dollar value of federal contracts awarded to such businesses during the preceding 12-month period; and (3) proposals to improve the access of such businesses to available assistance.\2\
\2\Veterans Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development Act of 1999 Sec.  603, 15 U.S.C. Sec.  657b note.
GAO found that the SBA's existing reporting and materials did not include the requisite information to satisfy the requirement.\3\ In response, the GAO issued a priority recommendation that the SBA establish policies and procedures to comply with the reporting requirement, to ensure it provides the Committee and others with information on the needs of veteran-owned small businesses. The SBA agreed with the recommendation.\4\
\3\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., supra note 1.
\4\Id.
By developing procedures for ensuring compliance with reporting requirements, the SBA will have better information with which to serve veteran-owned small businesses. Unfortunately, this priority recommendation has not yet been closed out. As of September 8, 2026, SBA has 59 open GAO recommendations, 14 of which are priority recommendations.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Small Business Payment for Performance Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Over the life of a contract, federal contracting officers frequently change the terms in ways that affect the costs to the contractor, through modifications known as ``change orders.'' Change orders can be done through: (1) a bilateral agreement where the government and contractors have negotiated and agreed upon the changes before work proceeds; or (2) a unilateral modification directed by the contracting officer without the agreement of the contractor before work proceeds. After a unilateral change is issued, the contractor may then submit a ``Request for Equitable Adjustment'' (REA) for any additional costs incurred.
These processes can be administratively burdensome and time-consuming for companies of all sizes, but can have a disproportionate impact on small businesses, especially with regard to cash flow.
The time frames and processes for change orders and REAs can vary significantly. When reviewing Army Corps of Engineering contracts between 2013 and 2018, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that while the majority of changes were finalized within 60 days; approximately 45 percent of the completed contract changes took more than 60 days to finalize, and a little more than 3 percent took more than 1 year.\1\
\1\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-19-500, Federal Construction: Army Corps of Engineers and GSA Need to Improve Data on Contract Changes (Jul. 2, 2019).
As a result of the GAO's conclusion that routine, central data collection on the construction contract change process was not occurring, but would be beneficial for agencies to understand the scope of any problems encountered, Congress enacted Section 855 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019 (FY 2019 NDAA).\2\ This provision required agencies to provide information on their policies regarding requests for equitable adjustments and the timeliness of payments.\3\
\2\John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019, Pub. L. No. 115-232, Sec.  855 (2018).
\3\15 U.S.C. Sec.  644(w).
Small businesses not only struggle with the costs of government-directed changes, the uncertainty around the process and timelines of payments remains an issue. The provisions of the bill are designed to help mitigate the impact of those costs by requiring half of the estimated cost to be paid earlier in the process. The Committee supports this goal but believes there are outstanding issues that should be addressed to ensure implementation matches intent. While the Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute made improvements, concerns remain regarding the bill's alignment with existing policies and requirements that vary across federal agencies, CBO's estimated costs, and the lack of definition and clarity for the terms and timelines. If left unaddressed, these issues may cause implementation challenges and delays.
Additionally, if SBA moves forward with an ill-advised proposed rule published in Federal Register on August 20, 2026, ``Small Business Size Standards'' (RIN: 3245-AI67)\4\ to redefine what is a small business government contractor, current authorities like those proposed in this bill will need reevaluation. While all contractors should be paid in a timely manner, these laws have been designed to address the disproportionate impact of limited cash flow on small firms. If they and other small business policies are now applicable to firms with very large contracts, thousands of employees and hundreds of millions in annual revenue, the consequences--as well as the costs--will change.
\4\Small Business Size Standards, 91 Fed. Reg. 53741 (proposed Aug. 20, 2026) (to be codified at 13 C.F.R. pt. 121).
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.

bill_title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act of 2026
content:
<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Digital tools are critical for workplaces of all kinds, including small businesses, and they require the use of cybersecurity and cyber hygiene infrastructure, systems and practices. According to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, 99 percent of small businesses use at least one technology platform, with 58 percent using at least four platforms. However, only 25 percent of small businesses use cybersecurity and malware detection tools. Unlike larger corporations, small business entrepreneurs and their staff lack the time, skills, and resources to adopt effective cybersecurity measures.
Multiple federal entities have developed and provided cybersecurity resources for small businesses. However, the Committee has heard feedback that awareness of these resources varies. While some federal agencies have created cybersecurity resources, it can be difficult for them to reach small businesses when those agencies lack the network and experience to perform effective small business outreach and counseling, as the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) does. The SBA, in consultation with other relevant federal entities, could be better utilized to provide assistance to small businesses on cybersecurity and technology use and adaptation, as well as disseminating information and resources.
One area of interest for small business government contractors is the cybersecurity standards and requirements that must be met to be eligible to receive a federal contract. Since 2019, the Department of Defense (DoD) has attempted to issue new cybersecurity regulations, known as the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) for defense contractors. CMMC sets a cybersecurity standard designed to ensure contractors have adequate security practices and processes in place to safeguard controlled information.
After years of mixed signals and delays, DoD formally established CMMC in a 2024 DoD rule.\1\ CMMC requires DoD prime- and sub-contractors to achieve and maintain a level of cyber hygiene and obtain a CMMC certification prior to contract award. The cost to the industrial base and the costs for each defense contractor are significant, reoccurring and vary based on level of certification needed.
\1\89 Fed. Reg. 83092 (2024).
To assist small businesses with understanding and complying with the requirements of CMMC and similar DoD regulations, Congress has authorized programs within DoD's Office of Small Business Programs and APEX Accelerators that provide resources such as assessment tools, counseling assistance and educational opportunities for small federal contractors.\2\
\2\See, e.g., Cyber Thursdays, Wis. Procurement Inst., https:// www.wispro.org/wpi-events/ featured-webinars/cyber-fridays (last visited Sep. 9, 2026); Cyber Self Assessments, Project Spectrum, U.S. Dep't of Def., https:// www.projectspectrum.io (last visited Sep. 10, 2026).
While there is universal acceptance that cybersecurity is priority, it is also widely acknowledged that CMMC is a costly, burdensome regulation that will act as a barrier to entry for small firms seeking to enter the defense industrial base and will likely accelerate the ongoing exodus of small businesses from the federal market. Accurate and timely information will assist small firms seeking to remain competitive in the federal market.
The Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute adds language that better defines an appropriate role for the SBA in cybersecurity efforts and maximize the SBA's resources by ensuring that they supplement, rather than duplicate, existing programs that are more suited for the task.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
